item.title: This Indigenous-led tour in BC is part of a Canada-wide initiative to put First Nations tourism in the spotlight
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.59
Seven in 10 Canadians say they’d enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures on their travels, but many don’t know how or where to find a tour. Indigenous-owned Talaysay Tours and B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel are hoping to fix that. “We are on the unceded territories of the Squamish and Lil’wat people,” says Talaysay Campo, whose name translates to ‘ocean breeze’, ‘wind blowing on the water’ or ‘whispering winds’. “There’s one thing I want to share, and that’s that the land is absolutely everything.” We’re just outside Whistler Village in British Columbia about to embark on a forest trail walk to Lost Lake (Sḵwiḵ), a critical stopping point for Indigenous communities to gather resources and fish when traveling between the coast and the interior. Today we’re on a preview of Campo’s new ‘We Are The Land’ tour. “The reason we chose this name for the tour is something my Aunty Talaysay would tell me when I was a little girl: ‘We are the land’. It means that we are the caretakers of the land,” she says. Campo is co-owner of Talaysay Tours, an Indigenous, women-owned tourism company offering Indigenous-led experiences across British Columbia. Founded by her mother Candace Campo, in 2002, the company is rooted in the traditions and knowledge of both the Shíshálh (Sechelt) and Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish) Nations, of which the women are members. Walking beneath a canopy of towering old-growth Western Hemlock trees, Campo points out the Devil’s club, a woody shrub used by her ancestors for pain relief. “It’s important to have Indigenous tourism so our local guests and out-of-town guests can build a stronger relationship with the land,” says Campo as we pause by a babbling brook, where glimmers of sunlight dance on the slow-moving creek. “There’s so much going on with logging, global warming—one thing I’ve realized is that if (people) don’t have a relationship with the land, how are they going to take care of it or know how to take care of it?” It’s a question that sits at the heart of a growing conversation about what responsible travel in Canada should look like. As part of this conversation, Talaysay Tours has partnered with B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel on this new ‘We Are The Land’ experience. It’s aim is to help bring place-based learning, cultural ecology, stewardship and storytelling to Intrepid’s 10-day Grand Canadian Rockies itinerary beginning in 2027. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism. We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” - Christian Wolters, Intrepid Travel Canada President The Talasay partnership is part of a broader initiative by Intrepid to include more Indigenous tourism across its Canadian itineraries, with the goal to have an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of Canada tours by the end of this year, and one on every Canadian itinerary by the end of 2031. According to new research from non-profit foundation Angus Reid, commissioned by Intrepid Travel in July this year and surveying a group of 1,507 Canadians, 57 percent say they are interested in participating in an Indigenous-led tourism experience within Canada, yet fewer than one in five have ever done so. Part of the problem may be visibility. Among Canadians who have never participated in an Indigenous-led experience, 42 percent say they have not encountered one while planning a trip, while another 30 percent say they don’t know where to find one. According to the survey, seven in 10 Canadians would enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures, while more than four in 10 would be more likely to choose a Canadian trip that includes an Indigenous-led tourism experience. The appetite is certainly there. For Intrepid Travel Canada President Christian Wolters, who has joined us on the walking trail, making these experiences easier to access is more than a business opportunity. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism,” he tells me, after stopping to taste a few reddish salmonberries, native to the Pacific Northwest. “We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” Intrepid is also working closely with the Indigenous Tourism Association of Canada (ITAC) and has committed over USD$350,000 over five years to support the growth and promotion of Indigenous tourism in Canada. This includes adding Indigenous experiences to existing tours, as well as developing new, bespoke experiences alongside Indigenous tourism operators. “Partnerships like this create tangible opportunities and ensure communities gain direct economic and cultural benefits, while supporting our vision of Canada becoming a world leader in Indigenous tourism by 2030,” said Keith Henry, chief executive officer and president of ITAC in a press release. Coming up in 2027, a Huron-Wendat experience in Wendake, Quebec, will be added to Intrepid’s Eastern Canada by Rail itinerary, which will include a guided visit to the Huron-Wendat longhouse at the Huron Traditional Site. This addition will see Intrepid reach its goal of an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of their Canada itineraries—a significant milestone on the road to integrating Indigenous-led experiences across every Canada trip. “When it comes to Indigenous tourism in Canada, we only take up five percent of tourism and that’s such a small percentage,” says Campo, as we stand before the lovely Lost Lake with its mountainous backdrop. “So this partnership with Intrepid and other Indigenous companies throughout Turtle Island—these are the partners I wanna work with.” As she distributes traditional ‘hush’ tea made with soothing raspberry leaf, refreshing mint sweet licorice root and vibrant rose hips, we talk of the importance of stories. “When it comes to a lot of Indigenous history and our government, they try to write our story for us,” she says. “We’re redirecting that chapter so we can write and share our stories ourselves.” The writer was hosted by Intrepid Travel **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. Journalist and wanderluster Charmaine Noronha is a travel writer with a penchant for adventure, culture and chocolate. She started her career as a reporter with The Toronto Star before becoming the EIC of Vervegirl Magazine for five years then reported on Canadian news for The Associated Press for 11 years. Most recently, she was a Lifestyle reporter/editor at HuffPost Canada.

item.title: The Ultralight Rebound: Why Everyone I Know Eventually Adds Weight Back
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.30
(Photo: Ayesha Cording) How we reported this story: Author Ayesha “Heaps” Cording is a thru-hiker who has completed the Pacific Crest Trail three times, as well as other long trails including the Continental Divide. She assembled this list of gear swaps after thousands of miles of trail. On my first PCT thru-hike in 2016, I found myself running into a storm with my arms tucked inside a sleeveless gas station poncho. I’d thrown out my heavy rain jacket, telling myself I’d buy a lighter one in the next town. Everything in my pack was already wet, thanks to the badly pitched poncho-tarp I’d lain awake under the night before. Shivering on the trail, I was trying to decide whether I’d rather freeze with my arms exposed or risk face-planting with them inside. By 2025, I had added a full 13.85 ounces back onto my gear list for the sake of my sanity. It’s a well-worn pattern among ultralight backpackers: We strip back to the absolute bones, only to eventually add weight back. The pillow we swore we didn’t need, the warmer pad, the bug net, or the sleep socks. After enough miles, the question changes from “Can I live without this?” to “What am I giving up by saving the weight?” That is the ultralight rebound. A decade and several thru-hikes later, I’m still a card-carrying gram nerd, but my pack looks a little different; here’s the gear I’ve added back. I’ve never possessed the ultralight superpower of sleeping on foam. I wish I could throw an 1/8-inch pad on any patch of dirt and just sleep. Instead, I ruined a perfectly fine air pad trying to make it torso-length to save a few ounces. It didn’t seal properly with my cheap hotel iron, so I spent 400 miles waking up deflated on the ground. The three-ounce weight penalty over my botched half-pad is barely noticeable in my pack, but I do notice it when I sleep. It feels decadent to stretch my legs out on a warm pad instead of resting them on my lumpy pack or in the freezing dirt, and I actually feel rested and recovered the next day. A stove was the “luxury” item I resisted longest. For years, I cold-soaked everything, resorting to eating out of a Ziploc bag so I didn’t have to carry a cold-soak jar. (Even my fellow ultralight zealots thought I had gone too far.) Then came September on the CDT in Colorado, when ice froze thick on both the inside and outside of my tarp overnight. Suddenly, a stove became a necessity for sleep. It meant the comfort of hot meals before bed and cradling a Nalgene full of boiling water tucked deep inside my quilt. Even Ray Jardine, the granddaddy of ultralight, eventually came around on the stove. Reflecting on his 1993 Appalachian Trail hike, he told Backpacker that the decision was “too bold” and that “the weight savings wasn’t worth it.” If the granddaddy of ultralight came around on the stove, I figured I can carry the tiny burden of the Soto Amicus to keep warm. Ten years ago, I shortsightedly hacked the hipbelt off my Hyperlite Windrider to “free the hips,” buying into the questionable mindset that the more miserable you are, the cooler you look. Three UL packs later, my shoulders protested. I started having nerve issues and eventually added a detachable hipbelt to my current pack, the Meadowphysics Crane. My shoulder is healing, the weight is better distributed, and longer food and water carries don’t fill me with dread. And a 2.1-ounce hit to the ego is a small price to pay to preserve my body. I’ll do anything to make sure I’m able to be out there with my legs covered in dirt in another ten years from now. These 3.2 oz wind pants have somehow become one of my non-negotiables. They add warmth while sleeping, keep dirt off my quilt, and mosquitoes off my ankles, but they’re as much a mental buffer as a physical one. After months of being exposed to everything the trail throws at me, even a little bit of protection is sweet relief. Sure, Body Wrappers are dorky and make an obnoxious nylon swish with every step, but I can live with a tiny weight penalty if it means feeling a little more at ease after a long day on the trail. My years on trail taught me that the lightest possible gear list isn’t automatically the best one. I still snap the handle off my toothbrush and smoosh everything down until my pack resembles a child’s school backpack. But I’ve learned there are worse things to carry than a few extra ounces, and there is something better than bragging rights: the sweet relief of having two dry arms on a rainy day.

item.title: Deep in the West’s Backcountry, These 6 Trails Lead to Sacred Rock Art and Ruins
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.02
(Photo: Josh Ewing/Getty Images) Every hike has a story to tell, but there’s something special about a trail that takes you to ancient dwellings or rock art. It forces the past into perspective. You visualize the people who existed there, walking the same trails, planting food in the surrounding fields, and imagine how they might have lived. I geek out over archeological and cultural heritage hikes. They make the hike itself feel more like a quest than just a stroll through nature. Every spring, I plan a backpacking trip specifically to explore a new site in the American West. Those trips have led me to some of the most interesting and beautiful places I’ve ever been. I know others share this interest, too. However, well-known sites like Mesa Verde National Park and Chaco Culture National Historical Park are easily accessible and tend to get crowded. And nothing kills a meditative journey into the past faster than being surrounded by families and sightseers. With that in mind, I compiled this list of hikes to ancient ruins that are off the beaten path. These are real trails that will take you back in time and deep into secluded backcountry. Believe me, I understand the temptation to interact with ancient art when you discover it on a trail. However, nothing could be worse for their conservation. Touching ancient structures, pulling potsherds out of the soil, or handling artifacts can be devastating to these sites. If you are interested enough in these structures to seek them out and hike to them, visit them with respect. Follow local guidelines and rules of the area you’re hiking in. Stay on the trails and always practice Leave No Trace. And while these sites may be part of history, it’s a living history: As one Bears Ears ranger explained to Backpacker, rock art and dwellings are sacred to the Native communities whose ancestors lived there. When you’re visiting, treat them with the same reverence people treat churches, temples, cathedrals, or other religious sites. Salt Creek Canyon is located in the southeastern part of Canyonlands National Park. You can thru-hike the north-south trail in either direction, or do an out-and-back from either trailhead. The canyon is chock-full of fantastic rock formations, natural arches, and Ancestral Puebloan ruins. Along the way, you’ll find granary after granary, where the Ute who lived here stored masa flour and corn. There is a large cliff dwelling on a spur off the main trail that you can hike to, and petroglyphs like “America Man,” and the “Five Faces” that are spectacularly well-preserved. At many of these sites, ancient potsherds litter the ground. Pro tip: Water can be hit or miss in Salt Creek, so most hikers tend to go in early spring. There are also numerous side trails to explore along the way, leading to arches and other ruin sites. Trail length: 22.5 miles (one way) Permit required: Yes; permits are required for camping in Salt Creek and are available on recreation.gov four months before the start of each seasonal block. There is also a $35 park entrance fee. Dogs allowed: No At 2.1 miles, the hike to House on Fire Ruin is short, but you can extend the hike past the ruin and follow the trail up Mule Creek for a longer, 6.4-mile out-and-back. This ruin is iconic. It’s built into a small sandstone alcove, and the rock above looks just like flames ejecting from the ruin’s roof. This is just one of over 100,000 known archeological sites within Bears Ears National Monument. Pro tip: If you want to backpack in the area, the nearby Arch Canyon is a 17.3-mile trail with better camping options. It follows a creek and exposes hikers to natural arches and smaller native cultural heritage sites and ruins. You could hike both trails on the same trip, as the trailheads are less than 5 miles apart, and one permit would work for both areas. Trail length: 2.1 miles out-and-back (to the ruin), or 6.4 miles out-and-back along the Mule Creek Trail Permit required: Yes; $6 reservation fee and $5 per person day-hiking fee Dogs allowed: Yes Just a few miles south of the House on Fire Ruin is another equally spectacular heritage site. Moon House Ruins are perched on a cliff overlooking McCloyd Canyon. One of the buildings has a room with the phases of the moon depicted inside—for all intents and purposes, an Ancestral Puebloan wall calendar. The hike to the structure is mostly moderate, though it involves some scrambling and sections with rope handlines. You’ll be treated to a great view of the ruins from a distance as you approach, so bring those binoculars. After 1.4 miles, you’ll descend into the canyon and cross it to Moon House. To the north and south of the main ruin site, there are other structures to check out as well. Pro tip: Visitors to Moon House Ruins are limited to 20 people per day. Reserve your permit online ahead of time on the recreation.gov Moon House Ruins webpage. Trail length: 4.5 miles out-and-back Permit required: Yes; $6 reservation fee and $5 per person day hiking fee Dogs allowed: No In southern Colorado, the Canyons of the Ancients National Monument is a must-see for anyone interested in the history of the southwest. The Sand Canyon to East Rock Creek Trail to Rock Creek Trail Loop is an 11.8-mile circuit that connects three trails. Along the way, you’ll encounter sandstone caves and views of Marble Mountain, Horseshoe Mountain, Black Mountain, and Ute Peak to the south. It makes for a long day, especially if you plan on stopping to take in the scenery and check out the Puebloan ruins along the way. Not all ruins are marked, so you’ll have to look carefully to find some of them. Dispersed camping is allowed in the Canyons of the Ancient National Monument, but try to find sites that have been used before and minimize your impact. Pro tip: You can hike the Sand Canyon Trail, which goes straight to the ruins and back. However, the loop is actually shorter than the direct out-and-back and has less elevation gain. Trail length: 11.8-mile loop Permit required: No Dogs allowed: Yes This trail starts in the Hovenweep National Monument in Utah and takes you over the border and into Colorado. It’s a 12.4-mile out-and-back that climbs and descends in both directions. The trail offers sweeping views of the monument and passes many unique rock formations. It’s also just north of a designated rare lizard and snake study area on the Colorado side, so keep your eyes open for critters. There are numerous Puebloan ruins along the way, like the “Twin Towers” and “Hovenweep Castle.” Pro tip: Hovenweep National Monument does not allow dispersed camping, but there is a large 31-site campground situated along this trail .3 miles past the trailhead. You can also connect this trail with others on the Colorado side that go into Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land, where dispersed camping options are available. Trail length: 12.4 miles out-and-back Permit required: No; however, there is a $20 entrance fee for Hovenweep National Monument Dogs allowed: Yes This is the one hike on this list that I included even though it requires a guide. Keet Seel is the largest Ancestral Puebloan structure in Arizona, and it is impressive. Unsupervised visits to the site are not allowed. However, the monument does offer seasonal guided overnight trips to Keet Seel in spring (April and May) and fall (September and October). The full out-and-back hike is a long 17.2 miles and can be very strenuous. It descends into a canyon and climbs back out, going both directions. But the reward is worth it. Daily visitors are limited to 20, and guides offer insight into the history of the ruins and the Puebloans who lived there. Pro tip: Plan several months ahead, and check the NPS Keet Seel webpage continually for updates on when you can apply for these trips. Guided overnight tours book up very fast and are only available when there is adequate staff. Trail length: 17.2 miles out-and-back Permit required: Yes; check the NPS Navajo Nation webpage for information on how and when to apply. Dogs allowed: No

item.title: How chislic became a South Dakota obsession
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.66
How a Crimean meat kebab travelled thousands of miles to become a South Dakota obsession Chislic may look like a simple meat skewer, but its journey from the Black Sea to the American Great Plains tells a much bigger story. At Meridian Corner, a roadhouse amid the corn and alfalfa fields of Freeman in South Dakota, my lunch took about 40 seconds to arrive at the table: five sticks of lamb and five of mutton, deep-fried and served with garlic salt and crackers. This is chislic – South Dakota's most beloved light bite, often eaten as an appetiser or snack between meals. Here in the town of Freeman, it's ubiquitous, served in bars, restaurants, and homes across this south-eastern pocket of the state. Drive much beyond it, however, and people may have no idea what you're talking about. "I grew up eating chislic and never thought much about it," town archivist Marnette Hofer told me. "Then I went to college in Kansas, and nobody knew about it. I don't think people in the Black Hills – in South Dakota! – had a clue." Chislic may be distinctly South Dakotan, but its roots lie thousands of miles away, around the Black Sea. So how did it become so thoroughly local that, in 2018, the state legislature made it the official state "nosh"? From Crimea to Dakota In the 1870s, Germans from Russia began arriving in what was then Dakota Territory, bringing with them traditions from their former homes around the Black Sea. Hofer, who grew up in the area and serves as the executive director of its Heritage Hall Museum & Archives, took me through its exhibits chronicling the historic passage. As she showed me around its exhibits, we discussed chislic and the unlikely chain of events that brought it here. While roasting meat on sticks is an ancient technique, peoples living around the Black Sea and the Caucasus traditionally cut their meat into small chunks before skewering it on metal rods, or even swords. Russian troops encountered this style of cooking among Tatars in Crimea and the Caucasus as the empire pushed south towards the Black Sea from the late 17th Century. Called "shashlyk", it was typically made with mutton, marinated in onions or vinegar and grilled on skewers – quick to prepare and easy to eat on the move. By the late 18th Century, shashlyk had become fashionable in parts of the Russian Empire and was enthusiastically taken up by German settlers who had been encouraged to settle in Russia under Catherine the Great, many of whom later established communities around the Black Sea. But in the 1870s, as Tsar Alexander II revoked privileges long granted to its German settlers, including their religious freedom and exemption from military service, many began emigrating. Among the things they carried with them were recipes. "And President Abraham Lincoln had eight years previously enacted the Homestead Act of 1862, promising cheap land on the American frontier," recounts Tim Waltner, the Heritage Hall's education and communication coordinator. "If you stayed on five years, the land was yours." The timing proved irresistible to immigrants from all over Europe, including some 115,000 Russo-Germans – or "Germans from Russia" as they would become known. Among them was farmer-turned-carpenter Johann Hoellwarth, who arrived in the growing town of Freeman in the 1870s. According to the earliest records available, said Hofer, Hoellwarth was the first to introduce shashlyk to Dakotan palates. "Only," she adds, "his accent was so thick people thought he was saying 'chislic'." How shashlyk became chislic The new name stuck, and more changes were ahead. Hoellwarth quickly discovered that the windswept Great Plains were very different from Crimea's milder landscape. While sheep farming was well established in the Dakotas by the early 1800s, there was no metal for skewers, no vinegar for marinating, and on the treeless prairies, hardwood was far too precious to burn. Even onions were relatively new. Like many immigrants before him, Hoellwarth made do with what he had: a cauldron, lard, garlic salt, hand-length sticks whittled from willow bushes, and 10ft (3m)-tall wild grasses that burned fast but hot. This is how a meal that was once marinated, grilled on a sword and eaten with flatbread became a deep-fried, salted bite-sized snack served on a glorified toothpick and eaten with crackers. "He would serve it during Fourth of July celebrations in Freeman," said Hofer. And just as Russian soldiers had discovered generations earlier, "it was popular." Inside the Chislic Circle At Meridian Corner, the chislic is traditional and the gossip, as the saying goes, could rip the paint off a barn. The roadhouse sits at the heart of the Chislic Circle, a term coined by writer Richard Preheim in 2005 for the roughly 30-mile radius around Freeman where devotion to chislic runs deep. It has also become something of a culinary bastion. Even after chislic was named the state's official "nosh" and chefs began serving beef, goat and pork versions, the Circle largely held to lamb and mutton. The legislature chose "nosh" rather than "dish" or "meal" because it considered the term a better fit for the snack-sized food. "When it became the state nosh, the definition of what chislic is really expanded," said Abby Streyle, Meridian Corner's manager, who is of German-Russian ancestry. "It's fun when people do different twists on a food, but it is important to keep some things old-school." More like this: But chislic has been evolving almost from the start. From Hoellwarth's introduction, as it passed down family lines the recipe picked up local peculiarities reflected in eateries across the area today. In the nearby town of Kaylor, the Kaylor Locker, the butcher supplying most of the Circle for the last 65 years, serves a venison version, the Circle's only acceptable stand-in for lamb or mutton. At Pep's Pub across the street, the chislic is griddled – not fried – with onions. In the town of Dimock, locally made cheese is added as a side along with crackers, while Bud's Tavern in Marion adds jalapeños to the onions and uses only "dirty oil" (previously used) to enhance the flavour. Some adaptations have been economic. Pep's Pub and Bud's Tavern serve their chislic "loose" – without skewers – a practice Cindy Fischer, owner of The Schnitz Bar in the town of Menno, says helped keep prices down. Others were practical. Over-fried chislic comes out hard as a rock, which may help explain the rise of griddles and air fryers to keep the meat juicy and evenly cooked. How far can chislic stretch? "When we began, we had a tasting competition and divided it into traditional and 'New Age Nosh' categories," she recalled. "Even then, there were some who scoffed that nothing other than traditional sheep chislic earned the name. But in the New Age Nosh category, someone wanted to enter alligator! That was going too far." Beyond the Chislic Circle, however, the rules remain loose. I tried beef chislic at the Blarney Stone in Sioux Falls – an hour's drive from Freeman – that bucked tradition further with horseradish and Carolina BBQ sauces. Delicious, but Hoellwarth's head would likely be exploding. "They called it steak tips before 2018," Streyle muttered. While the recipe continues to evolve, what chislic represents has remained remarkably consistent. "Chislic is hospitality in a simple, unassuming dish," Hofer told me. "Kind of a 'come as you are, we're glad you're here' type of food. It is a simple experience that reminds people of a community where hard work and honesty are important values. Where being real, down-to-earth and welcoming are just part of life." And one day, maybe even with alligator. --

item.title: What happens when a place has two different names?
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.44
Lake Ontario/Lake America: What happens when a place has two different names? Open the same map in the US and Canada and you may see two different names for the same lake. So, who decides what a place is really called? Open Google Maps in Toronto and you may see one name for a place. Open it in New York and you may see another. Increasingly, the map in your pocket can depend on where you're standing. That is what's happening with Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes that lie on the US-Canadian border. After President Trump ordered the US government to rename it "Lake America" following failed trade talks between the two nations this summer, the lake began appearing under different names on different maps. But changing a name on a government database doesn't necessarily change what the rest of the world calls it. From digital maps to tourism organisations and local communities, the Lake Ontario dispute shows how complicated it can be to rename a place – and who ultimately decides which name sticks. Who decides what goes on a map? Unsurprisingly, Canada has not entertained a change. In the US, the modification began with the federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the database used to standardise geographic names for federal use. Trump's executive order required "Lake America" to be added to the system and the former moniker removed. Google reflected the change in line with its long-standing policy of using official government naming sources, meaning US viewers now see "Lake America" while Canadian viewers continue to see "Lake Ontario". Apple Maps has also adopted the new name after pressure from Trump. But private mapping companies are not legally required to follow the federal designation. MapQuest, best known for being one of the earliest digital mapping tools, has refused to adopt the new name – and its refusal subsequently propelled MapQuest to number one overall on Apple's US App Store, with the company saying it had recorded more than 1.5 million installs across the US and Canada since the executive order was issued. "MapQuest focused on maintaining a name that people are familiar with," said Doug Berger, general manager at MapQuest. "When people need directions, they seek familiarity. It was an easy decision." What's in a name? The differing responses show how a federal name change can quickly produce multiple versions of the same geography. Oswego County in New York, which borders the lake, has chosen to retain Lake Ontario in its official and business materials, citing the historical significance of the name and expense to taxpayers and business owners for the cost of rebranding. "In our traditional Seneca language, its name is sga:nyodai:yoh, meaning 'beautiful lake'," said J Conrad Seneca, Seneca Nation President. "To us, Lake Ontario is not a political pawn. It does not separate the countries of the United States and Canada. It is all Indigenous land, which has been occupied by Indigenous people since time immemorial." When two names coexist But beyond the US and Canada, the impact of the name change may be limited. "The naming of bodies of water typically falls within national jurisdictions," explained Taufiq Rahim, senior fellow at non-partisan think tank New America and author of Trump 2.5: A Primer. "While there are international bodies like the IHO [International Hydrographic Organization], they do not have any authority to adjudicate disputes and typically when there is a dispute, two or multiple names can be used." A longstanding example is the dispute over "Persian Gulf" and "Arabian Gulf". Persian Gulf remains the standard name used by the UN, the IHO and most world atlases, while Arab states bordering the waterway – including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman – generally use Arabian Gulf and have encouraged allies to do so as well since the 1960s. More like this: A more recent example is Trump's January 2025 decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America". The new name was adopted on US federal maps and by some digital mapping services, while Mexico and international users continued to encounter "Gulf of Mexico" or both names. In Mobile, Alabama, the National Maritime Museum of the Gulf of Mexico had only recently spent nearly $100,000 (£74,000) rebranding when the federal name changed, leaving it with a newly minted identity tied to a now-disputed place name. At the time, its director told BBC Travel that another name change would require "a complete redo of the entire museum" and that she would follow the lead of city officials. Its website now identifies it simply as the National Maritime Museum of the Gulf. A similar issue is now playing out on the US side of Lake Ontario. The Lake Ontario National Marine Sanctuary, a federally designated protected area covering 1,722 sq miles (4,460 sq km) of waters and lakebed along the eastern New York shoreline, is retaining its name. The National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration, which comanages the sanctuary with New York State, says in a statement that the executive order applies to federal references to the lake itself but did not change the sanctuary's separately designated name. The agency is updating its materials to refer to the lake as "Lake America", while the sanctuary remains the Lake Ontario National Marine Sanctuary. A diplomatic wedge The organisational and financial burden of the name change will likely fall on the United States and its taxpayers. "This adds another unnecessary line to US expenses which in total can exceed hundreds of millions of dollars annually," said Usha Haley, Barton Distinguished Chair in International Business at Wichita State University. "People have to divert time, another important resource, to manage these changes for different audiences." While the change will have practical impacts, it's the symbolic implications that will likely have the most lasting effects. "Geographic naming becomes a proxy for sovereignty and power. It's geopolitical signalling on who controls national and bi-lateral narratives," said Haley. "The downstream symbolic and diplomatic consequences of a name change such as this can be much larger than the immediate commercial calculations." The change is likely to continue the erosion of diplomatic trust between Canada and the US, says Haley, hindering a weakening trading relationship between the two nations. Canada has long been a top destination for US exports, and the third-largest source of US imports, following Mexico and China. She said that symbolic disputes like this can become proxies for larger conflicts. --

item.title: Why Swedes think standing out is embarrassing
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.62
'You're not to think you're anything special': Why Swedes hate standing out Swedes prize equality, dislike boasting and are famously reluctant to stand out – yet they're also fiercely individualistic and know how to celebrate. The century-old idea of Jantelagen helps explain these contradictions, and offers visitors a fascinating key to decoding Swedish culture. As an utlandssvensk – a Swede who grew up abroad – I've always been fascinated by the unwritten rules that shape Swedish social life. I once got to chatting with a fellow Swede at a party. It was 4 July, and we discussed why our country didn't celebrate its national day as fervently as Americans. No fireworks, no parades – how come? "Well, it would be fairly embarrassing wouldn't it?" she said. "All that self-celebration. It's a bit over-the-top," she added, lowering her voice, as if there was an American hovering inches away from our table. As she explained, setting off fireworks for your nation (and therefore yourself) smacks of back-patting and ostentatiousness – two things that are anathema to much of Scandinavia. When I complimented my companion on how well she'd outlined the issue, she looked askance and waved my praise away like a bad smell. "No, please. That's just my little opinion, of course." A modest code of conduct To understand this aversion to basking in even the smallest of spotlights, many Swedes point to Jantelagen, or the Law of Jante: an unwritten social code embedded across Scandinavia that prizes humility, equality and not placing yourself above others. The term comes from Danish-Norwegian author Aksel Sandemose's satirical 1933 novel A Fugitive Crosses His Tracks, set in the fictional town of Jante. Sandemose used Jante to skewer the conformism of small-town Scandinavian life, laying out 10 "laws" designed to put anyone who considered themselves exceptional firmly back in their place. Rules such as "you're not to think you're anything special" and "you're not to think you're smarter than [anyone else]" leave the reader with a deliberately bruised ego – and that's the point. Nearly a century on, Sandemose's laws remain memorable and highly quotable, helping Jantelagen endure as cultural shorthand. How to connect with Swedes Be proactive: Small talk with strangers isn't the norm, so don't mistake reserve for unfriendliness. "Swedes tend to be very loyal and trustworthy once a friendship is established," says Gossner. "I often advise newcomers to take the initiative. Don't wait for Swedes to come to you, as they appreciate when others make the first move." Suggest fika: The Swedish ritual of cake and coffee offers a low-pressure way to socialise. Meet over coffee and a modest but delicious kanelbulle (cinnamon bun) rather than trying to force conversation in the street. Be punctual: Swedes place a high value on being on time, particularly when you're invited to someone's home. Stefan Dahlberg, a professor of political science at Mid Sweden University, has written a paper on Jantelagen's modern legacy. He sees the rules less as firm laws governing Swedish behaviour. Instead, he explains, "they are better understood as a cultural shorthand for a set of familiar norms […] that you can recognise in everyday Swedish interaction. Status differences tend to be played down, social relations are relatively informal and conspicuous self-promotion can be viewed negatively." Visitors to Sweden will likely see this in action when chatting to locals. Compliment a Swede on their English, for example, and they may quickly play it down – switching to Swedish and muttering, "Äsch, det är ju inte flytande…" (Shucks, it's not like it's fluent…). Sandemose would be proud. The qualities can also be seen in everyday Swedish rituals, from Fredagsmys – unpretentious "cosy Fridays" with friends or family – to Lördagsgodis ("Saturday-candy") that's practiced by parents as the one day that kids can unleash their sweet tooth after a week of modest abstention. That doesn't mean that Jantelagen functions as a literal rulebook – or identically across Scandinavia. Dahlberg's study of Jantelagen in Norway, a geographical and cultural neighbour, found the average respondent tended to disagree with the Jante statements. After all, Dahlberg explains, Sandemose invented the list as a scathing takedown of conformity. "So there are really two things mixed together in the concept: an egalitarian idea that nobody is inherently better than anyone else, and a more negative pressure not to distinguish yourself too much." Jante's mirror image Jantelagen has another, less obvious side. In a culture where seeking the limelight is usually frowned upon, Swedish reserve can disappear at parties when a tradition of snappsvisor (increasingly risqué songs belted out while drinking heroic amounts of aquavit) and performative speeches create safe social spaces to open up. So, while Jantelagen is often used as a reasoning for Swedish reserve and diffidence, it can also reveal the inverse. More like this: As Dahlberg notes, "'Don't think you are better than anyone else' can be read in the opposite direction: don't assume that somebody is better than you simply because they are richer, more successful or have a more prestigious title." With so much bubbling under the surface, Sweden can feel deceptively complex. Luckily, there are classes designed to help mystified foreigners. Yvonne Gossner runs Learn Swedish Culture AB – and business is booming. "I realised there was a big demand for practical insights into Swedish culture, especially for foreigners trying to navigate life here," she says. "Many felt lost or misunderstood in everyday settings, or even when trying to make Swedish friends." Case in point: a South American client once arrived at a Swedish woman's party an hour late, carrying a big dish of food as a surprise. The hostess "was not pleased" as the guests had already eaten, and the immodestly large, late-coming dish was left untouched in a bedroom. Swedes, Gossner says, place a high value on punctuality and politeness; if you're invited to a Swede's house, she suggests sending a post-party message of thanks. "There is even a Swedish joke: 'Don't forget to send a thank-you note for the thank-you note'," she adds. An unasked-for dish can risk looking like a statement that "my food is better than yours", while failing to acknowledge someone's politeness can jar the sense of social balance. Cracking the Swedish ice Lola Akinmade Åkerström, a Nigerian-American author, travel writer and photographer who moved to Sweden more than 15 years ago, was initially "a bit floored by the unspoken ethos" of Jantelagen, as well as the contradictory layers of national character. "Sweden is the most open society, run by the most private people," she says. If you want to deeply discomfit a Swede, she advises, just make eye contact on a quiet train, and hit them with "Hi! How you doing?" Yet they're not being cold, just respectful of the idea that no one should impose themselves on a stranger's space. That preference for understatement extends beyond social interactions. Travel through the countryside and you can see it reflected in the nation's beloved summer houses. "I think Swedes hold the world record in the number of summer houses per capita – around half the population has access to one," says Orvar Löfgren, professor emeritus of ethnology at Lund University. Yet these are rarely flashy second homes; instead, they reflect rustic, rural values, even among wealthy owners. (Don't think your cabin is better than other cabins, Sandemose might say.) While in Sweden, visitors might also notice small Swedish flags on birthday cakes, supermarket products and during student celebrations. "Swedes who love to see themselves as non-nationalistic are actually good at waving the flag," says Löfgren. And despite their quiet reputation, "Swedes are great at celebrating," he adds. Christmas, Easter, Midsummer, birthdays, and student exams are celebrated "with more intensity than in most European countries". You could say these occasions showcase Swedes at their best – not that they'd put it so boastfully, of course. --

item.title: Glamping on Vermont's newest bikepacking trail
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.55
The US's newest bikepacking trail is pioneering a whole new way to see Vermont The Heart of the Greens trail threads through Vermont's stunning Green Mountain wilderness, and is the first part of an ambitious bikepacking adventure that will someday span the state. My mountain bike tyres thud over pebbles and roots as I whizz through the darkening path. Dusk has fallen over Vermont's Green Mountain National Forest and nearly 400,000 acres of woods extend in every direction. In the distance, I spot pinpricks of light. The campsite is finally near. In the last fleeting moments of light, I arrive at the Chittenden Brook campground. As I wheel my bike past the welcome sign, I spy a slick, modern hut with pine siding. I'd planned to simply pitch a tent – to this weary bikepacker, the hut's glass windows and wraparound porch seem like the lap of luxury. Next time, I thought, I'm staying there. This hut is part of the Heart of the Greens Loop, a 38-mile (61km) bike trail loop and the first completed segment of an ambitious, continuous bikepacking network that, when completed, will stretch 485 miles (780km) and span the entire state. Plan your trip When to do it: Spring and summer are ideal, but tackle the trail in autumn to appreciate its stunning changing leaves. Most riders can expect to complete the loop in one to three days. How to get there: Rochester has limited bus service, so it's easiest to drive to the trailhead. Alternatively, park in Pittsfield and start your ride from there. What to eat: Bring your own provisions. The two villages anchoring the trail have a handful of eateries, like Rochester's farm-to-table Maple Soul and Pittsfield's Clear River Inn & Tavern. Sample dishes made with Vermont's famous maple syrup, like the iconic Creemee ice cream. Pittsfield has two general stores. Blazing a path for bikepackers My journey began that morning in Rochester, a picturesque village nestled in Vermont's mountainous White River Valley. I've driven through it dozens of times without stopping, but since it became the official start and end point of The Heart of the Greens when it opened in 2024, the tiny town has become a magnet for bikepackers. Like me, many are eager to blend the escapism of camping with the thrill of cycling through Vermont's glacial-carved wilderness and explosion of autumnal colours. The loop is a closed-circuit preview of the forthcoming Velomont, a bikepacking route through Central Vermont with a twist: it will be connected by 30 cleverly spaced off-grid huts allowing tired pedallers to bed down in protected forest shelter. On track to finish the first 200 miles (321km) within the next 10 years, the project echoes a larger trend in bicycle travel: statewide bikepacking routes are in development in Utah, Massachusetts and along the entire West Coast. I grew up near Rochester and have dreamed of such a multi-day bikepacking route. For now, I'm thrilled to take on the Heart of the Greens. Two huts are already placed along the trail, roughly 19 miles (30km) apart: the Chittenden Brook Hut, featuring simple bunks and a self-service kitchen, and Spikehorn Yurt. The yurt doesn't have electricity, and neither accommodation has running water. The route's huts will straddle a curious middle ground between camping and traditional stays, allowing bikepackers to carry lighter gear and immerse themselves in the wilderness. The Heart of the Greens may be considerably shorter than the Velomont, but with a cumulative ascent of nearly 6,000ft (1,830m) on largely unpaved forest roads and trails, it's no less intense. "It's a big walk on the wild side," says Doon Hinderyckx, owner of Green Mountain Bikes in Rochester, when I stop by before shoving off. Hinderyckx encourages visitors to hire e-bikes for navigating the steeper grades: "You're mixing mountain biking and the adventure of the challenging terrain. You're on and off the seat a lot." It also requires a bike with thick tyres and suspension, a water filter and provisions, since the current route passes through only two small backcountry villages – Rochester and, 9 miles (14km) south, Pittsfield. Like the huts, eateries and general stores along the trail itself are still in development, so I've packed several meals, plus rain gear and insect repellent, despite the beautiful late summer weather. Hinderyckx checks the air pressure in my inner tubes and oils my chain. He's the last mechanic I'll see for the next two days. Next door to Green Mountain Bikes stands the Stable Inn, run by Hinderyckx's wife, Anni MacKay. This handsome two-story guesthouse opened in 2023, with a range of rooms, Nordic-chic decor and rooftop solar panels, converted from a timber-frame warehouse from the 1840s. While not an official hut on the trail, the Stable Inn has become a base for many Heart of the Greens riders to unwind, or bookend their bikepacking journey with jaunts to the village's quaint art centres and shops. "[The loop is] a very strategic, positive thing," says MacKay. "People always want to have access to the backcountry, in a safe way, with the benediction of the community that is providing services. It's a complete win-win." Ups and downs in the Green Mountains I know Vermont well and have bike-toured widely, but this is harder than I expected. On asphalt, a 38-mile ride makes for a pleasant afternoon. The Heart of the Greens is far more demanding – and adventurous. Rugged roads lead to mountain bike trails, which scissor their way up the alpine forest. The first day, I coast south along Route 100 and turn onto State Garage Road, into a residential area. Houses disappear beyond the canopy, and I huff up one shelf of road, then another. All at once, the road transforms into steep gravel. I grind past the Spikehorn Yurt, the Loop's first hut, a rounded fabric enclosure with bunkbeds, a futon, homey furniture and a spacious terrace with views of the mountains. The route then devolves into two dirt tyre trenches cutting through the grass – what mountain bikers call "double track". My temples pound as I climb. Summer mosquitoes drone in the sultry air. After a couple of gruelling miles, the road finally descends, and so do the conditions. Logging lorries have shredded the ground into potting soil, my wheels sink into a mire of turned earth and broken branches. As I struggle, another cyclist pulls up behind me. "This is crazy, isn't it?" he wheezes. "I don't think I'd have made it if I wasn't on an e-bike." I can't help but agree. The grades are tough on my middle-aged thighs, and I frequently dismount and push. I got a late start to begin with, and as I reach the third major trail section of the day – a mile of switchbacks cheekily named "Perspiration" – my legs boil with lactic acid, and the Sun melts beyond the ridge. This is how I come to arrive at Chittenden Brook Campground after nightfall. I pitch my tent onto the cold ground and gaze longingly at the modern hut before me. Riding high After a decent night's sleep, I finally hit my stride. I sail down the smooth pavement of Route 73 and pedal through the pastoral scenery of the quiet, unpaved Bingo Brook Road. Dense trees all around, I pass occasional farmhouses and cottages, but most of this land is national forest. Fog lifts over a pond, and the air is cool and quiet. I try to imagine what the Velomont will look like in future decades. The Heart of the Greens now passes through just two village centres with a loose string of businesses straddling Route 100. As the Velomont expands, it will tether together more towns and country shops, making it easier for cyclists to resupply and interact with locals. Bikepackers will traverse ever-more-varied terrain and, like me, stop in towns they might never notice by car. "You're camping, but you're not really camping," says Georgia Grzywacz, a Maine resident who rode the loop and stayed at the Chittenden Brook Hut in June. She appreciated the kitchen, electricity and bunk mattresses, as well as the nearby brook. "You're without running water, but you have these creature comforts." Even the booking process was easy: "The [Vermont Huts] website is so navigable." I veer off Bingo Brook Road to find a final trailhead. Two mountains remain, totalling 12 miles (19km) and more than 2,000ft (609m) of climbing, but this time, I'm prepared. Teeth clenched, I grind my way up the switchbacks of Swan's Mill Trail, fighting for every foot of elevation. More like this: At last, my reward: Tunnel Ridge is a five-mile-long (8km) flow trail that snakes its way back down to Rochester, for a total of 110 switchbacks. My tyres shudder over washboard terrain and swerve around S-curves. I choke the brakes, my saddlebags bounce noisily over my rear rack. The forest becomes a wash of brown and green. Gravity lures me downward, into the valley. Endorphins flood my brain as I drift into The Stable Inn's parking lot, back to my waiting car. I'm euphoric but exhausted. For now, I'm closing the loop. But in time, there should be many miles, and many huts, more. And I'll be ready. --

item.title: A 2,500km road trip in search of wild lemurs
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.51
I drove 2,500km across Madagascar to find the world's last lemurs One epic road trip connects Madagascar's richest wildlife, most spectacular landscapes and the world's last lemurs. Sitting beneath a thick canopy of trees in Mitsinjo Reserve, I crane my neck skyward, straining beneath the weight of my camera. A flash of white and black fur leaps across my lens, much closer than anticipated. I drop the camera from my eye and the heavy jungle air erupts with the haunting, whale-like cries of the indri, the largest lemur species on Earth. Critically endangered, strictly arboreal and the origin of man, according to Malagasy lore, the indri is a wide-eyed, tuft-eared rarity known to few but the most exuberant wildlife enthusiasts. Madagascar's crown jewel of more than 150,000 endemic species is sitting just 3m (10ft) above my head. Madagascar is the only place on Earth where lemurs survive in the wild, and my husband and I had come here to see how much of that extraordinary wildlife we could encounter on an independent road trip. Over three weeks, our 2,500km (1,553-mile) route would take us from the capital, Antananarivo, through rainforest, rice paddies, prehistoric canyons and spiny desert to the island's west coast, linking eight national parks and reserves along the way. With a rented 4X4 and an ever-changing cast of park guides, the route offered a surprisingly achievable way to encounter species found nowhere else on the planet. The RN7: Madagascar's lemur highway We rented a 4x4 for the journey, and with the bustle of Antananarivo fading into our rear-view mirror, we rode the RN7's ribbon of freshly laid tarmac up into the central highlands where two-storey trano gasy homes made of red earthen bricks sat on the fringes of expansive rice paddies. Families watched from behind swinging wooden shutters as we passed by. Rolling green hills and terraced valleys grazed by long-horned zebu punctuated the winding roads between towns. Plan your trip: How to do it: Rent a 4x4 vehicle and camping gear from Roadtrip Africa. If you intend to depart the RN7, you can also organise a pisteur through them for a small fee. Best time to go: May to October, the island's dry season Don't-miss stops: Mitsinjo Reserve, Anja Reserve, Ranomafana and Isalo National Park offer the most diverse lemur sightings without venturing far from the tarmac. Our first wildlife stop was the dense jungle of Ranomafana National Park. Trudging through the rain, I followed a local guide – required in Madagascar's national parks and readily available at every park entrance – up the muddy trail. Walking with a slight limp, acquired while rescuing a traveller from a jungle waterfall years ago, he pointed out clumsy red-bellied lemurs, self-assured greater bamboo lemurs basking in the sun and ultra-rare golden bamboo lemurs. The latter survive largely on giant bamboo, consuming quantities of cyanide that would be lethal to most other mammals. The sheer variety is partly a product of Madagascar's fragmented habitats. "Lemurs are ultra-specialised creatures evolved to fill a single ecological niche," our guide explained. "Each forest in Madagascar hosts its own unique adapted species." More than 110 lemur species have been identified, many restricted to small pockets of forest. To see more of them, you have to keep moving. But the ease of the sightings has a darker explanation. Madagascar's forests are shrinking, our guide said, as communities cut down trees for fuel and agriculture, squeezing lemurs into ever-smaller fragments of habitat. Continuing south brought new species with each change in landscape. We sunned on chunky boulders surrounded by ring-tailed lemurs in Anja Community Reserve and searched for tree boas in the shadow of the Andringitra massif. Hiking within the ruiniform plateau and jagged canyons of Isalo National Park, the final stop on our voyage down the RN7, we stumbled through verdant foliage and went nearly nose-to-nose with Verreaux's sifaka, long-limbed lemurs famous for their sideways, dancing gait. Into Madagascar's wild west Reaching Tsingy required a four-day traverse across some of the roughest roads of the trip. For the most difficult stretch, between Manja and Morondava, we hired a local pisteur – a ride-along guide who knows every river crossing, mud pits and hidden routes through the maze of dirt tracks. More like this: We crossed rivers where the flow nearly crested the hood of our truck. Elsewhere, tall grass swallowed the track entirely. Without GPS or a reliable map, the pisteur became our eyes, picking a path through the endless web of sandy tracks and occasionally guiding us through isolated Sakalava communities. Careening around a particularly sandy corridor, we burst into a kianja, or village square, alive with a market and hundreds of shoppers. Thick ropes of tobacco, roasting cassava and an array of plastic trinkets were spread out on colorful lambahoany, the printed cotton wraps worn across Madagascar. It was a vibrant bazaar erected seemingly out of nowhere, surrounded by wooded savannah a day's drive in any direction. By the time we reached the town of Morondava in the dim evening light, after days of mud and river crossings, hitting tarmac again felt like a relief. We thanked our pisteur for his life-saving navigational services before setting up camp beneath the moonlit shade of a baobab, Madagascar's emblematic tree. Baobabs, fossa and Tsingy We woke at the edge of Avenue of the Baobabs – Madagascar's famous dirt road lined with towering baobab trees – in the soft pink light of dawn. For a few precious moments we had the country's most photographed landscape almost to ourselves before the tour groups arrived. Kirindy Reserve was a natural stop on our final stretch to Tsingy, and a welcome break before another gruelling day on the road. Kirindy is all about nocturnal wildlife. That night, our guide led us through the reserve, where in the glow of my headlamp, a Madame Berthe's mouse lemur scampered into the canopy while the wide, spectral eyes of a red-tailed sportive lemur reflected crimson in the beam. Back in camp, a particularly pudgy fossa – Madagascar's largest predator, with the long body of a mongoose and cat-like features – wandered from the treeline in the shadow of our tent. The next day, as we neared Tsingy, the hard dirt road devolved into a thick mud pit. Stranded vehicles littered both sides of the swampy mess and crowds from the nearby village gathered to haul drivers free. Before long, our 4X4 was bogged too. But Tsingy was worth every difficult kilometre. Its unique stone forests host many endemic lemurs, and we spent several days clipping into via ferrata lines and climbing through the Unesco-listed limestone pinnacles in search of aye-ayes, stump-tailed chameleons and tiny leaf chameleons. With our final park behind us, we turned the 4x4 back towards Antananarivo. After weeks of river crossing, mud and increasingly rough roads, the smooth tarmac through the central highlands felt strangely uneventful. We had succeeded in seeing Madagascar's extraordinary wildlife without joining a tour. But you never really travel "independently" here. Every national park guide who helped us track lemurs, the pisteurwho pointed the way andthe villagers who hauled us from the mud had made the journey possible. --

item.title: Inside the places that shaped Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.22
'Everything about her was East Tennessee': The places that shaped Dolly Parton From her Appalachian childhood to Nashville and Dollywood, a journey through the Tennessee she loved – and transformed in return. On a sunny day on 24 June 2026, hundreds of travellers, locals and Dolly Parton fans from across the US gathered in the small rural community of Cornersville, less than an hour's drive south of Nashville, for the unveiling of her Tennessean Travel Stop. It was the country star's last public appearance before her death just two months later. Wearing her signature fringe and rhinestones and a grin as bright as that Tennessee morning, Parton cut the ribbon and welcomed travellers to the new roadside stop, complete with a Southern meat-and-three restaurant, live music and – of course – a Dolly-themed gift shop. It was a fitting final chapter for an artist whose life and career were inseparable from Tennessee. From crooning about the Smoky Mountains to investing in rural East Tennessee where she grew up, Parton spent decades sharing her home state with the world – and transforming it in return. Explore Parton's Tennessee mountain home In 1964, US President Lyndon B Johnson launched the War on Poverty, a federal effort to reduce poverty and expand economic opportunity across the United States. Southern Appalachia, one of the nation's poorest regions, was thrust into the national spotlight. Media portrayals often depicted its residents as backward and destitute, reinforcing the caricature of the "hillbilly", a stereotype that had persisted since the 19th Century. But when Dolly Rebecca Parton came into the spotlight, this daughter of Appalachia who grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 brothers and sisters offered the world a different view of her home: one of joy, dignity and talent. Follow Dolly Parton's story across Tennessee Sevierville: See the bronze statue of Parton outside the Sevier County Courthouse and The Pines, where she performed for a paying audience for the first time at just 10 years old. RCA Studio B, Nashville: Visit the legendary recording studio on Music Row where Dolly Parton and other iconic artists like Elvis Presley recorded some of their greatest hits. The Country Music Hall of Fame, Nashville: A must-visit Nashville institution that chronicles the history of country music through artefacts, exhibits and the stories of the artists who trailblazed the genre. Dollywood, Pigeon Forge: Set in the Smoky Mountains that Parton loved so dearly, Dollywood takes guests on a journey through the singer's roots, from an exact replica of her childhood two-room cabin to the Dolly Parton Experience, which displays childhood memorabilia. "Dolly Parton told a new story about Appalachia that was rooted in her very particular experience," said Dr Jessie Wilkerson, a history professor and Appalachian scholar at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. "Yes, her family was poor, but they weren't desperate or hopeless, and they took care of one another. There was a lot of love and beauty in the place where she grew up, and so we get a different story about Appalachia through her." In the title track of her 1973 album, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Parton describes her Appalachian home as "peaceful as a baby's sigh". The landscape around her childhood home on the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains, along with Appalachia's storytelling traditions and bluegrass heritage, inspired much of Parton's music. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, a blue-grey mist that gives the Smokies its name settles over the peaks and valleys and waterfalls tumble through the forest. The 522,000-acre expanse is threaded with hiking trails and scenic overlooks, with autumn bringing a canvas of brilliant jewel tones and spring a kaleidoscope of wildflowers to the lower slopes. The landscape was a reoccurring muse, from the mountain blooms that inspired her 1987 ballad Wildflowers to the fog-covered peaks evoked in Blue Smoke, the title track of her 2014 album, and the pastoral idyll captured in My Tennessee Mountain Home. In nearby Sevierville, the main town serving rural Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up, the region's pride in its local legend is evident. A bronze statue on the courthouse lawn depicts her as a young girl playing guitar. Down the street is the Wings of Wander mural, inspired by her hit song Love Is Like a Butterfly, and the Red's Cafe mural, another larger-than-life depiction of Parton as a child, this time getting a cheeseburger from her favourite childhood restaurant. "People in East Tennessee really, really adore her, and it's something that's been important for the region to have someone who's really proud of coming from there, and who's a positive representation of Appalachia, when historically the representations of the region are the opposite," Wilkerson said. Retracing Parton's path in Nashville On the day Parton graduated from high school in 1964, she boarded a Greyhound bus headed west for the neon lights of Nashville. In a letter home shortly after arriving, feeling homesick and uncertain, she wrote, "Nashville isn't what I thought it was gonna be, but I think I'll like it once I get used to it." "When she came to Nashville, she came with a very distinct East Tennessee identity and made that very clear in both her music and her accent," said Robert K Oermann, co-author of her memoir Dolly Parton: Songteller, My Life in Lyrics and a longtime collaborator. "Everything about her was East Tennessee and mountain, and I think that was the message she brought to Nashville." Nashville looks very different today from when Parton first stepped off that bus 62 years ago, but visitors can still trace Parton's path from her early days fresh out of Sevier County to her rise as a country music icon who never lost the Appalachian sound of home even as she became one of Nashville's biggest stars. On Music Row, the city's historic record-industry district, visitors can step inside RCA Studio B where a blue X marks "The Sweet Spot" where Parton recorded hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You – both of which she wrote on the same day. Nearby, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum is featuring Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, an exhibition spanning her career and featuring memorabilia like her Gibson five-string banjo and handwritten music drafts. A few blocks away, the historic Ryman Auditorium is where a 13-year-old Parton made her Grand Ole Opry debut in 1959 and earned three encores. Murals of Parton dot the city in her honour, museum exhibits display her stage costumes and in the wake of her passing, fans have left flowers on her star on the Music City Walk of Fame. Visiting Parton's Appalachia Nashville, however, was never the end of Parton's journey. The further her career carried her from the mountains to Nashville and eventually Hollywood, the more firmly she seemed to plant her roots at the centre of her story. In 1982, she told Barbara Walters in an interview about her dream of opening a "mountain Disneyland" in her Appalachian home region. More like this: Today, that "mountain Disneyland" is Dollywood, a major tourist destination in Sevier County that invites visitors into the version of Appalachia Parton spent her career sharing with the world. Beyond the thrill rides and water park are shows featuring Parton's music, some performed by members of her own family. But to Parton, Dollywood was also a way to give back to the mountains and the community that nurtured her. "I think we owe a lot to Dolly Parton for Tennessee tourism and the kind of goodwill that she's helped create for the state," says Dr Celeste Carruthers, an economics professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. According to Carruthers, Dollywood draws millions of visitors and supports tens of thousands of tourism-related jobs in Sevier County, generating an estimated $1.8bn in direct economic impact annually. But Parton's investment in her home region extends well beyond tourism. In 1995, she launched the Imagination Library through the Dollywood Foundation in tribute to her father, who never learned to read or write. The programme's mission was to put a book in the hands of every child in Sevier County, with it later expanding around the world. "We really feel there's a responsibility going forward, that it's about more than just a theme park," says Andrew Wexler, CEO of Herschend, the family-owned entertainment company that co-founded Dollywood with Parton. "It's about the principles and values that Dolly had of family and love, generosity, community, faith and the idea that people's best experiences are shared with the people that matter most to them." --

item.title: How to Boil Potatoes (and How Long to Boil Them)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.37
So many potato recipes start with the same instruction: “Boil the potatoes.” Simple enough—until you’re wondering whether to start them in cold or boiling water, how much salt to add, or how long the potatoes actually need to cook. The short version: Start potatoes in cold, well-salted water, bring it to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer until tender. That’s it! Depending on their size and what you’re making, the actual cooking time could range from 8–40 minutes. A baby potato destined for smashing needs far less time than a big chunk of russet headed for mashed potatoes. Want to know more? Here’s how to get it right every time. How to boil potatoes The essential rule for boiling potatoes: Start them in cold water. When you drop potatoes into water that’s already boiling, the outsides overcook before the centers turn tender. Starting them cold lets the potatoes and water heat up together so they cook more evenly. Ingredients - 2 lb. potatoes, scrubbed, prepared as desired (more on that in a minute) - 1 cup Diamond Crystal or ½ cup Morton kosher salt - Place 2 lb. potatoes, scrubbed, in a large pot. Baby, small, and medium potatoes can stay whole; cut large potatoes into evenly sized pieces. Peel them first if your recipe calls for it. - Cover the potatoes with 3 qt. cold water and add 1 cup Diamond Crystal or ½ cup Morton kosher salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, stirring occasionally. Reduce the heat to maintain a simmer and cook until the potatoes reach the desired tenderness (more on that below). - Drain in a colander and let cool for 10 minutes, or proceed as directed in your recipe. Potatoes are dense, so seasoning only the exterior after boiling won’t give you the same deeply seasoned result. For 3 quarts of cold water, we recommend 1 cup of Diamond Crystal or ½ cup of Morton kosher salt (Morton is denser than Diamond Crystal, so you need less). Most of that salt goes down the drain with the cooking water, but the concentrated salt bath gives the potatoes a chance to absorb the seasoning as they cook. The time it takes to boil potatoes depends primarily on their size and how you plan to use them. Small potatoes can be ready in less than 15 minutes; larger pieces destined for mashed potatoes, gnocchi, or dumplings may need 30 minutes or more. | How long to boil potatoes for: | Smashed Potatoes | Potato Salad | Mashed Potatoes | Gnocchi and Dumplings | |---|---|---|---|---| | Fingerling potatoes | 8–12 minutes | 15–20 minutes | n/a | n/a | | Baby potatoes | 8–12 minutes | 10–15 minutes | n/a | n/a | | Medium potatoes | 18–22 minutes | 20–25 minutes | 30–35 minutes | 30–35 minutes | | Large potatoes (cut into 2" cubes) | n/a | 15–20 min | 20–25 minutes | 35–40 minutes | Large potatoes should be cut before boiling so they cook evenly—a whole russet may still be firm in the center by the time its exterior is overcooked. The exact dimensions matter less than consistency: Cut the pieces roughly the same size, and they should finish cooking at about the same time. Baby and other small potatoes can generally be boiled whole. Consider these time ranges as guidelines rather than deadlines. Start checking your potatoes at the low end of the range and let their texture—not the timer—tell you when they’re ready. How to tell when boiled potatoes are done “Fork-tender” is the usual cue: A fork, cake tester, or paring knife should pierce the potato easily. Exactly how tender you want it depends on what you’re making. A knife or cake tester should slide easily into and out of the potato. You want the potatoes fully tender all the way through, without any firm or crunchy spots. A knife or tester should slide in easily but meet a little resistance on the way out. The potatoes should be tender without falling apart when you toss or dress them. The best potatoes for boiling You can boil just about any potato, but the best variety depends on what you plan to do with it afterward. Idaho, russet, and other high-starch potatoes cook up fluffy and readily break down with a ricer or food mill, making them a classic choice for mashed potatoes. They’re also more prone to becoming waterlogged if overcooked, so keep an eye on them. New potatoes, Red Bliss, fingerlings, and other waxy varieties have a dense texture and hold their shape particularly well after boiling. That makes them a good choice for potato salad, niçoise, and other dishes where you want distinct, intact pieces. Yukon Golds land somewhere between starchy and waxy potatoes, with enough starch to make a creamy mash but enough structure to hold their shape. They’re the Test Kitchen favorite for ultra-creamy, buttery mashed potatoes—and a reliable all-purpose choice. Boiled potato FAQs Do you need to peel potatoes before boiling? Not necessarily. Thin-skinned potatoes like Yukon Golds, red potatoes, fingerlings, and baby potatoes can be boiled with their skins on after a good scrub. Whether you peel thicker-skinned potatoes like russets depends on the dish you’re making; peel them when you want an especially smooth final texture. Can you boil potatoes whole? Yes. Baby, small, and medium potatoes can be boiled whole. Large potatoes should be cut into evenly sized pieces so their centers cook through before their exteriors become overdone. Can you overboil potatoes? Yes. Cook potatoes too long and they can become waterlogged or start falling apart. Starchy potatoes like russets are particularly prone to breaking down, while waxy varieties tend to hold their shape better. Start checking for doneness at the low end of the suggested cooking-time range. Editor’s note: This article was originally published online in June 2019. It has been expanded and updated for style with further reporting by Zoe Denenberg and Hannah Lee Leidy.

item.title: Parker House Rolls
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.93
With burnished tops, buttery layers, and a sprinkle of flaky sea salt, Parker House rolls are the classic American dinner roll. Created at Boston’s Parker House Hotel in the 19th century, the soft, fluffy yeast rolls are sometimes called pocketbook rolls due to their signature folded shape. Serve them alongside Thanksgiving turkey or holiday ham, then pry open any leftovers to slather with honey or jam for breakfast. Adapted from The Fannie Farmer Baking Book, this Parker House roll recipe is straightforward enough for novice bread bakers: The dough is easy to knead by hand (though a stand mixer works too). Brushing each piece with melted butter before folding creates the rolls’ characteristic shape, while a second swab after baking gives them their sheen. Parker House rolls FAQ What makes a Parker House roll different from a regular dinner roll? It’s all in the fold. Instead of shaping the dough into balls, Parker House rolls are shaped into rectangles, brushed with butter, and folded over themselves. The result is their distinctive pocketbook shape and a buttery seam that makes them easy to pull apart. Can I make Parker House rolls ahead of time? Yes. Dough can be mixed 8 hours ahead. Cover and refrigerate. Once shaped, the rolls can be covered and refrigerated for at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours before baking. You can also bake them earlier in the day. Remove them from the oven about 5 minutes before they are done (they should be puffed and cooked through but not yet golden). Finish baking when ready to serve. Why did my Parker House rolls turn out dense? Too much flour or insufficient rising can produce dense rolls. For the most accurate measurement, weigh the flour rather than scooping it by volume and let the dough rise until doubled in size before shaping. Unfortunately, overproofing can also create a dense roll. To get it just right, use the poke test to determine when your rolls are ready to bake. Can I freeze Parker House rolls? Yes. Freeze baked and then cooled Parker House rolls up to a month. Thaw and rewarm them in a low oven to restore their soft texture. A spritz of water on top of the rolls will keep them plush and prevent them from becoming too dark. You can also freeze the risen, unbaked rolls for up to a month. Bake straight from the freezer, adding about 5 minutes of extra cooking time. This recipe was adapted for style from ‘The Fannie Farmer Baking Book’ by Marion Cunningham. Buy the full book on Amazon or ThriftBooks. Recipe information - Total Time 55 minutes plus chilling - Yield Makes 36 Ingredients 1 1 ¼ 3 1½ 1 3½ 4 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) and ¼ cup warm water (110°–115°) in a small bowl; let sit until foamy, about 5 minutes. Step 2Heat 1 cup whole milk in a small saucepan over medium until just warm. Combine ¼ cup vegetable shortening, 3 Tbsp. sugar, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Pour in warm milk, whisking constantly to blend and break up shortening into small clumps (it may not melt completely). Add yeast mixture and 1 large egg, room temperature, and whisk to combine. Add 3½ cups (438 g) all-purpose flour and stir vigorously with a wooden spoon until a dough forms. Step 3Turn dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead with lightly floured hands until smooth, about 5 minutes. Lightly coat a large bowl with vegetable oil; transfer dough to bowl and turn to coat. Cover loosely with plastic wrap. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in size, about 1½ hours. Do Ahead: Dough can be mixed 8 hours ahead. Cover and refrigerate, dough will rise more slowly as it chills. Step 4Lightly brush a 13x9" baking dish with some of the 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted. Punch down dough; divide into 4 equal pieces. Working one at a time, roll out pieces on a lightly floured surface into 12x6" rectangles. Cut each rectangle lengthwise into three 2"-wide strips; cut each strip crosswise to make three 4x2" rectangles (9 total per piece). Brush half of each rectangle (about 2x2") with melted butter, then fold unbuttered side up and over buttered side, leaving ¼" uncovered at the end. Starting in a corner of prepared dish, place rolls, flat side down, so folded edge is against a short side of the dish. Add rolls side by side to form a long row. Repeat with remaining rolls, facing folded edge toward rolls in previous row, until you have 4 rows total. Brush tops of rolls with melted butter, loosely cover with plastic wrap, and chill at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours. Step 5Preheat oven to 350°. Bake rolls until golden and puffed, 25–35 minutes. Brush with more melted butter and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Let cool slightly before serving. Editor’s note: This Parker House roll recipe was first printed in the 1984 edition of the ‘Fannie Farmer Baking Book,’ and appeared in our November 2012 Thanksgiving issue. Head this way for more of our best Thanksgiving recipes →

item.title: How to Build a Knife Set
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.63
For years we’ve been convinced that the best knife sets are made, knife by knife, by considering what you cook, how you cook, and the size of your space. Knife sets have their place, but really, we think of them as a stopgap as you assemble your own personal knife roll. Building a knife collection is extremely personal—the look, feel, and utility of each knife will read differently from person to person. And after all my time testing knives, the blades that became my go-tos have surprised me. I never expected a nakiri knife to be one of my daily drivers, and I never expected myself to own different styles of chef’s knives for different tasks.
