Not everyone is going to keep a gyuto around just to slice meat, but I was able to perfectly cut the flatiron steak I grilled the other week into thin strips that almost melted in my mouth because I had one. So this guide walks you through all the different categories of knives we’ve tested and how necessary they’re likely to be in your kitchen. Even though there’s a case to be made that you only need three knives, I think you should give yourself the opportunity to be surprised by some of the incredibly useful blades out there, just like I was. The essential knife You’re going to need a chef’s knife. Full stop. Many people prefer the durability of a Western chef’s knife, but some people might want the precision and steel quality of a Japanese chef’s knife. Most people will pick one or the other, but it’s also common for many home cooks to have one of each. Chef’s Knife The chef’s knife is the do-it-all star of any professional or home kitchen. This versatile blade can chop, slice, dice, even peel and core if you’re in a pinch. Generally defined by its tall heel, curved belly, and fine point, a good chef’s knife should be one of the first purchases you make for your kitchen. But because they have some of the most varied designs in the knife world, my full review of chef’s knives breaks down a large variety of top picks to help you find exactly what type of chef’s knife works best for you. Western chef’s knives tend to be sturdy, heavy, and made with slightly softer and more forgiving steel; Japanese chef’s knives (known as a gyuto), on the other hand, are designed to be sharp, nimble, and excellent slicers. Gyutos have finer edges made from harder steel, which helps them stay sharper longer but also makes them more vulnerable to chipping. If you’re looking for more precision and don’t mind a bit more maintenance, you might snag a Japanese chef’s knife for your daily use. Important knives you’ll use constantly: No matter how good your chef’s knife is, it won’t cut bread as well as a serrated knife. It will also feel ungainly for peeling or coring. That’s work for a paring knife. Bread knife Serrated knives cut bread without squishing it, which chef’s knives really can’t pull off. The best serrated knives are sharp, long enough to tackle big loaves, and sturdy enough to cut through a defined crust. They’re also useful for delicate tasks, like slicing tomatoes, and their overall size can help with big tasks, like splitting or peeling a watermelon. Paring knife Paring knives are great for coring and peeling, and their short blades give the user more control over small movements than a full-size chef’s knife or even a mid-size utility knife. They’re also useful for ultra-small tasks like slicing and hulling berries. But not all paring knives are designed the same, some have longer handles, some have narrow blades, some really can’t be sharpened. We tested and reviewed a wide variety of shapes, sizes, and price points to help you snag the type of paring knife you’ll find most useful. Useful knives you may not own: Adding a mid-size specialized knife to your kit, like a santoku, nakiri, or petty knife, brings more versatility while taking some workload off your other knives (meaning they’ll stay sharper longer). Most home cooks won’t need all three; most knife enthusiasts couldn’t imagine their collection without them. Santoku knife Named after the “three virtues,” santoku knives are great at chopping, slicing, and dicing. Their shape takes inspiration from a trio of other knives: the straight edge of the nakiri, the overall length of a petty knife, and the slight curve of a gyuto. They also have extremely pronounced sheep’s foot tips for precision point work. Santoku knives are great for a large variety of tasks and are often prized for their daily use for things like slicing cheese, cutting an apple, breaking down an onion, or chopping herbs. Nakiri knife Nakiri knives are traditional Japanese vegetable cleavers that feature a sturdy spine and a straight edge. These knives are great for breaking down tough vegetables like sweet potatoes and hard-skinned squash, and the straight edge is ideal for matchsticking carrots and cucumbers because the entire edge cuts all the way through to the cutting board (unlike the curved edge of a chef’s knife). If you have a fine-edged gyuto for an everyday chef’s knife, you might want a nakiri with its sturdy spine and heftier weight to handle some tougher jobs. Petty knife Petty knives are small Japanese utility knives that are great for precision work and slicing. Shaped like a gyuto, but with blades just a smidge longer than a paring knife, a petty knife is great for tasks like breaking down a whole chicken because they can easily fit between joints. The length of the blade gives you more freedom to tackle everyday tasks, and while they’re ideal for small tasks like dicing a shallot or cutting hard cheese, their nimbleness also makes them adept at slicing a steak. Nice-to-have knives: You may not ever need a heavy-duty meat cleaver, but you might be surprised at how versatile a Chinese cleaver is. Neither is essential in a kitchen, but both are great to have on hand when you need one. Same goes for the boning knife: You might not always bring home an entire striped bass, but on the occasion you do, you’ll be glad you have a boning knife on hand. Meat cleavers and Chinese cleavers Heavy-duty cleavers tend to be blunter than most knives, but that’s on purpose. Their edges are designed to crack through bone, so don’t expect them to slice through a delicate steak easily. Chinese cleavers, on the other hand, are thin and sharp, designed for precision push cuts. Our review breaks down the difference between the two in detail, while also showcasing why you might need one or the other more than you think. Boning knife Many home cooks get by just fine asking their butcher counter to portion their meat and fish, but more intrepid folks might find that breaking down a whole chicken, filleting a fresh-caught sea bream, or portioning a T-bone gives them more control over the meal they want to cook. A good boning knife is nimble, sharp, and easy to maneuver—it may be a specialized knife, but it excels at the task it was designed for. And don't forget… You’ll probably want to pick up a knife sharpener and honing rod to keep your knives pristine.

item.title: Onigiri (Japanese Rice Balls)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.58
Stuffed with savory fillings and wrapped in crisp nori, Japanese rice balls called onigiri are made for eating on the go. A convenience-store staple in Japan, they’re just as handy tucked into a lunch box or picnic basket. The key to onigiri that hold their shape is properly cooked Japanese short-grain rice. Rinsing and soaking the rice helps it cook evenly; shaping it while still slightly warm helps the grains stick together. Use damp, salted hands to prevent sticking—no rice cooker or onigiri mold required. This version offers three fillings: creamy tuna mayo, tart and salty umeboshi (pickled plums), or spicy kimchi. Once you’ve got the technique down, feel free to experiment with cooked salmon, spicy tuna, cod roe, leftover chicken salad, or crab meat. Just avoid anything too wet, which can make the rice balls difficult to shape. Onigiri FAQs What kind of rice is best for onigiri? Japanese short-grain rice, often labeled sushi rice at US supermarkets, is the best choice. When cooked, the grains cling together enough for the onigiri to hold their shape. Long-grain rice, such as jasmine or basmati, won’t hold together as well. How do you keep onigiri from falling apart? Shape the onigiri while the rice is still warm, using firm but gentle pressure to pack the grains together. Keep the remaining rice covered as you work so it doesn’t cool or dry out, and wet your hands with the salted water in the recipe to prevent sticking. What can you put inside onigiri? This recipe offers options including tuna mayo, umeboshi, and kimchi, but cooked salmon, spicy tuna, cod roe, leftover chicken salad, or crab meat are all fair game. Whatever you choose, avoid excessively wet fillings, which can make the onigiri harder to shape. Can you make onigiri ahead of time? Yes. These onigiri can be made up to two days ahead. Wrap each one tightly and refrigerate. For crisp nori, leave it off until you’re ready to eat; otherwise it will soften as it absorbs moisture from the rice. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 10 minutes (plus soaking) - Yield Makes 12–16 Ingredients 2 3 1 2 1 4 ⅓ ¾ ¼ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place 2 cups sushi rice in a large bowl and pour in cold water to cover by 2"–3". Gently swish around with your hands to rinse, then drain. Repeat process until water is almost clear (about 3 more times). Pour cold water over rice to cover by 1" and let soak 30 minutes (this will help the grains cook more evenly). Drain well in a fine-mesh sieve. Step 2Combine rice and 2½ cups water in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring occasionally. Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer until water is absorbed, 12–14 minutes. Remove from heat and let rice sit (still covered) 15 minutes. This will allow rice to steam and become tender. Uncover and gently fluff rice with a fork. Let sit until cool enough to handle but still warm. Step 3Meanwhile, cut three 8½x7½" toasted nori sheets into 3x1¼" strips with kitchen shears; set aside. Step 4Prepare the fillings. Mix one 5-oz. can tuna, drained, 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and 1 tsp. soy sauce in a small bowl to combine. Place 4 umeboshi (Japanese pickled plums) on a cutting board. Working 1 at a time, press a chef’s knife against fruit until pit is exposed; pull out and discard. Set fruit aside (no need to chop). Working over the sink and using your hands, squeeze liquid out of ⅓ cup Napa cabbage kimchi; chop into small pieces. Step 5Place 1 cup water in a small bowl and stir in ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Dip your hands into salted water, then scoop a little less than ⅓ cup rice into 1 hand. Form into a thick disk 3"–4" in diameter (keep remaining rice in pot covered). Create a small indentation in the center and add 1–2 tsp. tuna mixture or kimchi or a whole umeboshi. Mold rice up and over filling to create a sphere (filling should not be visible), then press firmly with index finger and thumb to form into a triangle. Place on cutting board or a baking sheet. Repeat with remaining rice and fillings, dipping your hands in salt water each time. (You’ll have extra tuna—save it for making a tuna salad sandwich or spooning onto crackers.) Step 6Place ¼ cup furikake or toasted sesame seeds on a small plate. Wrap bottom of each onigiri with a strip of reserved nori, then roll remaining exposed sides of onigiri in furikake. Do Ahead: Onigiri can be made 2 days ahead. Wrap tightly and chill. Editor’s note: This onigiri recipe was first published in September 2020. Head this way for our editors’ favorite ways to use leftover rice →

item.title: Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf Cake
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.48
Something about having a loaf of lemon poppy seed cake on the counter makes you feel like the star of a sitcom. As if you might drink your coffee from a thick-walled mug and scratch your cat under the chin just before you leave for work, a slice of said cake in your hand as you dash to the bus stop. Whether that rings true or not, know that this is a main character cake, worthy of its own show. Tall and hefty with a gentle tang and the crunchy burst of poppy seeds in every bite, it is completely unfussy yet still elegant. The bright loaf cake sings of sunny lemons thanks to the zest as well as juice. With the addition of oil and the insulating cap of snow-white glaze, it keeps nicely for a couple of days. Find more cheerful bakes here: Chocolate Guinness Cake; Apple Cider Doughnut Loaf Cake; and Preserved Lemon Tea Cake. Recipe information - Total Time 1½ hours - Yield one 9x5" loaf Ingredients Cake 2¼ 1½ 1½ ¾ 1½ 5 2 2 3 ¾ ¼ Glaze and Assembly 1 1–2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - CakeStep 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Generously coat a 9x5" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray or unsalted butter, room temperature; line with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Whisk 2¼ cups (281 g) all-purpose flour, 1½ tsp. baking powder, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Step 2Beat zest of 3 large lemons, ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, 5 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract on medium speed in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with paddle attachment until light and creamy, about 5 minutes. Step 3Add 3 large eggs, one at a time, beating after each addition to combine before adding the next one (batter may look curdled at this point). Scrape down sides of bowl with a rubber spatula, add half of dry ingredients, and beat on low speed just to combine. Add ¾ cup whole milk and remaining dry ingredients and mix until batter is smooth and creamy, about 1 minute. Add ¼ cup poppy seeds; scrape down bottom and sides of bowl and fold batter with spatula a few times to ensure it’s evenly mixed. Step 4Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. (If your pan looks more than three quarters full, transfer excess batter to a greased small ovenproof container and bake alongside cake as a cook’s treat). Generously coat the blade of a small paring knife with nonstick spray; run knife lengthwise through center of batter to make a shallow cut (this will help cake split cleanly along line as it bakes rather than cracking randomly). Step 5Bake cake until golden brown all over, it springs back when gently pressed, and a tester inserted into the center comes out with only a few moist crumbs attached, 60–65 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and let cake cool slightly in pan, about 15 minutes. Step 6Run a small offset spatula around edges of cake to loosen, then invert out onto rack. Turn cake right side up and let cool completely. - Glaze and AssemblyStep 7Stir 1 cup (110 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, and a pinch of kosher salt in small bowl, adding up to 1 Tbsp. additional lemon juice as needed, until thick but pourable. Pour glaze over cake, letting it drip down sides. Top with poppy seeds and thin strips of lemon zest if using while glaze is still wet; let sit until glaze is set, at least 45 minutes. Do Ahead: Cake can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

item.title: 53 Thanksgiving Recipes We Turn to Year After Year
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.05
Preparing and hosting a literal feast is hard enough without scouring the internet for the best Thanksgiving recipes—so we’ve done the work for you. A traditional Thanksgiving dinner might include roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes and gravy, cranberry sauce, sweet potatoes, green beans or brussels sprouts, dinner rolls, and pumpkin, apple, or pecan pie. You’ll find some version of all of those here, alongside the recipes we’re especially excited to put on the table right now. If turkey is nonnegotiable, we’ve got roasted, grilled, and smoked options, plus guides to turkey cooking times and carving the bird. Prefer a vegetarian Thanksgiving? There are plenty of meatless mains and sides too. And if 53 choices sound like about 48 too many, our Classic Thanksgiving Menu maps out the whole meal for you. Of course, the turkey is only the beginning. Browse our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes, then round out the feast with appetizers, cocktails, pies, cakes, and other desserts. And when the day is done, our leftover turkey recipes ensure the feast keeps giving.

item.title: Sweet and Tangy Collard Greens
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.68
Collard greens have deep roots in Southern cooking. They’re a fixture on New Year’s Day, when eating greens is said to bring prosperity in the year ahead. Chef Julia Sullivan of Henrietta Red in Nashville serves them alongside black-eyed peas every January 1. “It’s something my mom has always done, and I think my grandparents, too,” she says. “It’s a superstitious thing.” Sullivan’s collard greens get their savory, subtly smoky flavor from bacon, onion, garlic, and red pepper flakes. They simmer until silky-tender in just under an hour, then get a sweet-tart finish from apple cider vinegar and a little sugar. This recipe intentionally leans tangy. If you like your collard greens less acidic, start with 2 Tbsp. vinegar instead of the full ¼ cup, then add more to taste. Collard greens FAQs How do you clean and prep collard greens? Remove the tough center ribs and stems. Next, stack the leaves, roll them up, and slice them crosswise into 1"-thick strips. Dunk the prepped collard greens into a large bowl (or sink!) filled with water. Swish the leaves around to loosen the grit and let them sit for a few minutes. Remove the greens from their container (don’t pour them out or the grit will get back on the leaves) and shake to remove excess liquid. There is no need to dry the collard greens for this recipe; a little bit of water helps them steam and wilt down. Why do you add vinegar to collard greens? Vinegar balances collard greens’ earthy, slightly bitter flavor and cuts through the richness of the bacon and broth. Adding it near the end of cooking keeps its flavor bright. This recipe calls for ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, but you can start with half that amount and adjust to taste. Can I make these collard greens without bacon? Yes. The bacon is optional, so you can simply leave it out, or trade it for beef or turkey bacon. For vegetarian collard greens, also swap the chicken broth for water or vegetable broth and add savory depth with a spoonful of miso paste. What other types of greens work with this recipe? Any sturdy cooking greens can work here, but expect differences in flavor and cooking time. Mustard greens and turnip greens are equally beloved in the South; either will make a slightly sharper, more peppery batch of greens. Kale is also a fine alternative. More delicate Swiss chard will become tender much faster, so reduce the cooking time accordingly. Recipe information - Total Time 55 minutes - Yield 8 servings Ingredients 3 4 1 4 1 3 3 ¼ 2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 4 oz. slab bacon, finely chopped, if using, and cook, stirring occasionally, until some fat begins to collect in pot and bacon starts to look shiny, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, and cook, stirring occasionally, until golden and softened, 5–7 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Step 2Add 3 lb. collard greens (about 3 bunches), ribs and stems removed, leaves sliced crosswise 1" thick, to pot a large handful at a time, letting greens wilt slightly after each addition before adding more. Add 3 cups low-sodium chicken broth or water, bring to a simmer, and cook, stirring often, until greens are wilted and have lost about half of their volume, about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low, partially cover pot, and simmer gently, stirring occasionally, until greens are tender and liquid is almost completely evaporated, 25–30 minutes. Step 3Stir ¼ cup apple cider vinegar and 2 tsp. sugar into collard greens and cook until sugar dissolves, about 1 minute; season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Editor’s note: This recipe for collard greens was first published in our December 2017 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more ideas for your New Year’s table →

item.title: Cottage Cheese Lasagna
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.68
Cottage cheese lasagna skeptics, hear us out. Unlike ricotta, which can turn chalky, small-curd, whole-milk cottage cheese stays moist through the long bake. And when mixed with nutty Parmesan, melty Fontina, eggs, and garlic, it makes an exceptionally creamy lasagna filling. A combination of ground beef and hot Italian sausage brings plenty of flavor and richness to the meat sauce, while tomato paste and Worcestershire sauce give canned tomatoes long-simmered depth without the long simmer. Keep the sauce loose: That extra moisture is what cooks the regular dried lasagna noodles right in the baking dish. (Yep, no boiling required.) This may not be nonna’s classic (we’ve got BA’s Best Lasagna for that), but it’s deeply savory, exceptionally cheesy, and considerably easier to assemble. Cottage cheese lasagna FAQs What kind of cottage cheese should I use? Whole-milk cottage cheese is nonnegotiable. Lighter versions can make the lasagna watery and less flavorful. We prefer small-curd for texture, but large-curd works just fine if that’s what you have. Read more about our staff favorite cottage cheese brand: Do you have to boil lasagna noodles before baking? Regular dried lasagna noodles go directly into the baking dish—no boiling or soaking required. The relatively loose tomato sauce provides enough moisture to cook the noodles until al dente as the lasagna bakes. Can I make cottage cheese lasagna ahead of time? Yes. The baked lasagna can be refrigerated for up to 2 days. Let it cool completely, cover loosely with foil, and reheat, covered, in a 325° oven for 30–45 minutes, or until warmed through. You can also make the meat sauce up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate it in an airtight container; there’s no need to reheat it before assembling the lasagna, but you may need to add a few minutes to the baking time. You can also freeze the assembled, unbaked lasagna for up to 2 months. Thaw in the refrigerator overnight and then bake as directed. Can I use ground turkey? Absolutely. Swap the ground beef for ground dark meat turkey and the pork sausage for Italian-style turkey sausage. Because poultry is leaner, add an extra drizzle of olive oil if the pan looks dry. Recipe information - Total Time 2 hours (plus sitting time) - Yield 8–12 servings Ingredients 1 1 8 2 8 3 2 1 1 ¼ 1 2 6 12 2 24 12 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. ground beef (20% fat) and 8 oz. hot Italian sausage, casings removed, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until well browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer meat to a medium bowl, leaving fat behind. Step 2Add 2 large onions, finely chopped, 6 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to same pot; if pot looks dry, add up to 1 Tbsp. more oil. Cook, stirring often, until onions are translucent and golden around the edges, 8–10 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste and 1 Tbsp. dried oregano; cook, stirring constantly, until paste is brick red and beginning to stick to bottom of pot, 5–8 minutes. Return meat to pot. Step 3Add one 28-oz. can plus one 14.5-oz. can crushed tomatoes, ¼ cup Worcestershire sauce, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper to pot. Bring to a simmer, stirring occasionally and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pot. Remove from heat and stir in 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Taste tomato sauce and season with more salt if needed. Step 4Toss 12 oz. Fontina cheese, grated (about 3 cups), and remaining 4 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 2 cups), in a large bowl to combine; measure out 1 cup cheese and set aside for topping. Add 2 large eggs, 24 oz. whole-milk cottage cheese, and remaining 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper to remaining cheese in bowl. Mix vigorously with a wooden spoon until combined. Step 5Arrange 3 regular dried lasagna noodles in a single layer in a 13x9" baking dish. (If noodles are long, arrange parallel to long sides of baking dish; if noodles are short, arrange parallel to short sides of baking dish. Don’t worry about any gaps—noodles will swell as they cook.) Spread 1½ cups tomato sauce over noodles. Scatter one third of Fontina mixture evenly over sauce (mixture will be stiff; use hands to break off small pieces and scatter over sauce). Starting with another layer of noodles, repeat process, creating 4 layers of noodles in total and ending with a layer of tomato sauce. Top lasagna with reserved cheese. Step 6Place baking dish on a large rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake lasagna until sauce is bubbling around the edges, top is golden brown, and noodles are al dente (insert a skewer into center of lasagna to check), 75–85 minutes. Let sit at least 15 minutes and up to 45 minutes before serving. Do Ahead: Lasagna can be baked 2 days ahead. Let cool completely; cover loosely with foil and chill. Reheat, covered, in a 325° oven until warmed through, 30–45 minutes. Editor’s note: This cottage cheese lasagna recipe was first printed in September 2023. It has been updated for style.

item.title: Lasagna-Vibes Zucchini Skillet
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.56
For years, one of my go-to dinners in the summer was zucchini lasagna, where zucchini is used in place of noodles. It’s delightful, but it’s also very labor-intensive, requiring you to slice the zucchini into long, thin planks, salt each individual plank, wipe each individual plank, and then layer the zucchini “noodles” with ricotta, sauce, and mozzarella. Now I have far too many children to be salting individual planks of zucchini—so I make this. It’s a dump-and-go skillet meal that has all of those favorite flavors in a way, way quicker and easier format. Read More: Finding My Way Back to the Kitchen After Giving Birth Recipe information - Total Time 15 minutes - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 2 1 3 1¾ 1 2 1 ½ 1 4 4 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground turkey and cook, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until mostly cooked through with only a little pink remaining, about 4 minutes. Add 3 medium zucchini (about 20 oz.), halved lengthwise, sliced crosswise ⅛" thick, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt; season with freshly ground black pepper. Increase heat to high and cook, stirring often, until meat is cooked through and no longer pink and zucchini is tender, 6–8 minutes. Step 2Reduce heat to medium and stir in one 14.5-oz. can tomato sauce, 2 tsp. Italian seasoning, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. onion powder, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and half of 1 cup thinly sliced basil leaves. Taste zucchini mixture and season with more salt and pepper if needed. Swirl in spoonfuls of 4 oz. whole-milk ricotta (about ½ cup), then sprinkle 4 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over. Reduce heat to low, cover pan, and cook until mozzarella is melted, about 4 minutes. Step 3Top zucchini mixture with remaining basil and crushed red pepper flakes (if using) to serve.

item.title: What Are Budget-Friendly Recipes I Can Make for My 60-Person Wedding?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.39
There are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here. My 60-person wedding is going to be a DIY affair at a small inn-turned-Airbnb. The big meals are going to be handled by professionals, but there’s a couple meals—Friday breakfast and lunch, Saturday breakfast—that we’re hoping to cobble together ourselves in the inn’s commercial kitchen. While we regularly host groups of 20ish at our apartment, 60 people feels like an entirely different beast. How can we (simply! not-too-expensively!) scale up and make sure everyone is well-fed? We’re nominating some friends to help prep and serve food for each meal, but where do we start with the menu? How do you think about how much food you need? —I Do Congrats are in order! Thanks for writing in about your big day—I’m honored. This is a great size for a guest list. My husband and I invited a similar range (scandalous in pre-pandemic times) and the room was overflowing, bountiful, raucous at times. The funny thing about a small wedding is…it’s still a lot of people. And you’re right, it’s an entirely different beast than your everyday dinner party. I applaud you for tapping in friends. Delegation is—begging my editor to let me keep italics here—of the utmost importance. Not just because, unless you are a Top Chef contestant, feeding 60 people should not be a one-person endeavor. But also because, ahem, you’re the one getting married! As corny as it sounds, I hope that the top item on your to-do list is: Have fun. Everything else can wait, or should be someone else’s problem. Okay, speech over, taking a sip of pét-nat, onto the recipes! Breakfasts Not actually a recipe: My family has a reunion at the Shore every summer and our foolproof feed-a-crowd breakfast is bagels plus fixings. Can’t be beat. BA Bake Club has a wonderful homemade bagel recipe, which you should save for later and not use for this occasion. Now is the time to buy and assemble: bagels (if they’re fresh, skip toasting; if not, broil on a sheet pan); a few flavors of whipped cream cheese; smoked salmon (skip if this breaks the budget); sliced tomatoes and onion; capers; pickles. Optional fruit alongside. The math: - 1¼ bagels per person = 75 bagels - 1½ oz. cream cheese per person = 90 oz. (12 eight-oz. containers) - 2 oz. lox per person = 7½ lb. (Costco is your friend) - ⅓ tomato per person = 20 tomatoes - ⅙ onion per person = 10 onions - 1 tsp. capers per person = 1 giant jar - Who can say how many cornichons per person = 4 jars Ham-and-Cheese Croissant Bake. A charming, crowd-pleasing dish that you can assemble in advance, then bake the next day. Serve with some store-bought prewashed mixed greens splashed with Three-Minute Vinaigrette. Simple and chic. Mix the custard in two batches, each in a humongous bowl. (I have one of these and, honestly, can’t recommend it enough. Sure, it only comes in handy two-ish times a year, and my family makes fun of me for it, but when you need it, nothing else will do.) Bake in disposable aluminum pans. The math (recipe times eight for 64 servings): - 80 croissants (cheap supermarket ones! Lidl is known for them) - 3 lb. Gruyère (could do cheddar for a cheaper alt) - 3 lb. ham - 40 eggs - 8 pints heavy cream - 1 cup Dijon mustard - 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt* - 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper - 2 tsp. freshly grated nutmeg - 2 handfuls thinly sliced chives *Please get Diamond Crystal for this measurement or adjust the quantity for another brand. The type of salt always matters, but especially so in large batches. Lunches Olive Bar Pasta Salad. As my colleague Rebecca Firkser writes, “The beauty of this pasta salad is its flexibility.” In your case, I would actually avoid the supermarket olive bar; it can get pricey in large quantities. Instead, find a Trader Joe’s or Costco and make the most of their shelf-stable antipasti offerings: marinated artichokes, roasted peppers, pitted olives, white beans, etc. More cost effective and just as yum. If you have an ambitious pal who wants to grill or sear chicken for a crowd, that would be a nice addition, estimating ½ breast per serving, or 30 breasts total. But not needed by any means! The math (recipe times 10 for 60 servings): - 20 garlic cloves - 5 cups finely chopped oil-packed sun-dried tomatoes - 2½ cups sun-dried tomato oil (cut with olive oil if you don’t have enough) - 3 cups plus 2 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, plus more to taste - 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (optional) - 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper - 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt - 10 (1-lb.) boxes short pasta - 5 lb. small mozzarella balls or torn mozzarella - 10 quarts (40 cups) mixed antipasti (see above) Marinated Mixed Beans. I can hear someone scoffing in the distance at the audacity of the suggestion that you serve your beloved guests canned beans. But hear me out. They are delicious and cheap, can be assembled days in advance, and can confidently anchor an unfussy menu. Serve the beans in the same bowl linked above (see? Already coming in handy again), along with: crusty sliced bread; one to three cheeses (burrata, Brie, whatever strikes your fancy); soft-boiled eggs; olives and pickles; maybe some charcuterie. Nosh-y and fun. The math (recipe times 15—gasp—for 1 cup per person): - 15 shallots, finely chopped (use a food processor if you have one) - 2¾ cups plus 1 Tbsp. white wine vinegar, plus more to taste - 7½ cups finely chopped tender herbs (again with the food processor) - 5 cups olive oil - 30 (15.5-oz.) cans beans (bride’s pick!) - 5 Tbsp. Aleppo-style pepper or gochugaru - Kosher salt, to taste Drinks For breakfast, get some travel boxes of joe from a nearby coffee shop and call it a day. For either lunch: If one of your friends (read: not you) wants to go the extra mile, set up a vermouth-spritz bar with: bottles of rogue and blanc vermouth; cans of seltzer; lots of ice; lemon and lime wedges. Celebratory but won’t have everyone sloshed in the middle of the day. Readers, what’s the best wedding food you’ve ever had? (Yes, sure, it can be from your own wedding. But only if you’re telling the truth!) Share in the comments. Warmly, Emma Questions may be lightly edited for clarity, length, and style.

item.title: The Great Date Boom is Here
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.92
There's nothing the internet loves more than a trendy ingredient. A few years ago, tinned fish became the It girl of the proverbial pantry, inspiring folks to swap their cheese boards for brinier, braver "seacuteries." Then cottage cheese blew up. Creators on TikTok and Reels proved that the creamy breakfast staple could be whipped, baked, blended, braised, and even frozen and churned for a delicious, protein-packed snack. Now, in 2026, we've seemingly reached peak pickle, with pickle-flavored everything from lip balms to (yes, even) lube. But the newest snack darling is one of the oldest ingredients in the world: the date. We saw it firsthand during Pantry Awards judging, when date-based products started landing in our submissions pile in numbers we hadn't seen before. These fiber-filled fruits are having a moment, in new and unexpected ways. Sour date snacks, date-sweetened boxed cakes, date-based candies and syrups, even the world's first soft drink made from dates—the primordial fruit is being reimagined for modern times, and people love it. "Consumers are starting to see dates as more than just a traditional dried fruit," says Amanda Sains-Harris, vice president of marketing for the date-based snack brand Joolies. Sains-Harris explains that the date boom has been a long time coming: Dates have been gaining popularity on social media and at industry trade shows for years. Now the fruits are flying off shelves. The category is up 24.1 percent in conventional grocery channels through June 2026, she says, citing point-of-sale data from the market-intelligence platform SPINS. As with cottage-cheese ice cream and tinned-fish cheese boards, folks seem to be looking for a healthy snack that still tastes good. Cardboard protein bars and chemical-tasting sodas are a thing of the past. "[Dates] check a lot of boxes without feeling overly engineered," Sains-Harris says. "Consumers also don't necessarily want to choose between better-for-you and indulgent anymore. They want both. Dates naturally live in that sweet spot." Grace Finerman founded Date Smarter!, which makes decadent chocolate-covered date caramels (and won one of our 2026 Pantry Awards, BTW). She agrees that consumers are seeking out healthier alternatives to sugary snacks—but they don't want zero-sugar, either. "Five years ago people were really turning to stevia," Finerman says. "I think the pendulum has kind of switched to people now wanting not cane sugar, but something sweet that's not processed." Despite their sticky sweetness, she says, dates are naturally low-glycemic. They're also high in fiber (6.7 to 8 grams per 100 grams), which is a tempting proposition in the age of GLP-1s and fiber-maxxing. And they make great fuel, especially when filled with protein-packed nut butters. "We actually have a large customer base of endurance athletes, professional and collegiate athletes, and overall fitness enthusiasts," says Sophia Karbowski, co-founder of Realsy, which specializes in date snacks stuffed with different nut butters. "The natural combination of carbs, sugar, and fiber in dates—plus a bit of added protein and fat from the natural nut butter filling—is the perfect source of clean energy athletes are looking for." Dates are also incredibly versatile, which makes them attractive to brands, too. On their own, the dried fruits are indulgent. But wrap 'em in bacon or stuff 'em with something sweet, and they're practically heaven. Since they're so sticky, they make excellent binders. Mashed together à la the viral peanut butter date bark that's taken over TikTok, or blended into a paste, they hold nuts, fruits, and other ingredients together. And when they're dried and powdered, they make an excellent refined-sugar substitute in baking mixes, syrups, and more. "We [Date Smarter!] use date powder, which is when you take a date that's dehydrated and run it through a processor," says Finerman. "We make all our caramel with that." Food trends come and go, but these brands are all betting that dates are here to stay (and given that they've been around since literally Mesopotamia, we think so, too). Karbowski expects to see dates on labels across the whole grocery store, from beverages to baking mixes. Sains-Harris wants to push the boundaries of where the fruits can go, and she's already getting creative: In May 2026, Joolies launched Date Sours, which swap the traditional buttery fillings for flavors like sour blue raspberry and cherry cola. "We always say dates are 'the original palm tree candy,'" says Sains-Harris. "And I think they're finally getting the spotlight they deserve." Whatever happens, we're here for it.

item.title: 5 Easy Ways Our Editors Turn Store-Bought Gnocchi Into Dinner
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.80
Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month it’s all about shelf-stable gnocchi. You would never expect an unassuming pouch of store-bought gnocchi, tucked tautly in plastic, to be good. But it is! The little potato dumplings have a pleasantly chew and just enough earthy savoriness to make them feel like more than a pantry fallback. The trick is how it’s made. Most shelf-stable gnocchi starts with dehydrated potato flakes, which give each dumpling a consistent texture and make the product stable enough to be stashed away in your pantry. A clever little bit of food engineering. And there’s no shortage of ways to put this ingredient to work. Stir-fry gnocchi in a hot skillet until they crisp up. Plop them into creamy sauces, where they bob along like buoys. Roast them alongside veg for a one-and-done dinner. There’s a whole lot this humble little pouch can do. Read on for how our editors cook with store-bought gnocchi at home. This Crispy Gnocchi Caprese is a staple in my household. Oddly enough, the last time I made it, I could only find the mini shelf-stable gnocchi in my grocery store. Who knew that even existed? Not me. Because of their small size, the little dots of pasta cooked up quicker than the standard ones, which means dinner was ready in no time. I used a haul of Sun Golds and cherry tomatoes, plus balls of mozzarella and torn basil dressed in bracing vinegar and fruity olive oil. Shoveling into my mouth with a spoon was the only correct way to eat. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking I love busting out shelf-stable gnocchi anytime I need to round out a meal with a carb and don’t want to make rice or pasta. While boiling them and tossing them in sauce is great, I also like to roast them on a sheet-pan so the outside gets crisp while the centers stay pillowy. You don’t have to schlep out a pot, don’t have to wait for water to boil, and you can snuggle them up next to proteins and veggies so everything cooks at once. My current favorite combo is sausage and broccoli rabe; the fat from the sausage sizzles the pasta while the broccoli rabe adds a peppery bite. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor I bought my first package of shelf-stable gnocchi to make a sheet-pan recipe that everyone in the office couldn’t stop talking about. And wow did it upend everything I’d assumed about the premade pasta. It now ends up in my shopping cart more often than not. But what a revelation trying former staffer Kendra Vaculin’s Gnocchi-Leek Soup With Greens still was. So enchanted by the crispy texture the oven provided, I’d entirely missed out on the plushy goodness of these little dumplings in soup. They’re the perfect addition to this weeknight-friendly dinner, adding heft and chew to an otherwise bright meal. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor Many, if not most, of my meals during the week are sheet-pan dinners. I love being able to toss something in the oven, then forget about it. Store-bought gnocchi is perfect for this treatment, and you don’t even need a recipe. Just preheat the oven to 400° or 425°. Dump a bag of gnocchi onto a sheet pan along with your vegetable of choice; say, broccoli florets, chopped bell peppers and onions, or halved brussels sprouts. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and sprinkle of salt and pepper. Roast until the gnocchi are browned and the vegetables are tender. Add some melty cheese on top—funky raclette is my vote here. Keep baking (or even broil) until the cheese melts into gooey puddles. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director The first time I consumed vacuum-packed gnocchi was in 2022 when deputy food editor Hana Asbrink developed her recipe for Sheet-Pan Gnocchi With Soy-Dressed Mushrooms. I was taken aback. These little nondescript nubbins were…good?! A few months later, it was again Hana who introduced another new-to-me food, rosé tteokbokki. Completely smitten by this stew, I started to think about what I could use in place of the tteok, an ingredient my colleagues and I love very much, but can’t always find in every grocery store. The answer, it turns out, is a pouch of gnocchi. They’re doughy and dense, but in this recipe, that’s a good thing. As the gnocchi cook, their starch gently thickens the auburn sauce, and they soften into a comforting bite. —Shilpa Uskokovic, senior Test Kitchen editor

item.title: Everything is a Luxury Item Now
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.14
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the rise of AI-made reservations. We must address one oft-ignored issue that’s become too acute to overlook: Whoever is in charge of wine at Trader Joe’s needs a wellness check. I’m seeing apple pie wine. I’m seeing pumpkin spice chardonnay. I’m concerned and I want to help. This week chef Daniel Humm of Eleven Madison Park fame entered the consumer packaged goods (CPG) game. His new product is called Riff, a line of boxed pasta dishes that come with seasoning mixes and crunchy toppings, plus suggestions on each box for how you can incorporate fresh ingredients. (Riffs—get it?) Also important: 13,000 cases later, the CDC has announced the Cyclospora outbreak is over. Phew! One less concern among the many other food safety issues currently unfolding—like “small stones and other hard objects” in ice cream. Also in this week’s Open Tab: why every food item seems like it’s a luxury item, Chipotle’s shiny new partnership with Palantir, China’s blueberry scam, and the legacy of Prince’s favorite cheesecake. The era of expensive everything A burger at DC’s Le Diplomate will set you back $29—more than twice what it cost 13 years ago, as The Washington Post reports. In New York, Gigi’s set off a wave of menu pricing discourse with a $77 roast chicken, they’re doing $100 hot dogs in Florida, and across the country, prices at McDonald’s have doubled over the last decade—even as serving sizes have gotten smaller. Why is everything so much more expensive now? The answer is multifaceted: The war in Iran is skyrocketing fuel prices which, in turn, has a profound impact on global food systems, plus inflation is rising steeply—hence this week’s Fed rate bump—and, finally, restaurants’ supply, labor, and utility costs are still rising. A lot of restaurant items are priced as luxuries, but our sense of luxury has also skewed in recent years. Caviar, once rarified, is now par for the course. Wagyu beef, a high-end, hard-to-source import years ago, is on countless menus at all price points. For $158—that’s two roast chickens at Gigi’s—you can indulge in an all-you-can-eat Wagyu and seafood experience, in fact. All this means diners will learn to be more discerning. With prices like these, determining which meals warrant this kind of spending is all the more important. Why is Chipotle working with Palantir? What’s the opposite of a joint slay? Whatever that term might be, that’s how I’d describe an international fast-casual restaurant chain partnering with a multibillion dollar tech giant hell-bent on destroying every last scrap of data privacy for normal people. I am talking, as you may have guessed, about the new collab between Chipotle and Palantir. Palantir, which has been contracted to work with ICE to track migrants’ movements, will be working with Chipotle on a food safety risk platform—essentially a means to try to reduce the number of food safety incidents at the chain’s locations. “The platform brings key information together in one place, enabling our teams to more effectively identify trends, prioritize follow-up, and make proactive, data-informed decisions,” Laurie Schalow, Chipotle’s chief corporate affairs and food safety officer, in a statement to Wired. Will all of this actually result in greater food safety at Chipotle or is this simply a scheme to collect data on your burrito order? Well, reader, at this juncture it’s hard to say. Approximately a decade and a half ago, the fruit giant Driscoll entered the Chinese market to make blueberries happen, bringing in growing technology to lay claim to the best blueberries with the best genetics, according to The Wall Street Journal. By 2025, Chinese production of blueberries doubled that of the US. But Driscoll wasn’t the only one cashing in on the blueberry rush. Chinese business owners allegedly copied those blueberry-growing technologies, and some even stole Driscoll’s copyrighted blueberry varieties. The blueberry market in China is booming, but Driscoll has filed more than 20 lawsuits (and won two) seeking damages against Chinese companies, according to WSJ’s report. Vanessa Drews started making cheesecakes just for the love of the game—a cheesecake-head, if you will. That all changed when Prince (yes, that Prince) developed a taste for Drews’s desserts. Last September, she opened up a brick-and-mortar shop four miles from the late icon’s Paisley Park home, where she serves up the same Prince-approved recipes. Read on to discover the rest of Drews’s story.

item.title: Prince's Favorite Cheesecake Delivers the Funk
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.13
About 20 miles southwest of downtown Minneapolis, in the small town of Excelsior, a curiously named business sits wedged in a strip mall among a taqueria, a nail salon, and a pet groomer. Wander inside and you might think you’re in a museum dedicated to Prince, the Minneapolis-born musical genius who lived just four miles south of here at his private home and recording studio complex, Paisley Park. The purple walls are dotted with photos of the homegrown superstar, who passed away 10 years ago this year. The business may double as a de facto homage to the self-proclaimed Purple Yoda, but it’s actually one of the hottest bakeries in the Midwest. Welcome to Cheesecake Funk. When owner Vanessa Drews opened the cheesecake bakery in September 2025, it quickly became the talk of the baked good loving Twin Cities. And the Prince connection goes far beyond the bakery’s purple walls. But for lovers of all things sweet and creamy, Cheesecake Funk is today a veritable mecca for those in the know. Dig, if you will, the superlative turtle cheesecake laden with rich dark chocolate, gooey caramel, and crunchy toasted pecans, with a crispy bottom crust. The exact recipe for that crust is a secret, but Drews admits to using cinnamon and a healthy portion of brown butter. It’s a masterpiece of contrasting textures and layered flavors, which perhaps explains why it’s Cheesecake Funk’s best seller. For Drews, a single Black mother of two, it all started back in 2002 when she was still a hobby baker. A lifelong lover of cheesecakes, she baked them for family and friends who began requesting them for every party and holiday gathering. “I started tweaking the recipe over time, mixing the crust with brown butter, adding cinnamon here and there,” Drews says. At the time she was working a day job as a senior paralegal and making cheesecake in her free time. But money was tight, and she picked up a part-time gig selling merchandise at Paisley Park on the occasional evenings that Prince threw open-to-the-public parties. One day in 2013, she showed up with a cheesecake. “Prince always had band members and other employees coming here from other parts of the country and the world,” Drews recalls. “So, I put the cheesecake in the fridge with a note saying that anyone was welcome to a piece. I wanted to provide some good food for them and say: ‘Welcome to Minnesota.’” Stocking the fridge with cheesecake became a ritual. Soon Drews noticed the speed with which her cheesecakes were devoured. Who could be responsible? And then, scrolling through the social media site formerly known as Twitter, a particular post caught her attention: A meme of two monkeys trying to resuscitate a fellow simian that featured the words, “The moment you find out somebody ate the last piece of Vanessa’s cheesecake.” It was uploaded from an account managed by Prince. “I thought: ‘Oh my God, I’m the Vanessa he’s referring to!’” she says. “I was euphoric." Prince began calling her edible handiwork “cheesecake funk,” often including the phrase on invitations to parties at Paisley Park, writing “HELPYOSELFTOSOMECHEESECAKEFUNK.” After that, at Paisley Park parties, Prince would occasionally walk by Drews and, with his trademark smirk, say, “What’s for dessert, Vanessa?” before walking away. (This anecdote may surprise Prince fans—there’s a common misconception that he was 100% vegan. Not so, at least when it came to cheesecake.) While Prince’s endorsement certainly boosted her confidence, she didn’t feel ready to quit her job and become a full-time baker. But then, a big break: In 2019, a friend of a friend offered a bite of Drews’s cheesecake to Kam Talebi, founder and CEO of Kaskaid Hospitality, the Twin Cities–based enterprise with 18 restaurants nationwide. He loved it enough to put it on the dessert menu of the Eden Prairie location of Crave American Kitchen & Sushi Bar, a small chain of restaurants scattered across the Midwest. “A few months later, Kam called me and he said, ‘You’d better prepare for volume. I’m adding your cheesecake to all eight Twin Cities locations of Crave,’” Drews recounts. “I remember sitting at my desk at the law office and thinking, Oh my gosh! Is this really happening?” She decided to pull the proverbial trigger. Drews dipped into some of her 401(k) plan to buy baking equipment and set up shop in a rented hotel kitchen. Fast-forward to September 2025, when she opened a bakery near her home in Excelsior, using the moniker Prince came up with, Cheesecake Funk. Prince’s favorite variety, turtle, is decidedly bold, but there are no wallflowers among the 17-plus flavors on offer at any given time, many of them seasonal. This past summer’s flavor, lingonberry, was appropriately Minnesotan given the state’s large population of people with Scandinavian heritage, and it was enough of a hit that Drews added it to the permanent menu. “It’s very tart, but has bursts of sweetness, similar to strawberry,” Drews says. “It’s just really refreshing and light, perfect for summer.” As the weather shifts, it’s on to the next: The current fall seasonal flavors include a deceptively simple apple cheesecake topped with stewed fruit laced with cinnamon. These days, one has ample options when seeking Cheesecake Funk products in the Twin Cities. In downtown Minneapolis, stop by Union Rooftop, Brit’s Pub, Butcher’s Table, Wood + Paddle, or one of a handful of locations of Crave in and around the Twin Cities, or even Paisley Park. Or you can go to the original Cheesecake Funk in Excelsior and say hello to Drews. Prince fans have begun stopping there on their way to or from Paisley Park. “The other day I had a couple from Germany, and this afternoon, these sweet ladies came in from the Netherlands,” Drews says. “People come to find me because they appreciate Prince.” “I’m so thankful to him,” she continues. “Prince is like the gift that keeps on giving.”

item.title: The Best Time to Visit Greece For Island-Hopping, Fewer Crowds, and Ideal Temperatures
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 6.94
Many people travel to Greece to spend time along its coast or on one of its myriad islands—a holiday destination that leaves salt on your skin. And there's good reason to come for that alone, although it gives little sense of a country that is roughly 80 percent mountainous. Beyond the beach there are farming villages where a scenic adventure can segue into local wine and seasonal, farm-to-table food. Some places are worth visiting for a particular occasion: the grape harvest, or an Orthodox feast that brings a village’s scattered families home. Naturally, the best time to visit Greece depends on which of those pleasures you want to build a trip around. An Easter visit calls for early hotel reservations, while an island holiday late in the year needs a close look at ferry schedules and hotel closing dates. For help with those choices, we draw on recommendations from Curated Greece co-founders Vasilis Sarmantas and Seetha Ramanathan, along with Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist Ronnie Liadis of Liadis Travel. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date. When is the best month to travel to Greece? September is the best month for a first visit to Greece that combines Athens with an island. The sea has had all summer to warm up, and ferries still serve the main routes frequently. Sarmantas and Ramanathan recommend it for beach holidays with fewer crowds than midsummer: In the Cyclades, the Aegean island group that includes Mykonos and Santorini, the most sought-after hotels remain busy well into the month of September, and sometimes even October. Late May to early June is these experts' other preferred window, near the start of a beach season —which generally lasts until early October. Liadis favors May for wildflowers and comfortable weather, though the sea can feel cool this time of year. The water is warmest from July to September, Sarmantas and Ramanathan told us. April and May are good months to visit Greece for sightseeing. Cooler weather lets you linger at exposed sites such as the Acropolis, the ancient hilltop citadel of Athens, and the open-air theater at Epidaurus on the Peloponnese peninsula southwest of Athens. For a trip in late October, look to Athens or larger southern islands such as Crete and Rhodes, where more hotels stay open year-round. On smaller resort islands, check hotel closing dates alongside ferry schedules before settling on a destination. What is the temperature in Greece by month? July and August are the hottest months, but keep in mind that an Athens forecast tells you little about a village high in the Pindus mountains of the northern mainland. The table below gives a broad seasonal guide using historical monthly averages for five destinations: Athens, the northern city of Thessaloniki, Corfu Town, Heraklion (on Crete), and Rhodes Town. Each range spans the lowest and highest city average in that group. These are benchmarks, so individual days, especially during heat waves, can be considerably hotter. | Month | Typical daytime high | Typical overnight low | |---|---|---| | January | 49–60°F | 34–48°F | | February | 52–60°F | 36–48°F | | March | 58–62°F | 40–50°F | | April | 66–68°F | 46–55°F | | May | 74–79°F | 54–60°F | | June | 81–88°F | 61–68°F | | July | 84–92°F | 65–72°F | | August | 83–92°F | 65–73°F | | September | 80–85°F | 59–69°F | | October | 70–76°F | 51–62°F | | November | 60–68°F | 44–56°F | | December | 52–63°F | 37–51°F | In summer, plan archaeological visits for the earliest entry time available, and check the site’s hours that morning since extreme heat can bring abrupt closures. The EU’s Copernicus climate service recorded extreme heat stress in parts of Greece during summer 2025. Hot, dry, and windy conditions also raise wildfire risk: consult Civil Protection’s daily risk map before a rural excursion and follow local restrictions and any 112 evacuation alerts. Keep in mind that a clear sky does not guarantee a smooth ferry crossing. The meltemi, a northerly wind over the Aegean, can take the edge off a hot beach afternoon while roughening the sea enough to disrupt ferries. When strong winds are forecast, confirm your sailing with the operator before heading to the port. What is the cheapest time to go to Greece? November through March is generally the cheapest time to go to Greece (apart from Christmas and New Year’s). Sarmantas and Ramanathan put the potential savings on international flights at 30 to 50 percent of high season's prices. In Athens and Thessaloniki, that lower hotel bill still comes with plenty to do: Museums stay open and neighborhood restaurants have local regulars to feed through winter. On the islands, check what will be open around your hotel, since many resorts close from roughly November to April. For an island holiday, compare May with late September and early October, when rates can ease before seasonal businesses close. Check the connections while you compare hotels. An extra flight or an overnight stay between ferries can easily absorb what you saved on the room. Orthodox Easter fills rooms in places known for their Holy Week traditions, and its date may differ from Western Easter. Keep an eye on those dates, and if they align with your travel plans, book early and plan to arrive before the weekend. On Good Friday, worshippers follow an epitaphios, a flower-covered bier representing Christ’s tomb, through the streets. The mood changes at midnight on Holy Saturday, when candles are lit to cries of Christos Anesti, “Christ is risen.” By Sunday, families are gathering around tables of roast lamb. In Corfu, the island’s philharmonics, or local brass bands, accompany the Good Friday processions. At 11 a.m. on Holy Saturday, residents drop botides, large clay pots, from balconies. An Easter Sunday arrival would miss both. Patmos, in the eastern Aegean, draws pilgrims to the cave where tradition places St. John’s writing of Revelation. During Holy Week, the abbot of the Monastery of St. John washes the feet of 12 monks in the square of Chora, the island’s capital, reenacting Christ’s gesture to his disciples. In the Peloponnese town of Leonidio, the midnight Resurrection service is the moment to be there, as illuminated paper balloons rise from parishes across town. When is peak season in Greece? July and August are the busiest and most expensive months, although the folks from Curated Greece say the broader high season now extends from early June into mid- or late September. This is when island travelers have the fullest choice of hotels and ferry departures. Book ahead for a particular room or sailing, especially if your dates leave little room to adjust. Around August 15, Greece’s own summer holidays add to the international rush. The Feast of the Dormition, known as Dekapentavgoustos and often called “summer Easter,” commemorates the Virgin Mary’s death. Many families return to their home villages, while pilgrims sail to the Cycladic island of Tinos to visit the revered icon at the Church of Panagia Evangelistria. Some make the ascent from the port on their knees. At village panigiria, the communal feasts held for religious holidays, music, and dancing continue long after church. These homecomings help explain why a ferry can be full even when its destination is absent from the usual resort itineraries. If you want to visit such destinations, book your ferry tickets as soon as the relevant schedule is available, particularly if you need space for a car. How many days are enough for a trip to Greece? If you’re visiting Greece for the first time, try to go for about seven nights for a mix of city and island experiences. “With a week, you can comfortably explore Athens in two or three days, spend a couple of days on one or two islands like Santorini for iconic views or Mykonos for beach time and night life, and possibly include a day trip to a key mainland cultural site like Delphi or Meteora,” as suggested by Sarmantas and Ramanathan. If you have extra time, an additional stop on the mainland or another island, such as Crete or the Peloponnese, can provide further depth, from archaeological wonders to beautiful natural landscapes. Liadis offers a helpful reminder about factoring in travel time: “I don’t recommend less than three nights on any island because a good part of the time is spent transferring from island to island. There are flights that connect to the islands via Athens, but the ferry system is reliable and convenient.” What is the nicest part of Greece to visit? For a first visit, Crete can fill a week without another ferry crossing. Of its two main cities, Heraklion puts you near Knossos, the Bronze Age Minoan palace, while Chania gives easier access to the western beaches and White Mountains. Either lets you combine the coast with lunches in mountain villages, though trying to cover both ends of Greece’s largest island leaves too much of the week to driving. In the village of Elos near Chania, chestnut celebrations in late October or early November put roasted nuts and sweets preserved in syrup on the table. In the Cyclades, decide how much of the holiday you want to spend looking at the sea and how much in it. Santorini’s caldera hotels overlook a sea-filled volcanic basin with steep shores, so the famous view does not come with a long sandy beach below. For that, consider Naxos, where inland farming villages also give you reasons to venture away from the coast. On nearby Paros, look around the fishing village of Naoussa for restaurants and hotels within reach of the beach. May and early fall allow more comfortable exploring, with warmer water at the later end of the season. Corfu, in the Ionian Sea, is a good option if you don't want to rely solely on the beach because there is a substantial town to explore. Centuries of Venetian rule shaped its old streets and its cooking. Order pastitsada, meat in a spiced tomato sauce served with pasta, for a sense of how that history survives at lunch. On Kefalonia, another Ionian island, more of the holiday involves driving through mountain country to reach the next cove, so it is a better choice when beach weather is the priority. Spring and fall are good times for a road trip through the Peloponnese. Stay in the harbor town of Nafplio for visits to Mycenae, a Bronze Age citadel, and the theater at Epidaurus. From there, head south toward the Mani peninsula’s stone tower houses or inland to mountainous Arcadia. Here, the roughly 47-mile Menalon Trail connects villages in eight sections of varying difficulty—the stage between Stemnitsa and Dimitsana, for example, follows old mule tracks past cliffside monasteries above the Lousios River and is demanding. Choose your section based on local advice rather than assuming that any village-to-village walk will be gentle. In central Greece, Athenians spend ski weekends in Arachova, a mountain town below Parnassos Ski Centre. Its tavernas serve grilled formaela, the peppery local cheese made from sheep’s or goat’s milk. Farther south in Arcadia, the village of Vytina puts the eight slopes of Mainalo Ski Centre within reach of a village stay. The nearby MANNA hotel occupies a restored 1929 sanatorium, surrounded by fir trees at about 3,900 feet. The forest also merits a visit after the spring or autumn rains, when local guides lead mushroom hunts. Snow has become less dependable in Greece’s mountains, so check lift conditions close to departure and choose bookings you can change. Zagori, in the mountainous Epirus region of northwestern Greece, deserves several days on foot. Its UNESCO-listed landscape includes stone villages connected by old paths and arched bridges, with forests around the Vikos Gorge that turn color in autumn. The stone staircase into Vradeto was the village’s only approach until 1973. Walking it makes the region’s former isolation easier to grasp, and the route can continue to the Beloi viewpoint above the gorge. The village of Aristi is a convenient base near the Voidomatis River, while Papigo gives access to hikes in the Tymfi mountains. Save high routes for snow-free conditions and ask locally about trails after rain. For a fall trip built around wine, start in Thessaloniki and explore the vineyards of Macedonia in northern Greece. The Naoussa here is a wine town, distinct from its namesake on Paros, and the surrounding vineyards grow the red grape Xinomavro. The Kir-Yianni wine estate offers tastings and vineyard tours year-round by reservation. For a harvest visit, ask the estate when it expects to pick before booking your dates. The timing can differ by several weeks between vineyards, even in the same year. Do Americans need a visa for Greece? US tourists can visit Greece without a visa for up to 90 days in any 180-day period, counting time spent elsewhere in the Schengen Area toward the same limit. According to the Department of State, the passport must be valid for at least three months beyond departure, with a blank page available for each stamp. ETIAS, the European Union’s planned travel authorization for visa-exempt visitors, is not yet operating and is not accepting applications. Its timetable has changed, so check the official EU site before departure for the launch date and any new requirements. Plan your stay • Where to Eat, Stay, and Play in Athens: From modern art galleries and tsipouro bars to traditional live-music rebetadikos for dancing the night away, • The Best Airbnbs in Santorini: Where to rent for a private slice of the Greek Island this summer. • A ‘Mamma Mia’–Inspired Packing List for Greece: Flowy white dresses, linen skirts, and overalls included. • 11 Best Hotels in Mykonos: Smart, stylish, and supremely laidback places to stay.

item.title: Disneyland Discount Tickets: September 2026 Guide
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 6.05
You just can’t argue with that Disney magic. Whether you’re a Disney adult or a begrudging occasional visitor, at some point throughout the day, a little bit of Disney dust will hit you. Maybe it’s the fireworks, or the rides, or the many, many Disney-shaped food items. If not that, it might be seeing the excitement on kids’ faces when they run into a princess, Avenger, or cartoon character IRL. I’m no Disney evangelist, but I would say that if you can’t have fun at a theme park, consider looking inward. (And okay, as a former resident of both California and Florida, I have spent more than my fair share of time at the parks on both coasts.) All that aside, trips to the parks are expensive, so if you’re here to find ways to save, I get it—below, find all the current discounts and promotions to be aware of before planning your next trip to Disneyland. Disneyland discounts for Magic Key holders For the uninitiated, annual passholders are called Magic Key holders, and they can pop in and out of Disneyland as they please (with some terms and conditions in there). Through September 7, these theme park enthusiasts can save up to 20% on select Standard and Premium room types at premium Disneyland Resort hotels. The offer is tailored to Sunday through Thursday night stays at Disney’s Grand Californian Hotel & Spa, Disneyland Hotel, The Villas at Disneyland Hotel, and Pixar Place Hotel. Of note, you must present a valid active Magic Key pass at check-in to secure the discounted rate. Disneyland discounts for military members Savings are available on an ongoing basis for active-duty and retired US military personnel, including the National Guard, Reservists, the US Coast Guard, the US Space Force, the Commissioned Corps of the Public Health Service (PHS), and the Commissioned Corps of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Tickets start at $98 for kids of these travelers and $104 for adults purchasing a one-day, one-park ticket. These tickets may not be combined with other ticket discounts or promotions, and cannot be sold or transferred. Locals get discounted Disney tickets for as little as $71 Through October 8, 2026, Anaheim, California, residents can purchase one-day passes for as little as $71. This is valid for any day visit taken by October 8. Proof of eligible residency, including a valid government-issued photo ID, is required for both purchase and admission. Save on multi-day Disneyland tickets While going to the parks for just one day is the most cost-effective option, your per-day cost does go down when you opt for multi-day tickets instead. For example, a one-day ticket will run you between $104 and $224 based on the date you select. If you go for two days, your price per day starts at $168; for three days, it drops to $142 and up per day; for four days, from $120 per day; and for five days, from $104 per day. A few things to note: Disneyland is much smaller than Disney World, with just two parks, so it is possible to cover a good amount of ground in a single day. However, especially if you’re coming from out of town, you may want a few days there so there’s less pressure to squeeze every ride and meal into a single day. There’s also the question of purchasing one-park-per-day tickets or upgrading to a Park Hopper ticket (an extra $100 per day). If you’re visiting for just one day, I’d suggest the Park Hopper ticket so you get to experience both parks. For multi-day trips, it really comes down to preference; you’ll want to decide between chunking out your park visits or having the freedom to roam back and forth between parks throughout the day (which, size-wise, is definitely doable). Save on food, merchandise, and add-ons with Disneyland discounts beyond tickets Tickets are one thing, but once you’re inside the park, it’s easy to rack up charges on dining, souvenirs, and add-on experiences. If you’re concerned about sticking to a budget, there are a few surefire ways to cut costs. For one, take a look at the gift card section next time you're at Target, Costco, or Sam’s Club, as they sometimes sell discounted Disney Gift Cards. If you’re interested in an additional credit card, new Disney Inspire Visa Card holders can earn up to $500 in the form of a $300 eGift to spend at the park and a $200 statement credit after you spend $1,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. You’ll also earn Disney Rewards Dollars on all card purchases, including: - 10% on card purchases made directly with Disney+, Hulu, and Stream.ESPN.com - 3% on card purchases at gas stations and most Disney US locations - 2% on card purchases at grocery stores and restaurants - 1% on all other card purchases When it comes to food, placing mobile orders via the Disneyland App can help you track food spending more easily and find quick options in place of more expensive sit-down meals. Lastly, consider dining off-property or at Downtown Disney to curb costs. On my last visit to Disneyland, I stayed right across the street from the entrance at Park Vue Inn—the proximity was amazing, and it had a pool and hot tub. Rates start at $229 a night, and rooms with kitchenettes are available, which make coming back midday to prep meals a breeze.
