item.title: The Most Remote Places on Earth You Can Actually Visit
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.24
Reaching the most remote places on Earth takes more than just a plane ticket—it takes patience, endurance, and often a string of connections that make the arrival feel like an achievement in itself. These are places where airports are rare, ships arrive only a handful of times a year, and the communities you meet are outnumbered by wildlife. What they offer in return is a kind of distance that feels almost impossible in the modern world—skies free of light pollution, landscapes shaped by extremes, and the rare quiet that comes from being far beyond the usual travel circuit. Why do we seek remoteness? Journeys to places like these are rarely simple, but that difficulty is part of the allure. They remind us what travel feels like when the destination is hard-won, when the act of arriving carries its own reward. In the Kerguelen Islands, there are no hotels or tour buses, only wind, sea, and wildlife. In Russia's Oymyakon, for example, just stepping outside is an act of endurance. And on South Georgia, hundreds of thousands of penguins gather on beaches once scarred by whaling. In a world where so much feels accessible, true remoteness has become rare. These are the most remote places on Earth that shift our sense of scale and remind us that there are still corners of this planet where distance is intact. Kerguelen Islands, Southern Indian Ocean Nicknamed the “Desolation Islands,” this French territory sits marooned in the southern Indian Ocean, approximately 1,865 miles from Madagascar. Few places feel so utterly cut off. Volcanic cliffs plunge into storm-lashed seas, while king penguins and elephant seals crowd the beaches in their thousands. Nobody lives here permanently—only rotating teams of scientists, engineers, and unconventional travelers. What surrounds you is a world sculpted by wind, sea, and stone, where humanity has left little mark. How to get there: The French supply vessel Marion Dufresne II sails from Réunion Island several times a year. The voyage takes around six days. Quttinirpaaq National Park, Canada On the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, just shy of 500 miles from the North Pole, Quttinirpaaq lives up to its Inuktitut name: “top of the world.” It is a place of extremes—glaciers stretch for miles, jagged peaks rise from polar deserts, and the summer sun never sets. Muskoxen graze the tundra, Arctic wolves hunt in silence, and traces of ancient Inuit encampments remind you how long people have endured at this latitude. Few visitors make it here, but those who do find a landscape that feels infinite. How to get there: Travel first to Resolute Bay in Nunavut, then connect by charter plane to Tanquary Fiord, open only in the summer months. Ittoqqortoormiit, Greenland Few places capture the human will to survive like Ittoqqortoormiit, a settlement of around 450 people perched at the edge of Scoresby Sound, the world's largest fjord system. Wooden houses painted red, blue, and yellow dot the snowy cliffs, while rhythms of life here still follow the seasons: hunting and fishing sustain families, sled dogs line the streets, and in winter the sea ice seals the town off from the outside world completely. The surrounding waters carry drifting icebergs, and it's not unusual to see polar bears wandering the coast. How to get there: Reachable by helicopter from Nerlerit Inaat Airport, itself connected by small aircraft from Reykjavik, Iceland. Longyearbyen, Norway Longyearbyen, in the Svalbard archipelago, is the northernmost town of its size in the world. Despite its isolation, it's surprisingly lived-in, with cafés, a craft brewery, and even a fine-dining restaurant. Beyond town, reindeer roam freely, glaciers carve the landscape, and the Global Seed Vault safeguards the world's crops in a frozen hillside. Here, summers pass in endless daylight; winters in an unbroken stretch of night. How to get there: Daily flights connect Oslo and Tromsø to Svalbard Airport, making it one of the more accessible remote places. South Georgia, South Atlantic Ocean A remote island once known for whaling, South Georgia is now a sanctuary where wildlife has reclaimed the land. More than half a million king penguins gather on its beaches, while elephant seals occupy the shore in extraordinary numbers. Rusting relics of abandoned whaling stations remain, and the grave of polar explorer Ernest Shackleton—the Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer who led three British expeditions to the Antarctic—lies at Grytviken, a pilgrimage for history enthusiasts. After decades of ecological strain, including the introduction of reindeer by whalers, conservation projects are now restoring the island’s native habitats and protecting its fragile ecosystem. How to get there: No airports exist—visitors arrive by expedition ship, usually as part of cruises departing from Ushuaia, Argentina. McMurdo Station, Antarctica On Ross Island, McMurdo Station is the largest research base on the continent, supporting around 1,000 people each summer. It has been the launch point for many of Antarctica’s most important expeditions, from early 20th-century journeys led by Scott and Shackleton to modern scientific studies on climate change and glaciology. The surrounding landscape—glaciers, volcanic peaks, and the vast Ross Ice Shelf—has shaped much of what we know about the polar world. Travelers can’t stay at McMurdo, but expedition cruises to the Ross Sea sometimes include landings nearby, offering the rare chance to stand at the centre of Antarctic exploration. How to get there: Expedition cruises to the Ross Sea depart from New Zealand or Australia, with limited charter flights from Christchurch supporting specialist itineraries. Pitcairn Islands, South Pacific Ocean Home to just under 50 people, the Pitcairn Islands are one of the world’s least populated territories. Settled by the HMS Bounty mutineers in 1790, the community is still made up of their descendants. Life moves at a slow rhythm, shaped by the island’s rugged volcanic terrain and the surrounding Pacific waters. For visitors, the appeal lies in the intimacy: hiking to hidden caves, diving into crystalline waters, and being welcomed by almost every resident. How to get there: Fly to Tahiti, then on to Mangareva in French Polynesia. From there, a supply ship makes the 32-hour crossing to Pitcairn several times a year. Changthang, Ladakh, India High on the Tibetan Plateau, Changthang is a high-altitude desert where the air is thin and the landscape seems endless. Nomadic Changpa herders graze yak and goats across sweeping plains, while saltwater lakes like Tso Moriri and Pangong Tso shimmer beneath snow-capped peaks. Black-necked cranes, wild asses, and even snow leopards are spotted here, adding to its sense of undisturbed isolation. How to get there: Flights run from Delhi to Leh, followed by an overland journey across rugged mountain passes into the plateau. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: The 12 Best Places to Go Apple Picking Near New York City
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.76
As the leaves start to don their sienna coats and the mercury drops into the comfortable-sweater- weather range, autumn's many joys come to the fore. Whether it's the morning PSLs or decorating everything head-to-toe for Halloween, it's no secret why the year's third season is oft-cited as a favorite. And one of the best ways to celebrate fall is by going apple picking, as crowd-pleasers like Galas and Honeycrisps begin blushing into their reddish-gold skins. If you're based in the Big Apple (pun definitely intended), you'll be happy to know that several pastoral orchards and farms lie but a stone's throw away from New York City. Think New Jersey boltholes and easy upstate pit stops where you can fill your wicker basket to your heart's content and then some. And apples aren't the only fruit on offer—prepare to pick out pears for your next holiday dinner, or a pumpkin brimming with the potential to become a fearsome jack-o'-lantern. You can also extend your farm life fantasies by grabbing a seat on a family-friendly hayride, visiting a petting zoo, or being the hero of Thanksgiving by taking home a bottle or two of home-brew cider. Without further ado and in no particular order, here's where to find some of the best apple picking near New York City. Location: 1 Alstede Farms Ln, Chester, NJ Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 15 minutes by car If your palate asks for more than just the crisp bite of an heirloom apple, how about a satisfying bowl of homemade ice cream, smears of fresh-churned Amish butter, or steaming pans of ratatouille packed with farm-fresh produce? At Alstede, you're in luck—the farm has an online store that can deliver right to your door or local farmers market. Beyond apples, your whole grocery run practically lives here, whether you’re looking for eggplant, potatoes, or blueberries. But if it’s the ambience of the grounds that you find yourself obsessed with, they also host regular tours, seasonal harvest moon nights, and weddings for those who are truly in love with the venue. Where to stay nearby: Situated an eight-minute drive away from Chester in Peapack, New Jersey, Pendry Natirar charms with its historic brick mansion façade, incredible spa, and over 500 acres of parkland. Location: 9 Fishkill Farm Rd, Hopewell Junction, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 45 minutes by car Sample the Champagne of ciders when you have a sip of this farm's tree-to-bottle Treasury Cider. A family-run operation, as some of the best apple-picking orchards are, Fishkill Farms presses its own special breeds of dessert and bittersweet apples on-site to achieve the label's signature taste. And that's just one example of the level of effort you can expect here. Not only does the farm grow organic Crimson Crisp and Spartan apples, but it also farms most produce according to eco-certified and ecologically grown standards, which both have rigorous requirements for what the fruit is exposed to from seed to sale. But the fun’s not just in the fruit—dine at the Fishkill Farms Grill with all the Catskills surrounding you, or catch an evening performance of live music from a visiting band. Where to stay nearby: If you're apple picking here, you're practically steps away from Beacon and Cold Spring, two of upstate's most accessible gems (just hop on the Metro-North commuter line). We recommend staying at The Roundhouse in Beacon, a property that is a destination in and of itself for food, art, and shopping. Location: 306 NY-304, Congers, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour by car Welcome to your classic apple and pumpkin picking experience, where the beauty of the tried-and-true shines through. Having been around since 1891, the farm, now run by the practiced hands of fourth- and fifth-generation Davies family members, runs like a well-oiled machine. Admission is $17 in cash per person, and if you don’t know where to start with the over 5,000 trees and 27 different apple varieties on the farm, the website has a “Meet Our Apples” page where each is identified with a well-lit picture, ripening timeline, and flavor profile. If you’d like to enjoy even more fruits from the farm but not your own labor, the brewery arm, Red Barn Cidery, produces a host of its own ciders, local beers, and nonalcoholic options. Where to stay nearby: Stay right on the Hudson at a warm Airbnb that sets the mood with a crackling fireplace and wooden rafters across from Congers, in Ossining, New York. With four beds and two-and-a-half baths, this Hudson Valley escape is plenty capable of hosting the whole family. Location: 45 Ball Rd, Warwick, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 45 minutes by car; 3 hours by train Sprawling orchard grounds have never been more accessible than at Masker—open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day of the week rather than being condition- or season-dependent. The orchard is also designed for driving through, so you can take your car right up to the trees you want to pick from or picnic under. Beforehand, consult the website banner that clearly states which varieties are ready for picking, and download the map of the orchard so you’ll know ahead of time that Red Delicious apples can be found on the corner of “Strudel” and “Pie” lanes. Where to stay nearby: Sometimes, the greatest gift our travels can bestow upon us is a true sense of quiet. There's no better place to seek it in Warwick than at this cozy cabin Airbnb you'll want to claim as your own neck of the woods. Location: 250 Hurds Rd, Clintondale, NY Distance from NYC: About 2 hours by car The name might’ve already clued you in, but this farm goes all out for the kids—there’s a busy bee train, chances to leave their mark on the Chalk Bus, a tire climbing wall, a giant bounce pillow, and that’s not even to mention the petting zoo or 2.5-acre corn maze. While there’s more than enough to keep the whole family engaged with those activities alone, the best time to visit is throughout October, when the lion’s share of the farm’s apples are ripe, and the pumpkins are ready to pick too. Where to stay nearby: Check in a 15-minute drive across the river at The Heartwood at Vassar in Poughkeepsie, a gorgeous college town. Soak in the autumnal, academic atmosphere from one of the 50 rooms and suites at this recently opened property. Location: 244 Werimus Rd, Hillsdale, NJ Distance from NYC: About 1 hour by car; 1 hour and 30 minutes by train This farm puts its vast-spanning orchards to use as a canvas for one of the best light shows in the tristate area. In the daytime throughout the summer and fall months, peaches and apples are the main attraction, but when the sun sets during the Halloween season, new life is breathed into the orchards as they host a ghoulish light extravaganza peppered with skeletons, jack-o'-lanterns, and a gallery of classic monsters. During the winter months, the Orchard of Lights features giant snowflakes, reindeer, and even Dr. Seuss’s Grinch. Where to stay nearby: If fall doesn't feel complete to you without a little side of spookiness, get right in the middle of the action at the Sleepy Hollow Hotel. The property features weeknight fall specials, reduced rates for locals interested in a staycation, and a restaurant that's open all day. Location: 91 Wemrock Rd, Freehold, NJ Distance from NYC: About 2 hours by car Owned and operated by the Applegate family for the past 118 years, Battleview is the oldest pick-your-own farm in New Jersey. This year, the orchard is offering 19 varieties of apples throughout the fall, and it also has year-round opportunities to pick sour cherries, strawberries, peaches, and pumpkins. As kids explore some of the 130-acre grounds on the seasonal hayride, parents can walk the aisles of the on-site country store stocked with favorites like house-made cider and fresh-baked pies, and speciality items such as the customizable fruit baskets. Its website has Applegate family recipes for every variety of fruit the orchard cultivates. Where to stay nearby: Did someone call for a Hallmark movie set? Look no further than this quiet and cozy Airbnb in Monroe Township that boasts plenty of space, perfect for a multigenerational outing. The wraparound porch was practically made for fall evenings spent watching the wind rustle through the tree line. Location: 139 Hardscrabble Rd, North Salem, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 30 minutes by car These orchards don't just offer some of the best apple picking near New York City—they're a celebration of all things autumnal. The best time to visit is throughout September and October, when Outhouse puts on its Fall Festival. Every corner of the grounds offers something built to entertain, whether it's racing rubber ducks or blowing bubbles for the little ones, hayrides for the whole family, or snacking on wood-fired pizza and washing it down with homemade hard cider for food lovers. With 12 apple varieties that ripen during the pick-your-own season, there’s enough diversity to satisfy fans of tangy McIntoshes and honey-sweet Jonamacs alike. Where to stay nearby: When it comes to a weekend escape near North Salem, you don't have to choose between woodsy or luxurious. Instead, ask yourself, “por qué no los dos?” with stays like the Martha Stewart–approved Bedford Post Inn waiting to welcome you in. Location: 82 Four Corners Rd, Warwick, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 45 minutes by car If you’ve ever wanted to live inside a Bob Ross painting, this is the orchard for you. At Apple Dave’s, the farm’s own lake is a backdrop for sweeping views of the northern Appalachian Mountains. Meandering walking trails through the trees plus an on-site store filled with fresh produce and charming Halloween decor provide casual yet engaging activities for a fun day out with the family. But for the 21+ crowd, the distillery offers Apple Jacks, Shawangunk wines, and cocktails enhanced by the farm’s produce amongst the usual suspects of local beers and ciders. Where to stay nearby: Cozy and tiny are two words that fit hand-in-hand, and you'll find both qualities in spades at this minimalist cottage that subtly signals “designer” with its muted tones and plush Scandi-coded furnishings. Location: 62 Granite Springs Rd, Granite Springs, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour and 30 minutes by car Beyond its orchards, Stuart’s is also home to a Christmas tree farm and bakery that churns out irresistible cider donuts and fresh-baked pies. The farm also does not charge entrance or parking fees, meaning visitors are only charged for what they pick and purchase at the store. But this is definitely one of those trips where the journey getting there is just as worth it as the destination—driving through Granite Springs, visitors get to experience Westchester at its autumnal best, as the mountains pass by in a montage of gold and orange. Where to stay nearby: Extend your itinerary beyond the main event of apple picking by staying the weekend at Hotel MTK Mount Kisco, which sits at the junction of the Caramoor Center for Music and the Arts and Rockefeller State Park Preserve. Location: 155 N Ohioville Rd, New Paltz, NY Distance from NYC: About 2 hours by car This is an orchard for the epicurean. After you spend an afternoon at the orchard plucking Fujis, Galas, Honeycrisps, and Cortlandts, take the load off at Twin Star’s on-site restaurant. Wood-fired pizzas are sumptuous and savory, with options such as sweet sausage and broccoli rabe and Dragon’s Breath for the daring. Inclusive items like the vegan pizza and black bean burger also feature on the menu to accommodate dietary preferences. And for those truly looking to indulge, be sure to visit on Saturdays and Sundays for the low-and-slow barbecue and to stack your plate with fall-apart ribs and brisket. Where to stay nearby: Experience living history at Mohonk Mountain House, where you will be immersed in the wholesome pastimes and stunning natural beauty of an American icon. This historic backdrop stays revitalized with a slate of fresh offerings—don't skip the spa. Location: 2 S Mountain Rd, Pomona, NY Distance from NYC: About 1 hour by car; 2 hours by train These orchards in the quaint town of Pomona are the ideal weekend day trip out of the city. In addition to sampling some of the newest and coolest apple varieties on the market (who wouldn’t want to take a bite out of a Ludacrisp?), the bakery offers everything from timeless apple pies to peanut butter custard pies that are begging to be your next holiday dinner centerpiece. While there’s enough to occupy your Saturday and Sunday afternoons, the farm also has a strong presence at local farmers markets such as Bronxville, Riverdale, and White Plains. Where to stay nearby: Don't just stop at the leaf-peeping. Take in everything fall has to offer by the water at AMC Corman Harriman Outdoor Center hotel, where guests can take out free kayaks and paddleboats for a new flavor of fall adventure.

item.title: At Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy, Exploring Eastern Indonesia by Boat and Board
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.52
There are not many places left in the world like the tip of Rote. It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell, and bathymetry. There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach—good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there. Amid all this remoteness, the first top-end resort has just opened, Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy, sister property to Nihi Sumba, west of here. Both these hotels—a few hundred miles apart—front one of the most coveted waves in the world. When I visit, the hotel is still taking shape. At the eastern end of the bay is a clutch of thoughtfully designed, thatched, low-rise villas, each with a swimming pool; the interiors in mine use local materials such as lontar palm and ikat textiles. The gathering place is beach club Nammo, with its poolside restaurant and watersports instructors, smack in front of Bo’a break. Here I wait for the tide to turn before paddling out. When Nihi Rote launches fully in October, there will be 21 villas, three pools, a spa, a pump track, and a golf simulator. It is also planning to build and sell multimillion-dollar residences alongside the property. One night, I’m invited to Rote Hospitality Academy, where Timorese trainees have prepared an endearing evening of traditional song and dance; storytelling; and a feast of coconut rice with lemongrass, rendang beef stew, and grilled fish with sambal. Sitting around the fire pit, toes in the sand, the students share stories with me about the cuisine; traditional string instrument sasando, made of bamboo; and their struggles with learning to swim. For many, it is their first job, or their first job in hospitality, and it’s been a fast-track whirlwind. Before the hotel opened, they had already hosted a big-splash 50th birthday party for its owner, Michael Schwab, son of investment firm founder Charles Schwab. “We’ve never seen anything like this on Rote,” says one student. Change is not always easy, especially in a place that, until recently, relied on seaweed farming and fishing. I feel a pang as I drive past Rote’s cinder-block and tin-roof huts, women on the porch pausing to wave as they plait each other’s hair, sepia-tinged frangipani blossoms strewn on the ground. Rote has long been open to outsiders—and that is increasingly rare in this world of ours. “Do you live here?” is a regular refrain from locals as I freewheel around town. It is always uttered with a smile—on the harbor, at a café, down on the beach. When I reply that I am passing through, they say: Come and live here, you are welcome, bring your family. Many have taken up such invitations, seduced by the island’s stress-free, go-slow rhythm. “We were also passing through,” a South African surfer tells me, echoing my line. “But that was two years ago.” He and his partner have had a baby, bought some land, and are now building a cottage. I borrow a bike to explore the main coastal road, sealed but potholed and set back from the seafront, with sandy lanes trailing down to the beaches. Village merges into village, and the only demarcations are bollards painted “selamat datang" (meaning welcome) or a trio of life-sized crucifixes, prettily decorated despite being a symbol of execution. One is painted lavender, another strewn with flowers. The churches here are enormous and numerous, towering vaulted monuments, one resembling a gigantic Noah’s Ark. Catholic, a man tells me, then to be contradicted by his wife: no, Presbyterian. Another says Methodist. The pastor tells me Calvinist. Tropical Christianity, let’s agree on, and fervent. At Easter, I’m told, crowds enact the Stations of the Cross, parading through the streets in the garb of Roman soldiers. The rest of the year, there’s not much more than a scrap of traffic. One day I drive 40 minutes and count two motorbikes and one water bowser. I reach the end of a road that peters out into scrub, nothing beyond and nowhere for me to go. Although there are few vehicles, there are scads of roadside vendors selling gasoline in fancy glass bottles that look more like love potions. Lines of laundry flap. Animals are everywhere: languorous cows, silky-haired goats atop bathroom-tiled gravestones, and broods of chickens crossing the road, I could only assume, to get to the other side. This easy-going scene belies the region’s bloody colonial history. Timor was fought over by the Dutch and Portuguese—a battle rooted in the sandalwood and spice trade—resulting in its split into East and West. The British muscled in, but only for a few years, and the Japanese occupied the area during the Second World War. Remnants of history and cultural heritage are not obvious at first glance; some can be seen in the weaving of tessellated tenun ikat textiles and the ti’i langga, resembling a ten-gallon cowboy hat made of lontar palm, worn by men, with a phallic spike on the brim. The best way to explore Rote, with its offshore islands, reefs, and consistent breaks, is by boat. At one rocky outcrop I find a vast cave of screeching fruit bats. I drop into the water with a mask and snorkel and fast-float in the choppy current to spy on triggerfish and parrotfish. I was told oceanic manta ray and whale sharks congregate here, so I focus my eyes towards the deep, which falls away fast; the next strike of land is Australia. I check out surf sites, ending up on the far side of Ndana Island, Indonesia’s most southerly point. Nobody is around. I spend most of my time crashing and splashing, but nothing can beat the occasional moment standing aloft, feeling the push of a wave, the water so clear I can see fish dashing about the coral. A couple of haggard, sun-smashed Aussie surfers arrive close to the end of the day, so I bow out of the wave, instead bobbing about straddling my board to watch the colors of the sky shift. Back on land I meet locals and newcomers with surf shacks, market stalls, and motorbike hire shops. Hotelier Mick Fogarty is just opening on Rote, after more than 30 years in Bali running the fabled Mick’s Place on Bingin Beach. When I ask him if he feels an ache about leaving Bali, he says “no” before I’ve finished the question. He and his Danish wife, Sascha Hansen, have three pretty self-catering bungalows, and, sensibly, used the best land to build a house for themselves. “We were going to build a restaurant but then thought, why don’t we build a home,” says Fogarty. That sums up the spirit of those who come to Rote. “Everyone moves here for the lifestyle,” he continues, “not to turn a profit, just to sustain a life.” After sunset, when everyone lopes back from the beach, there are a few couples hitching their gear onto motor scooters and a few families carrying babies, bags, and boards, toddlers in tow. Everyone’s sandy with wet, tangled hair. It’s a strong, fit, healthy scene. “No drugs, no nightclubs," as I keep hearing on repeat. One hotel owner points out, “many of the people here already had their 20 crazy years, so now we can all chill.” Another labels Rote a “retirement village for surfers, who come for peace and quiet." Carla Lázaro Ferro from the Canary Islands calls it differently. She lived here, then moved to Berlin, where she found herself “crying for Rote." “Here you feel you can give back. Life is more meaningful, more chaotic, more free,” she tells me. On my last night, I sleep out on the deck of my villa at Ferro’s Bo’a Vida resort, overlooking the Bo’a wave and the Timor Sea. Here on the southern edge of Indonesia, the stars glow like light bulbs, even on the horizon. Only the dazzle of the rising moon dims them. I feel as far away as I could be. Where to stay Following the success of its sister resort in Sumba (to the west of Rote), the 21-villa Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy on Bo’a Beach opens the renowned surf sites to top-end travelers. Villas are a mix of one-bedroom, duplex, and family-style set-ups, and larger residences are planned. The westerly rooms have the best views of the Bo’a break. Bo'a Vida owner Carla Lázaro Ferro opened a thatched shack 15 years ago atop a rocky outcrop at the end of Bo’a Beach, overlooking the legendary wave of the same name and the sunset beyond. Now she has six climate-conscious villas, five of which were designed by her husband, award-winning architect Álvaro Carrillo Eguilaz, with stone paths meandering down to slips of sand and the yoga sala. Ferro also runs the café Indika in town, which serves fruit bowls until 5:30 p.m., when everyone heads out to catch a wave. Nat and Matt Thistlewaite of Rote Island Huts came here from Australia in 2011 after finding the island of Rote on Google Earth. They arrived with the aim of creating a nonprofit holiday retreat that channeled income into local education and the community. There are five simple huts: three are family-style with bunks, all have beachfront access. It’s a heartening enterprise, and they are now preparing to hand over management to local Rotenese, as they always intended. Pika and Pascal Chevillot, a Slovenian and a Frenchman, used to own Sardine, one of Bali’s top restaurants. At Sardine Beach Rote, they’ve created a spectacular three-villa property in five acres of gardens on one of the island’s best beaches. The rooms use lontar palm and coconut leaf to create traditional roofing, paneled walls, and sconces. Pascal’s breakfast is a real event, with Parmesan omelettes and smoked Spanish mackerel. I notice a copy of Tao Te Ching on a side table, which just about sums up the place. Aussie Mick Fogarty and Sascha Hansen from Denmark are the creators of Mick’s Place Rote, three delightful beachfront bungalows with private courtyards in a glade of coconut trees. The couple are strong on sustainability, harnessing solar power, reusing grey water for the gardens, and lending bicycles for guests to get around on. There's a one-week stay minimum, and the lap pool is set to be the gathering place. Close to the T-Land break at Nemberala Beach, Spaniards Julia Davila Solana and Jose Miguel Murgui have built 81 Palms and its six A-frame cabins on the soft sand, plus they’ve recently opened four smaller bungalows at their new Next Door property. The Spanish restaurant is the best place for dinner in Rote, with former Michelin-starred Murgui in the kitchen cooking up gazpacho, tapas, and seafood paella. Natural World Safaris can arrange an 11-day trip combining a B&B stay at COMO Uma Ubud on Bali and a seven-night full-board stay at NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy on Rote, from £5,800 per person. The price is based on two people sharing and includes all transfers and domestic flights. International airfare is excluded. This story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Sennheiser Coupon Codes & Discounts | September 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.28
German audio brand Sennheiser has made its mark on all types of travel experiences, from providing the ideal in-flight headphones for the Concorde, to developing microphones favored by artists on stages across the globe, to launching immersive, speakerless audio for vehicles. To put it simply, you can’t travel well without good sound, and if you’re in the market for noise-canceling headphones that’ll get you through that next long-haul flight, this audio brand’s got you covered. Established in 1945, Sennheiser has long been a household name among audiophiles, but has also won the ears of casual listeners. It all began when Dr. Ing. Fritz Sennheiser founded Laboratorium Wennebostel outside of Hanover, which later became Sennheiser Electronic. The first product was the DM 1 microphone, made for Siemens. The company has been credited with creating the world’s first open-back headphones in 1968, and in 1991, it launched the legendary Orpheus electrostatic headphone (whose successor would be the HE 1 in 2015), followed by the Evolution Microphone Series in 1999. The very best in sound technology doesn’t come cheap; if you’d like to shop the Sennheiser brand, read on for the coupon codes, discounts, and free shipping offers to use before making a purchase. Use a Sennheiser coupon code for 10% off your first order If you’re new to the brand, you’re in luck: First-time customers can sign up for the official Sennheiser newsletter to receive an exclusive 10% off coupon for their initial purchase, up to $100. And once you’re subscribed, you can stay informed about new product launches, flash sales, and subscriber-only promotions—all delivered directly to your inbox. Subscribers can also benefit from free shipping on all orders sitewide with no minimum spend, ensuring extra savings on every purchase. Once you sign up, the discount and free shipping will expire by December 31, 2026, so make sure you put it to use before then. Keep an eye out for limited-time offers at Sennheiser Sennheiser is currently offering limited-time discounts on industry-standard gear, including headphones and soundbars—often available without a specific code. Right now, for instance, the AMBEO Soundbar Max Refurbished has been marked down from $2,999 to $1,299.5, rounding out to a total saving of $1,700. This home theater tool will level up how you watch movies, with a 3D audio experience. Students, military members, and first responders can enjoy a 15% discount Sennheiser is committed to honoring those who serve our communities, from students learning how to make music to nurses who commute to work with a pair of headphones. As a gesture of gratitude, the company offers a 15% discount code to military personnel, veterans, government employees, medical professionals, first responders, seniors, students, and teachers. All you have to do is verify your status through ID.me. Once you’ve completed your verification, you’ll be given a unique promo code, which you can enter into the “Discount Code” field when purchasing an item on the Sennheiser site. Unfortunately, this code can’t be combined with other offers. Shop refurbished Sennheiser products at a discount without a code If you don’t mind giving up on that shiny new toy feeling, Sennheiser offers discounts on "like-new" products that have undergone professional inspection, testing, and restoration to meet original performance standards. You can find previous-generation models, open-box items, or cosmetic-blemish products—like the HD 560S or HD 599 headphones—at a fraction of their price. All refurbished products typically come with a warranty, ensuring peace of mind with your purchase, similar to new items. What to do if your Sennheiser coupon code isn’t working If your Sennheiser coupon code isn't working, be sure to check for typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization, as well as any terms and conditions. The 10% newsletter sign-up promo code, for instance, is capped at a $100 discount and limited to first-time users only. You can also try clearing your browser’s cache and cookies, or switching devices or browsers. When all else fails, Sennheiser's Consumer Experience team is there to help.

item.title: These US Airlines Have Mishandled the Most Bags in 2026, According to New Data
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.16
Most travelers have experienced that sinking feeling at baggage claim when the carousel stops and their checked luggage is still nowhere to be seen. While lost or delayed bags are sometimes just an unfortunate part of air travel, there are some airlines that statistically mishandle checked bags more often than others. The situation can be extra frustrating in 2026, as most carriers have significantly raised the cost of checking luggage on domestic and short-haul international routes to an average of $45 for the first bag. Despite the elevated fee, US airlines have collectively mishandled 1,120,760 checked bags in the first six months of 2026, according to new data from the Department of Transportation (DOT). That’s an average of about 0.5 bags mishandled per 100 bags enplaned. Although those numbers can seem shocking, they’re similar to mishandled baggage rates for the same stretch in 2025, which saw an average of 0.52 bags mishandled for every 100 loaded into planes’ cargo holds. If you’d like to avoid your carefully packed luggage being on the wrong side of those statistics, it’s a good idea to know which airlines routinely have the highest rates of mishandled bags. The DOT’s monthly air travel consumer reports compare the 13 largest US airlines and how many bags each carrier mishandles per 100 loaded onto planes. A mishandled bag includes baggage that is lost, delayed, damaged, or stolen. In the first half of 2026, American Airlines had the highest rate of mishandled bags, with an average rate of 0.73 mishandled bags per 100 enplaned, the DOT data shows. Closely following is American’s wholly owned regional subsidiary Envoy Air, which mishandled an average of 0.72 bags per 100 enplaned. United Airlines was next, with a mishandled baggage rate of 0.66 bags per 100 enplaned from January to June 2026. On the flip side, low-cost carrier Allegiant Air had the best baggage handling rate, with just 0.12 bags mishandled per 100 enplaned. Travelers who want to keep close tabs on their checked luggage can put devices like Apple Air Tags into their bags and track them during each stage of the flight. Many airlines now integrate Air Tag data into their baggage tracking process, allowing travelers to share the device location with customer service representatives through their mobile apps. Here’s a look at the DOT’s full US airline rankings for the most mishandled bags per 100 enplaned for the first half of 2026: - American Airlines: 0.73 bags - Envoy Air: 0.72 bags - United Airlines: 0.66 bags - Skywest: 0.55 bags - Republic Airways: 0.53 bags - Alaska Airlines/Hawaiian Airlines: 0.53 bags - Frontier Airlines: 0.51 bags - Spirit Airlines: 0.47 bags - PSA Airlines: 0.44 bags - Delta Air Lines: 0.38 bags - Southwest Airlines: 0.32 bags - JetBlue Airways: 0.31 bags - Allegiant Air: 0.12 bags

item.title: The Best Beaches in Italy, From Sicily to Puglia
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.92
You’d be hard-pressed to find a more quintessential Italian pastime than spending a summer day at the beach—and the best beaches in Italy lend themselves to precisely that kind of leisurely indulgence. The country has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, so you can bet there’s a piece of waterfront for everyone. Some are long, wide strips of sand dotted by neat rows of lounge chairs and umbrellas, while others are rocky inlets or hidden coves reachable only by boat or hike. The list below culls our picks for the best beaches all along the peninsula and on the islands, from Liguria in the north to Sicily in the south, along with tips on where to stay near each. Some are accessible by train or public ferry, while others require a car (road trip, anyone?). Keep in mind that summer (especially July and August) is the high season, so expect beaches to be more crowded than at other times of the year. For fewer crowds, consider shoulder season months like May, early June, and September. Tips for visiting the best beaches in Italy For some expert advice on planning a beach-oriented itinerary in Italy, we tapped Georgia Yuill, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and Butterfield & Robinson’s region director for Italy. Though the best time to visit Italy can vary depending on the type of trip you want to have, a beach vacation warrants some summer vibes—and strategy. “The best time to go to the beaches of Italy are on the weekdays of June, early July, and September,” Yuill says. “Waterfronts in Sardinia and Sicily are particularly lovely in September with the water warmed up over the previous months and visitor numbers low, leaving you with a tranquil and gorgeous setting.” Yuill says the beaches can get crowded on the weekends in June, July, and August, when you’re competing not only with fellow tourists for spots on the sand but also with Italians who are on their own vacations as well. “That said, experiencing the coastline or islands such as Sardinia by gulet or catamaran is an excellent solution to finding quiet inlets and harder-to-reach beaches,” says Yuill. This list features beaches that are free to access, but if you can swing it, private strips of sand at beach clubs are a great option as well. “Not only are they perfect for people-watching, but they provide all the things travelers may not have packed, like umbrellas and lounge chairs,” Yuill says. Plus, families traveling to Italy with kids will especially appreciate the lifeguards on duty. And who can say no to the convenience of showers, changing areas, and eateries? Finally, Yuill suggests choosing an area designated as a Blue Flag Beach, which indicates that it is clean and well cared for from an environmental perspective. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Kris Fordham and Caitlin Morton.

item.title: The Best Things to Do in Monaco—the Crown Jewel of the French Riviera
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.58
Monaco’s ritzy reputation began more than 150 years ago with the debut of the James Bond-famous Belle Époque-style Casino de Monte-Carlo. Throw in a fresco-adorned clifftop palace, the super yacht–lined harbor, and one of the most anticipated events in the luxury sports industry’s social calendar (the Monaco Grand Prix), and it’s no wonder the principality has emerged as a summertime playground for jetsetters and royalty alike. Flanked by the Mediterranean Sea and the French Alps, the petite principality may be the world’s second-smallest state, but with freshly revamped grande dame hotels, a sleek new seaside promenade, and two billion dollar land expansion project Mareterra—which rapidly earned the nickname “world’s most expensive neighborhood”—Monaco is proving it’s more than royals and race cars. There’s also the prestigious Rolex Monte-Carlo Masters tennis tournament—and some seats even come with panoramic Mediterranean Sea views, too. While the principality may claim a few superlatives—with the annual Monaco Yacht Show, the unofficial closer to high season, often touting the world’s priciest super yacht—it’s much more accessible than most travelers realize. And thanks to an uptick in direct seasonal flights, it’s even easier to reach. Here’s where to go and what to do when you get there. Getting there and around The Nice airport is the gateway to the French Riviera, and now you can fly direct year-round from New York (JFK) or Newark with business-class-only La Compagnie; seasonally from Atlanta, Philadelphia, and Washington, DC; or from most major cities in Europe. If you’re taking a train from another part of France or Italy, you’ll have to connect in Nice or the Italian border town of Ventimiglia. From Nice, it’s a 25-minute drive or seven-minute helicopter ride to the principality via Blade. Once you arrive in Monaco, the easiest way to get around is by foot or bus (you can tap a credit card or pay for a ticket onboard). Carshare services like Uber and Bolt will drop you in the principality, but you can’t request a car to take you from Monaco to another destination. You can, however, order a taxi or request one through your hotel and charge it to your room, if you’re staying at one of the Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer properties. The best things to do in Monaco Monaco’s rocky shoreline doesn’t sport the same swaths of sandy beaches as some of its neighbors, which is why so much real estate is dedicated to pools (there’s even an open-air, Olympic-sized saltwater pool on the port). Sunbathe along the waterfront solarium that's the Côte d'Azur version of Scandinavia's floating saunas, or set off on a half-day whale-watching safari around the coast to spot migrating fin and sperm whales. While Cannes is defined by La Croisette and Nice’s pebble-strewn shores are bordered by the Promenade des Anglais, Monaco’s main beachside stretch, the crescent-shaped sliver Larvotto, recently received a modern makeover helmed by Renzo Piano. A handful of beach clubs and restaurants spill out along the palm-fringed promenade. For a more subdued scene than Saint-Tropez that’s every bit as glamorous, sprawl on a floral-patterned sunbed (a nod to the 1960s-era motif designed for Princess Grace) at La Rose des Vents’s seasonal, Gucci-themed beach club. If you don’t want to peel yourself away from the plage for lunch (and who could blame you?), you can dine on caviar and king crab tacos (a definite must-order) at your lounger. Across the bay, cliffside La Vigie Zanoni, chef Simone Zanoni’s al fresco Italian eatery, resembles an intimate, unfussy version of Capri. The sweeping views of the principality alone are worth it—and if you’re taking part in a boat day, you can even pull up to the restaurant’s private dock. Rooftop Nikki Beach Monte Carlo’s cabana-clad pool embraces the Riviera’s party-heavy beach club vibes, but for something more understated, cruise over to La Môme Riviera’s rose-striped parasols and Italian restaurant, which hover along the rocks in nearby Roquebrune-Cap-Martin. When you arrive at the private pontoon via boat (Star Boat Luxury offers shuttles departing from Port Hercule), the tucked-away enclave feels like you’ve stumbled upon a private island. Nearby Loulou Pirate is a spruced-up take on a fisherman’s hut and embraces the same barefoot-chic vibe today as when the original locale was a hotspot for the likes of Brigitte Bardot in the 1960s and ‘70s. At Monaco’s newish fashion district, One Monte-Carlo, near the casino, splurge or window shop at designer boutiques like Cartier and Saint Laurent, or sip a glass of champagne under the Art Nouveau-style pavilions at Le Jardin Belle Epoque by Perrier Jouët’s pop-up outside Hôtel Hermitage Monte-Carlo. For vintage and second-hand luxury finds, browse Le Dressing’s two boutiques in the portside La Condamine district. If your trip falls over a Friday, hop on a direct, 30-minute train to Ventimiglia for the open-air weekly market—among the largest in Italy—and pause for lunch at waterfront stalwart Marco Polo 1960. In the evening, catch a performance by the likes of Norah Jones, James Blunt, and John Legend during the Monte-Carlo Summer Festival; take a seat for a classical concert or opera like Carmen at Opéra de Monte-Carlo; or watch a film under the stars at the open-air cinema beneath the Oceanographic Museum. Where to eat and drink The French Riviera is dotted with Michelin-starred restaurants running from the coast up to perched medieval villages like Èze and the neighboring town of Menton, where for the past 20 years Mauro Colagreco’s three-star Mirazur has been as revolutionary for France’s culinary scene as Noma for Denmark’s. Inside Monaco’s covered Condamine market hall in the Place d’Armes square, Colagreco’s Mitron Bakery features a selection of sourdough loaves that are milled and baked daily in Menton. (While the indoor market is closed for construction, vendors are serving from kiosks in the square.) If the weather is nice, head to the smaller port in Fontvieille to Les Perles de Monte-Carlo for platters of freshly shucked oysters and perfectly seasoned sea bass (this place fills up fast, so reserve in advance). Nearby, the original Beefbar—which has expanded to include a swish collection of restaurants everywhere from Saint-Tropez to luxury cruise ships and private flights—draws a local crowd for lunch (the smash cheeseburger is one of the house favorites). The terrace of Liguria-born Zeffirino is another go-to for its Genovese pesto coating fresh, square-shaped mandilli pasta (even Frank Sinatra was a fan of the namesake chef Zeffirino’s pesto). At new eco-district Mareterra—where homes and buildings were designed by Renzo Piano, Tadao Ando, and Sir Norman Foster and residents include billionaires and Formula 1 local legend Charles Leclerc—a handful of shops and restaurants have also opened their doors, including London transplant zēphyr, anchored by its own sultry cocktail bar Naked & Famous. Throughout the principality, young chefs are shaking up stuffy fine-dining concepts, replacing decadent, drenched-in-sauce dishes with lighter fare that lets the Riviera’s seasonal ingredients shine. One of the best examples is Blue Bay Marcel Ravin, where subtle flavors of the Caribbean and its distinct spices are infused into the Martinique-born chef’s cuisine. Picture artisanal plates dressed with vanilla sugar cane vinegar and cassava crumble. The open kitchen unfolds into the airy dining room accented by natural materials like sleek wood paneling and coral-inspired screens disguising tables, so they feel more like private booths—but the true showstopper is the seaside terrace, especially at sunset. There’s no shortage of places to see-and-be-seen in the principality, from Roaring Twenties-inspired rooftop restaurant La Môme Monte-Carlo, where a singer serenades tables that peer over the port and Prince’s Palace, to Amazónico, another rooftop setting that overlooks the glistening casino and where entertainment ranges from Bossa Nova and Cuban music to DJs spinning “electro-tropical” beats. Across the square, book dinner at Greek-Mediterranean GAIA, which draws a fashionable crowd of locals and famous faces year-round (discretion is key, so avoid trying to snap shots of F1 drivers). Take a seat in the foliage-filled terrace, which feels plucked out of the Athens Riviera, and sip a selection of expertly curated Greek Assyrtiko wines. Share classic spreads like taramosalata before ordering from the restaurant’s own fish market, where options include carpaccio or ceviche, as well as grilled whole fish with a drizzle of lemon oil. Then, as the evening progresses, join the well-heeled crowd filing into speakeasy-style, members-only lounge NYX. Monaco’s nightlife ranges from bottle service at late-night lounges like velvet-lined SASS CAFE to DJs spinning tribal house beats at nearby COYA Monte-Carlo, a waterfront, Peruvian-fusion eatery with a pisco bar and lounge. (If you’re after a cavernous, late-night club, you’ll find a few of those, too, including Twiga and Jimmy’z Monte-Carlo). For something more lowkey, start or end your evening with apéro (pre-dinner drinks and light bites) or a nightcap under the Eiffel-designed glass dome at Gustave at Hôtel Hermitage or at Hôtel de Paris’s legendary Le Bar Américain, a 1920s-era haunt popular with everyone from Joséphine Baker and Cary Grant to Lady Gaga. Open year-round, jazz, swing, blues, and soul performers entertain every evening and bar snacks include some of the best barbajuans (Swiss chard-filled fritters) in town. Where to stay Monaco’s sprinkling of five-star Belle Époque hotels are huddled around the Carré d’Or (Golden Square), crowned by the historic centerpiece Casino de Monte-Carlo. The independently owned, Jacques Garcia-designed Hôtel Métropole Monte-Carlo boasts designer names like the Spa Métropole by Guerlain and the Karl Lagerfeld-designed Odyssey, an urban rooftop oasis with a heated saltwater pool and Italian poolside restaurant Zia. Reviving Joël Robuchon's longstanding institution, the late chef’s former right hand is at the helm of the namesake, two Michelin-starred Les Ambassadeurs by Christophe Cussac. Jacques Garcia was brought back on board to spearhead the two-year renovation of the restaurant, which features an open-kitchen concept, chef’s table with 360-degree views of the team at work, and cigar lounge in the extended lobby bar, where a trio of museum-worthy pieces by Pablo Picasso, Francis Bacon, and Andy Warhol anchor the space. One other aspect popular with fans of the former Robuchon eatery has also been brought back: the legendary bread and dessert trolleys. Facing the casino, the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo is perhaps the most emblematic of Monaco, and after a multi-year, multimillion-dollar renovation, it’s among the most modern as well. You’ll still see timeless glamour in the gilded dining room of three-star Le Louis XV – Alain Ducasse, with its gold leaf-painted frescoes and columns (and Bordeaux-modeled wine cellar lined with more than 350,000 bottles). But with revamped Art Deco rotunda rooms overlooking the super yacht-filled harbor, and the expansive Prince Rainier III Suite, outfitted with a two-level outdoor lounge and infinity pool perched over the casino, rooms not only offer some of the best views, they’re some of the most luxurious in the South of France. The family-friendly Monte-Carlo Bay Hotel & Resort feels like more of a Mediterranean island retreat, with seaside sun beds and beach fare from two Michelin-starred chef Marcel Ravin; Balinese-style beds by the sand-bottom lagoon; and water sports like parasailing and tubing available off the hotel’s pontoon. At the opposite end of the principality, in what’s technically considered France, the terra cotta-colored Monte Carlo Beach exudes retro, 1930s charm with Art Deco, California villa-inspired rooms hugging the coastline, and an Olympic-sized saltwater pool that served as a backdrop for Helmut Newton’s Vogue and Vanity Fair shoots. A perk for guests staying at Monte-Carlo Beach, Hôtel de Paris, and Hôtel Hermitage: access to the pool and private plage at Monte-Carlo Beach Club, which sports a Jacquemus-themed pontoon with matching striped beach beds. For a stay that comes with sky-high rooms showing off sweeping views of the principality, modernist The Maybourne Riviera is perched along the rocky peninsula of Roquebrune-Cap-Martin and features chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s New York transplant, abc kitchens riviera, plus a striking infinity pool suspended nearly a thousand feet above the sea.

item.title: 11 Scenic Train Rides in the US Worth Booking for the Views Alone
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.27
Every year, instead of flying home to southeastern Virginia, I always opt to take the train. My journey typically starts in New York, winding down the Northeast Corridor before stopping in Washington, DC. While this busy stretch of track is far from the most scenic train ride in the US, there were still moments when I found my face pressed against the window—like near Havre de Grace, Maryland where the Susquehanna River widens—unable to look away. It was a reminder of how the joys of slow travel can sneak up on you, even in familiar places you may have traveled through countless times before. That said, there are certain train routes in the US with scenery so mesmerizing that they are worth taking for the sights alone. Amtrak, of course, has more than 30 different train routes crisscrossing every US region, from the vast deserts of the Southwest to the sparkling coast of California, and majestic mountain ranges in between. But even more private rail operators in states like Alaska and Hawaii offer their own scenic train rides that shouldn't be overlooked. The challenge, then, becomes picking which train trip to take—and when. Below, we’ve selected 13 of the most scenic train rides in the US that are worth booking for the views alone. item.title: The Best Hotels Near the Sphere in Las Vegas
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.14
I’ve been taking trips to Las Vegas since long before the Sphere was there, and half the fun—for me, at least—has always been staying somewhere central in this wonderfully over-the-top city. A good Vegas hotel should make it easy to slip between a long lunch, a pool afternoon, a big dinner, and whatever you’ve got planned after dark without spending precious vacation time stuck in traffic—and since the Sphere opened in September 2023, there’s a new glowing landmark to factor into that equation. The enormous exosphere has become essential to the Vegas skyline, but the real draw is inside: an immersive venue unlike anything else in the city (or the world, really), where the scale of the screen, sound, and space makes going to a show feel like a transformative event. Booking a hotel nearby is ideal if you're eager to be a quick walk or drive from the venue but also want to keep the neon, restaurants, casinos, pools, and beautiful absurdity of the Strip within reach. Whether you’re planning around the event of your dreams or simply want to experience Vegas’s newest and most iconic orb in all its glory, these are the hotels worth checking into less than a 10-minute drive from the Sphere. FAQ: What big shows are coming up at the Sphere? The Sphere’s fall-through-winter calendar is especially stacked: The Eagles return September 18 through January 23, while Metallica takes over October 1 through March 13. The iconic Wizard of Oz experience goes through December 7, and the Backstreet Boys are back for a New Year’s run from December 26 through January 2. Looking ahead, Oprah Winfrey’s AHA live immersive experience will take place April 2 to 4. You can always stay up to date on the Sphere's website. What to know when walking to the Sphere: While an over-20-minute walk might sound daunting to some, walking to the Sphere in Las Vegas is highly efficient via the indoor, climate-controlled pedestrian bridge connected directly to The Venetian Resort. Visitors arriving from other Las Vegas Strip properties should anticipate a 15-to-30-minute walk through connecting hotel corridors or along Sands Avenue. Due to the venue's grand scale and layout, wear comfortable shoes to easily navigate the extensive walkways and stairways. Also remember to pack light before making your way—the Sphere enforces a strict bag size limit of six by six by two inches, and does not have on-site storage facilities. How we choose the best hotels near the Sphere in Las Vegas: Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

item.title: 13 Best Hotels in Key West, From Historic Inns to Private Islands
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.92
Long known for its free-spirited vibe and its identity as the iconoclastic “Conch Republic,” Key West welcomes you to come as you are, whether that means strolling past street-roaming roosters in your finest cowboy hat and Daisy Dukes, joining the revelers on Duval Street à la Mardi Gras, enjoying family time on the beach, or just staying put around your hotel pool “wasting away again in Margaritaville.” (Jimmy Buffett actually wrote the final verses of the song circa 1977 while stuck in traffic on the Seven Mile Bridge heading back to the Florida Keys, then debuted it on Duval Street shortly thereafter.) It’s definitely a place that caters to hedonistic tendencies at land’s end, especially during Fantasy Fest and other wild celebrations throughout the year, but it’s equally suited to soaking up the sun and embracing an IDGAF attitude. Beneath the more recent commercialization of Key West lies a deeper charm, reflected in its eclectic mix of resorts. The most sought-after stays are in Old Town, which occupies the island’s western edge, touching both the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. Old Town is remarkably walkable, with fabulous restaurants, historic sites, and kitschy dive bars never more than a short stroll away. True, there are plenty of places to stay in New Town, often at lower rates. But why rely on an hourly shuttle to Old Town or stare at a chain mall parking lot from your room when so much of the fun of Key West is crawling back to your hotel through picturesque neighborhoods and lush gardens after a night of debauchery? There’s also something to be said for actually sleeping in one of the historic cottages and buildings that speak to Key West's earlier days, recalling the words of Hemingway and lyrics of Buffett. Whether you’re after a romantic retreat, a fun weekend with your besties, a gay nudist escape, or a laid-back family vacation, you’ll find it among our picks for the best hotels in Key West. item.title: This Dual-Voltage Hair Dryer Is Actually Lightweight and Compact Enough to Pack
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.83
I envy my friends who arrive at the airport with nothing but a slim carry-on in tow. I, on the other hand, check a bag every time. And yes, I do overpack, but I really try not to; by the time I lay all my hair tools on one side of my suitcase, it's halfway full. So, I accepted the fact that I'll never be a carry-on-only traveler a long time ago. But recently, I got my hands on Dyson's new Supersonic travel hair dryer—and for the first time, I might actually be able to save some space in my suitcase. Dyson's latest hair tool is specifically designed with travelers in mind—it's 32% smaller and 25% lighter than the brand's OG best-selling Supersonic hair dryer, meaning it can be tucked away in the corner of a suitcase or pocket of a weekender bag with ease. I've had the Dyson Airwrap for years, and don't get me wrong, it's great—but between the long barrel, the multiple attachments, and the thick cord, it's usually way too bulky for me to pack. When I'm traveling, I want something easy, fuss-free, and overpacker-friendly. On a recent bachelorette trip to Rosemary Beach, Florida, I easily packed my Dyson Supersonic travel hair dryer in my suitcase. And because my friends and I were staying in an Airbnb, a hair dryer wasn't provided, so it was even more important that I bring one. If you, like me, are tired of filling up the majority of your suitcase by packing a bulky hair dryer or styling system, Dyson's new travel tool is worth checking out. I had two main concerns when the hair tool arrived. First, is it actually smaller and lighter than your average hair dryer? And yes, it absolutely is. It's really not much bigger than my iPhone, and takes up a fraction of the space in my bag that my Airwrap does. Second, I wanted to know if it actually worked as well as other Dyson hair tools—or if this smaller version would mean I sacrificed power. Within seconds of turning it on, I could tell this mini hair dryer packed a serious punch. It heats up in seconds and has just as much strength as my full-size Dyson Airwrap. The major pro for this travel hair dryer is that it's dual voltage, meaning you can safely use it in outlets abroad too—unlike the Dyson Airwrap and original Supersonic hair dryer. I love knowing I can take this tool anywhere, whether I'm at home in New Jersey or traveling to Europe. I also love the look of it sitting on a hotel bathroom counter. It's so simple and sleek—and the slim barrel is easy to grip and hold while drying. Its design is simple: There's a button to turn it on and off, a button to control the three heat settings, and another for its two speeds. I have long hair, and the Dyson can fully dry it in about 10 minutes—even when it's sopping wet right out of the shower. It also leaves my hair with a glossy, shiny finish—unlike the hair dryer usually found at hotels that can sometimes leave my hair feeling dry and brittle. I like that the cable length is shorter than most tools (it's only 6.5 feet, compared to the original model that is 8.6 feet). It also comes with a Styling Concentrator, a small attachment that helps prevent frizz and leaves your hair a little smoother. Another cool perk is that it's compatible with attachments for the original Supersonic hair dryer, so you don't have to buy additional parts if you want to mix and match. My only gripe with this hair tool is the price. $300 for a hair dryer is expensive—a lot pricier than others I've used in the past. But it does work way better than any hair dryer I've tried before and is much lighter and smaller. Given its compact size, impressive power, and dual-voltage capabilities, I say it's worth it. I originally got this hair dryer with only travel in mind. But for the past two months, it's been my go-to hair tool, even when I'm home. Call me lazy, but it's so much easier to pull this thing out than my bulkier Airwrap to dry my hair. I recommend Dyson's new hair dryer for any frequent travelers looking for something compact, lightweight, and dual voltage. Or anyone wanting a go-to hair dryer that's less bulky but works just as well as larger hair tools on the market (perfect for those with limited storage space in their bathroom). Whether I'm packing for a two-week trip overseas or a quick weekend escape, you'll definitely find this small-but-mighty hair tool in my bag.

item.title: 29 Best Hotels in Miami (2026), From Key Biscayne to Wynwood
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.79
Once dominated by pastel Art Deco and late-night bass, the best hotels in Miami have evolved into an eclectic, high-design, sprawling ecosystem. Beyond the legendary oceanfront icons of South Beach lie moody art-filled sanctuaries, discreet European-style retreats, and soaring glass towers anchored in the cosmopolitan energy of Brickell. Luckily, when it comes to picking the right one, towering Downtown Miami and iconic Miami Beach alike have a wide variety of top-tier accommodations for every need (and bank account). City-loving travelers will be pleasantly surprised by the sophisticated hotels in Miami’s dense urban core. Beach-goers can look forward to thousands of square feet of pristine beach to enjoy at a number of oceanfront resorts. Whether you are chasing Damien Hirst gold, rooftop bars, or pristine (and velvet-rope-free) beaches, here are the absolute best places to check in right now. Our top picks: - Best overall: 1 Hotel South Beach - Best for beach access: Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club - Most romantic: Faena Hotel Miami Beach - Best for families: Loews Miami Beach Hotel - Best for first-timers: Andaz Miami Beach by Hyatt - Read Full ReviewAfter a six-year closure and a $100 million restoration, the Delano Miami Beach returns knowing exactly what made it legendary in the first place: design, drama, and glamor with a sense of place. Elastic Architects resisted turning the hotel into a museum of its former selves, instead weaving together restored favorites like the Rose Bar with guestrooms that feel warmer and more inviting than before, especially the two-story Poolside Bungalows just steps from the hotel's iconic pool. In the Delano’s third incarnation, one of Miami Beach's best beach-and-pool scenes returns (both cocktail- and kid-friendly this go’round), paired with high profile restaurants by Paris Society, namely Gigi Rigolatto and Mimi Kakushi, where locals often outnumber overnight guests. Add Café Delano's irresistible pistachio croissants, heartfelt service, an immaculate art collection, and members programming open to hotel guests, and the Delano once again is all the hype on South Beach. - Read Full ReviewA crisp, minimalist European import that seamlessly blends modern corporate cool with Miami's vibrant rooftop culture all while being tucked away on a quiet leafy street in Brickell’s bustling neighborhood. The 275 rooms here are a calm and cool retreat from Miami’s loud and frenetic downtown. Spacious and flooded with natural light, thanks to floor-to-ceiling windows, the rooms lean into a soothing palette of cool grays, warm wood accents, and pops of yellow. Brickell’s glittering skyline envelopes this high-rise and, depending on where your room is situated, you can catch a glimpse of Biscayne Bay or the lush Simpson Park that cuts through a swath of downtown. Bathrooms are streamlined and modern with expansive glass walk-in showers and all rooms include Lavazza coffee makers and mini-fridges. - Read Full ReviewArriving at the Surfcomber feels a bit like hopscotching through Miami Beach history. The hotel's Collins Avenue neighbors—The Sagamore, National, SLS, among others—line the street in linen white. Not one to break dress code, the Surfcomber's façade is also marked by sharp lines; a dramatic, semicircle driveway to coast into; and smooth, matte-white walls—a fitting canvas for the party lights that paint the South Beach streets neon. With 186 rooms, there is a box-of-chocolates variety of accommodations to choose from, whether you're a solo traveler just looking for a place to settle at night, or you're looking to really treat yourself by booking an oceanfront suite with your own private balcony. All rooms come with luxury Atelier Bloem bath products, and keep to a generally neutral palette to keep the attention on the view from your room. A visit to the pool and backyard space is just about necessary when it comes to staying at the Surfcomber. Be amazed by the difference the distance of the lobby can make between the bass-boosted streets and the secluded beach bar and stunning pool—go ahead, rent that cabana. - Read Full ReviewUnframed, Autograph Collection signals a fun, cutting-edge design chapter for Miami Beach—with bold, curvy architecture and easygoing spaces that invite you to stay a while. Behind its sculptural façade, you’ll find plush rooms, a rooftop pool for lingering, and a French Riviera–inspired dining scene that gives the hotel its own personality. It’s a stylish home base for exploring South Beach—close enough to the action, but with plenty of reasons to come back before the night is over. The 149 rooms feel like a cool retreat from the buzz of Miami Beach. Rich velvet headboards, warm wood finishes, and pops of blush and rust make the spaces feel inviting and chic, while details like marble vanities and sleek microcement showers add just the right amount of drama. - Read Full ReviewBlink and you might think you mistakenly hopped a plane to Savannah instead of South Beach: At the northernmost end of Ocean Drive, this hotel’s Florida-Georgia style of architecture sticks out like a colonial masterpiece in a sea of pastel-colored Art Deco gems. While some people head to the neighborhood with only late nights out on their mind, The Betsy attracts a different, more erudite crowd. Yes, they love being in the thick of all that touristy mayhem, but prefer that it not happen right outside their window. And it’s not just the hotel’s quaint façade that seems to attract a different type of South Beach reveler; inside, the public spaces act as a sort of art gallery, with photo exhibitions rotating throughout the year. Rooms are spacious and have mini libraries, writing desks, and oversized marble bathrooms; the hotel also counts two pools and a rooftop ocean deck among its attractions. - Read Full ReviewThe first new hotel to grace South Beach’s storied Española Way in a decade, the enchanting Esme Miami Beach is all about the boutique hotel charms. Rather than replicate the easy, breezy, sand-in-your-toes style of South Beach’s grand dames, this restored enclave (which comprises eight buildings connected by charming paseos) offers a well-placed base from which to explore South Beach. You know you’re in for a unique experience as soon as you walk in the door; the lobby is outfitted with thick crimson carpeting, Moroccan-style benches, and accents of brass and dark green, setting the tone for the Moorish influence on decor throughout the property. The rooftop pool is small but striking (and not really made for anything other than dipping), but it’s a perfect spot for catching sun under the connected peach and white striped daybeds that line the deck. - Read Full ReviewLocated in the trendy Brickell neighborhood, this Four Seasons lets you discover Miami beyond just the beach—without sacrificing those turquoise water views. With a two-acre, palm tree-lined rooftop pool overlooking Biscayne Bay, you can access the best of the city’s vibrant downtown area while still enjoying the tropical relaxation one deserves when vacationing in South Florida. Most of the guests here are well-heeled business travelers, but there were also a fair amount of (well-behaved) young families and friend groups on vacation mode at the property’s sprawling pool facilities. Among Miamians, the hotel is best known for its extravagant Sunday Brunch; all tables become immediately filled with a combination of local residents and hotel guests, a natural overlap felt throughout the property, which is also home to the Four Seasons Residences. - Read Full ReviewJust as he did back in the 1990s with the Delano, Ian Schrager is reinventing the Miami Beach experience with The Edition. Here, every amenity a person could want (or even know was possible) is there for the taking—ice skating rink included—and the hotel has five fabulous drinking and dining options, including Matador Room, Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s innovative Latin fusion restaurant. There’s no detail in the rooms that hasn't been scrutinized in an attempt to exceed guests’ every expectation, and the heavenly, low-slung bed—which sits atop a light oak frame that blends in with the walls, and is topped with a down comforter and pillows—is no exception. - Read Full ReviewThere are two entry points to the Gale: through the high-ceilinged, grand valet on one side, and rose-hued in-house restaurant Casa Gianna on the other. Either route makes for quite the entrance to this sparkling 51-story tower, where glamorous people with things to do come and go at a steady clip. This is an affordable, reliable stay smack dab in the thick of Downtown Miami that feels impenetrably tranquil despite the noise all around. The rooms here mirror the residences in the same building, so you can book a studio, one-bedroom, or two-bedroom ranging from 410 to 910 square feet. Most of these have full kitchens and washer-dryers, so you can really set up shop. Decor is minimal and modern, with black-and-white photography on the walls and furniture in neutral colors. The windows are floor-to-ceiling for the most part, meaning massive Miami views. Take out a bike to Miami Beach—you’ll fly past traffic and will not regret it. - Read Full ReviewThe Ritz-Carlton South Beach, one of a string of hotels on Miami’s destination waterfront, is a refined respite from the area’s pool parties and 'til-the-sun-rises nightlife, while still providing easy access to the city’s best restaurants, a great lobby bar scene, and ocean views. The rooms are crisp and modern, with white walls and linens punctuated by deep cerulean blue furniture—a velvet bed frame, plush chaise—and midcentury-style accents like bronze reading lamps and caned armchairs. In the ocean-view rooms and suites, which make up a majority of the room categories, the brilliant Atlantic out of the window is the real star of the show, just as it should be. Like most Ritz-Carltons, the experience is reliably five-star: service is fantastic, the decor is elevated and modern while nodding to the destination, amenities leave little to be desired, and the location is ideal. - Read Full ReviewThe first hotel to officially open in Wynwood, Miami’s graffiti-clad neighborhood that’s now home to dozens of galleries, shops, and restaurants—the Arlo is an art-filled oasis that seeks to strike a balance between being a splashy getaway and a vibrant urban hotel. The hotel’s aesthetic draws on the neighborhood’s high concentration of street art, with the property's exterior walls featuring works by Miami-based artist Hoxxoh, and 250 pieces of contemporary art positioned throughout the public spaces and guest rooms. There’s an inviting ninth-floor rooftop pool with a cocktail bar and views of the Miami skyline. The hotel also strives to be a hub of activity for its guests with weekly programming like comedy nights, fitness classes, and space devoted to loungey coworking environments with a pool table and a yoga deck. While the hotel is lacking in certain frills (like room service), there are also thoughtful touches like complimentary fortune cookies in the rooms with unique fortunes and bicycles for guests to explore the neighborhood. - Read Full ReviewMiami Beach’s midcentury Art Deco scene may have cemented its place in design history, but today a new, grown-up iteration can be found in the form of The Shelborne By Proper. Guest rooms are reflective of the entire property’s mood: elevated yet easy. My room on the sixth floor featured a partial ocean view, just enough of a glimpse of that turquoise blue water to whet my palate. The room’s design feels calm and grounded, which I owe to the soft, earthy tones and warm, natural textiles. It’s a nice counterbalance to the energetic vibe that Miami Beach naturally offers, a true retreat that feels intentionally devoid of flashy artwork and instead focuses on curved, architectural furnishings that are low-profile and slim. Also noteworthy is that the design is nowhere near that stereotypical Florida coastal-chic image with wooden floors and shiplapped walls. Instead, the rooms are elevated with marble flooring that is warmed up with a textured off-white rug. - Read Full ReviewEven amid the architectural exhibitionism of Miami Beach, the gleaming curved main tower of the 1,500-room Fontainebleau Miami Beach is a knockout. The design of this essentially launched the so-called Miami-Modern style, and the resort dominates its stretch of Miami Beach. It’s a clean and classic escape where contemporary vibes meet retro in a flash of glamour. Although the Fontainebleau has been upgraded at no small expense, guests still feel like they’re part of its storied past. - Read Full ReviewOpened in 2024, this 13-room hotel is nestled inside the four-story landmark Moore building, which also houses a posh coworking space, private club, art gallery, and restaurant on the ground floor. Upon walking inside, you’re immediately struck by the Zaha Hadid site-specific installation Elastika that spans the light-filled atrium connecting the different levels with stretches of web-like material. It’s both cheeky and iconic. The main spot here is Torno Subito, located on the ground floor of the atrium and headed up by famed Italian chef Massimo Bottura and his team. The menu focuses on modern Italian cuisine and includes dishes like Mediterranean Sea Bass stuffed with pork, tiny, handmade tortellini served in a rich Parmigiano broth, and “Oops, I burned the Key lime pie”—a South Florida-inspired reimagining of Bottura's iconic "Oops, I dropped the lemon tart" dessert. Guests of the hotel can also dine on the second-floor balcony restaurant that is part of the members’ club. My lunch there included a delicious hen-of-the-woods mushroom pizza and spicy tuna crispy rice from the sushi bar. During city-wide events like Art Basel and Formula 1, the place is a hive of activity. FAQ: How we choose the best hotels in Miami Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property.
