item.title: Claude Monet’s most famous paintings are coming to Tate Modern in a major 2027 exhibition
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.21
Culture-loving Londoners have been treated to a string of excellent exhibitions this year. From Queen Elizabeth II: Her Life in Style at The King's Gallery to The Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum, there has been no shortage of showcases to capture our imaginations. As summer draws to a close, more details about the exhibitions we can look forward to next year are emerging. The latest? Tate Modern’s first-ever exhibition focused on the world-renowned work of French painter Claude Monet, of course. Set to open its doors on 25 February 2027 and run until 27 June 2027, the exhibition will feature more than 60 paintings in what’s said to be the UK’s largest presentation of the Impressionist’s work in nearly a decade. Coinciding with the 100th anniversary of Monet’s death, Monet: Painting Time will span masterpieces from the 1870s to the 1920s, tracing the artist’s lifelong entanglement with nature. Highlights to see along the gallery walls will include iconic paintings such as Cathédrale de Rouen, effet de soleil, fin de journée (1892) and a selection of rarely exhibited loans from private collections like Branch of the Seine near Giverny (Sunrise) (1897). In a statement announcing the exhibition, Sasha de Marigny, Anthropic’s chief brand and communications officer, said: "Alive to colour, light, and shimmering motion, Monet uniquely captured a mood and a moment in a world that never held still. A century on, his work asks us to slow down, notice each carefully placed brushstroke and dash of colour, and find the world more vivid for it. Anthropic is proud to support Tate Modern's first solo exhibition dedicated to his work." Monet transformed the way artists painted modern life, capturing the effects of light, atmosphere and time through rapid, expressive brushstrokes. The master artist repeatedly returned to the same subjects, including haystacks, cathedrals, poplars and the Seine, painting them at different times of day and year to reveal nature’s constant transformation. At Giverny, where he settled in 1883, his garden and pond inspired his monumental Water Lily series, which occupied the final three decades of his career. As museums and galleries continue to announce their 2027 programmes, we’re all eyes and ears, anticipating the year’s hottest tickets.

item.title: Where was 'Slow Horses' filmed? 5 London locations to look out for in the Apple TV+ series
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.16
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Slow Horses filmed? In 2022, Apple TV+ viewers were introduced to sinister forces and an underground world of espionage via London’s Slough House. Here, a dysfunctional team of British intelligence agents, all of whom have committed career-ending mistakes, work behind the scenes in an MI5 ‘dumping ground’. Across five seasons, chaos has followed the Slow Horses as they duck and dive their way through the city, uncovering plots and secrets along the way. Now, Emmy Award and BAFTA winner Sir Gary Oldman returns as Jackson Lamb for Slow Horses’ highly anticipated sixth season – with plenty of recognisable London locations to look out for. Here, we highlight some of the key filming locations across the city so you can turn them into a set-jetting walking route – free of menacing encounters, hopefully. Aldersgate Street The Slow Horses’ base, Slough House, has remained the same since the show first aired. You can find the dumping ground on Aldersgate Street, just around the corner from Barbican Underground Station. The office site sits next to Vecchio Parioli, a family-run Italian restaurant that’s been serving up hearty fare since 1950. Duke of York statue This London landmark, a column dedicated to Prince Frederick, the second son of King George III, is the backdrop of Lamb and Taverner’s final exchange in season one. Regent’s Park Eagle-eyed viewers will have spotted filming across parts of Regent’s Park in season three, as Taverner (played by Kristin Scott Thomas) and Lamb meet away from prying eyes. Scenes use the park’s North Gate entrance and one of the canalside benches. Granary Square Fountains River (played by Jack Lowden) and Frank’s season four showdown takes place in Granary Square Fountains. While this takes place on the banks of the River Thames in the novels, it proved a bit of a logistical nightmare on-screen – it turns out that having actors chucked into the Thames isn't the most health-and-safety-friendly stunt. Beppe's Cafe This is the real cafe that Jackson Lamb visits for his breakfasts. The hideout is a greasy spoon popular with those who live and work around Smithfield Market. Season 1 - 5 of Slow Horses is available to watch on Apple TV+ now. Season 6 airs weekly until 21 October 2026.

item.title: Inside the secret Yorkshire art walk that’s harder to get into than Glastonbury
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.15
I love walking. As a Cotswolds countryside resident, my once-concrete jaunts across east London have been swapped for crunchy grass stomps through cow-laden fields or floating across rolling hills just out my front door. I also love art. Exhibitions and retrospectives are often what dictate my travels. A recent dash on the Eurostar brought me to a speedy 48-hour whip around the late David Hockney exhibition at the Louis Vuitton Museum in Paris, in between long bistro meals and a snoop around the city’s latest new hotel opening. So when a few art-obsessed friends returned from what they called the most incredible walk of their lives up in the North York Moors, but said that they couldn't really tell me why, I was immediately intrigued. I began researching and uncovered an outdoor art walk where tickets to gain access to were as hard as heading to Glastonbury. The walk is, rather intriguingly, called Hanging Stones. I'd heard about artist Andy Goldsworthy from my mother. The contemporary English land artist has been shaping, morphing and discerningly using his hands to form large scale works using natural materials we might often overlook in everyday life: stones, snow, rock, leaves, iron, twigs, mud and more. One of his most talked-about pieces involved transporting 13 one-tonne snowballs from Scotland and placing them on the streets of London during a hot summer's day. He challenges and inspires conversation about our world and its precious land, and for his ongoing project up in Yorkshire – commissioned by the David Ross Foundation – he shifts the focus to the raw beauty of the Moors. To get tickets, eager hikers need to set reminders to check the website. Slots open at hangingstones.org – it’s currently booked out for the rest of the year, but new releases come out regularly. It costs £10 per adult; under-18s and students go free. There’s a maximum of four groups of six allowed each day. On the day, collect your laminated map and keys from Sevenford House B&B, then head to the Milburn Arms in Rosedale Abbey where the circular walk begins and ends. Allow five to six hours... you’ll need it, and wear proper boots (once you have your slot, I’d advise against trying to change it, so prepare for all weather conditions) and bring your own food and water – there are no facilities en route. My husband and I set off up north for a six-mile hike through farmers' fields and dormant heather hills to to pick up an instruction guide and a set of dangling keys… Here's everything we found along the way. To Goldsworthy, the whole walk is an artwork in itself. There are ten stone outbuildings, some rebuilt from ruin, all immaculately beautiful and each with its own installation inside. The tenth, titled Heygate Thorns, is currently in the works, but there’s a tiny window Goldsworthy left for you to have a special glimpse. My favourite stretch was the uphill push to the furthest point you reach before looping back, which is surrounded by hazy gorse and heather. There’s magic in unlocking giant padlocks and not knowing what’s inside. The signposts felt straight out of Lord of the Rings; little slits of eyes hammered into stone are your earmarks to keep you on your way. Don’t forget to look up. The light can change everything. Goldsworthy makes the mundane something joyful to look at. Perhaps the perfect picnic spot, or keep on pushing to the highest point of the walk for a chapel- like shelter on a particularly blustering day.

item.title: The best villas in Morocco for group getaways in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.95
Glittering Morocco’s diverse landscapes, azure coastlines and breathless, eclectic cityscapes make it an attractive destination to visit year-round and the best villas in Morocco offer an especially memorable way to see it all. There’s no shortage of wonderful hotels, but for a group trip without the crowds, a private villa is best. For families and big groups of friends, they offer the best of both worlds: the privacy and space to settle in on your own terms, often with the pools, sprawling gardens and attentive service you’d expect from a luxury hotel. Around Marrakech in particular, villas offer a chance to dip into the energy of the medina before retreating to a quieter base, with many properties looking towards the peaks of the Atlas Mountains. The bustling capital city has perennial charm, but beyond its walls, there’s so much more to Morocco worth exploring. Whether you’re gearing up for a hiking trip to the Atlas mountains, looking to immerse yourself in the sights and sounds of the buzzy souks or headed out to the coast, there’s a fantastic nearby address to know. Most of our favourite Morocco villas pair idyllic views with in-house chefs, housekeepers and even security staff for a hotel-worthy break in your own space. Below are ten of the best villa rentals in Morocco to know about in 2026. Editor's picks: For big groups: Fabulous riad with garden, Marrakech For sea views: Rustic farmhouse, Essaouira For an afforable stay: Breezy minimal villa, Essaouira How we choose the best villas in Morocco We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. All listings featured on Condé Nast Traveller are independently selected by our editors. If you book something through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This is our pick of the best villas in Morocco.

item.title: The other side of Capri: Why Anacapri is the island’s best-kept secret
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.45
I have been visiting Capri for nearly two decades, but it took me surprisingly long to discover Anacapri. For years, my trips comprised people watching on La Piazzetta, browsing the fabulous boutiques, a boat trip over to Bagni Tiberio for lunch and a dip, followed by dinner under the lemon trees at Da Paolino. Do not get me wrong, I still adore all of those things, but a few years ago, I began spending more time on the western side of the island, taking the winding road upwards from Capri town to Anacapri. With its name stemming from the Greek anás (“above”), it felt like discovering a different destination altogether. Set 300 meters above sea level, Anacapri has a slower, more local pace. Its pedestrian lanes lead past whitewashed houses, artisan workshops and tiny piazzas, while the landscape quickly gives way to vineyards, olive groves and dramatic sea views. It is not that Anacapri is untouched by Capri’s glamour; the Jumeirah Capri Palace has been one of the island’s grand addresses for decades and the likes of Jackie O, Gwyneth Paltrow, Mariah Carey and Julia Roberts have chosen this as their more discreet base. However, it still retains a strong sense of village life and is a haven from the crowds, for those in the know. Its character is rooted in its history. Anacapri was once connected to the coast below by the Phoenician Steps, a steep flight of 921 steps that still climbs up from Marina Grande. At the top, the historic centre unfolds around Piazza Vittoria and Via Giuseppe Orlandi, where churches, ceramics shops and family-run restaurants reveal a side of the island that can be easily missed on a day trip. This is where Roman Emperor Tiberius built many of his villas during the 1st century AD. The village has long attracted outsiders, too. Swedish doctor and writer Axel Munthe built the breathtaking Villa San Michele here in the late 19th century, creating a home filled with antiquities and gardens overlooking the Bay of Naples. His villa, now open to the public, has become part of a longer tradition of artists, writers and intellectuals being drawn to Anacapri for its landscape, light and sense of escape. I properly fell for Anacapri in 2021, when I booked a few nights at what was then called 2 Pini, a small, family-run residence tucked away behind the main piazza, next to the Monte Solaro chairlift. We had planned a short stay but ended up extending it (twice). There was something about waking up here, wandering into the village for an espresso and being greeted by Anacaprese people that made it difficult to leave. The property has since been renamed Relais Caposcuro and is being run by the fourth generation of the family, Guido D'Auria, alongside his lovely wife Martina. I have been returning ever since. “Anacapri is where you come to discover the authentic side of the island,” Martina tells me. “If you want to find peace, relaxation, and nature, this is the right place. That is why Axel Munthe, Norman Douglas and Karl Wilhelm Diefenbach chose to spend their days here.” She recalls how visitors are made to feel like locals. “The strength of Anacapri is hidden in its local people. They all know each other but welcome new guests. When you dine at a restaurant, the owner calls you by your name; you are not simply a tourist.” Anacapri is having something of a moment. The arrival of new places to stay is giving visitors more reason to base themselves here. Next year, Casa Caprile will open as part of the Small Luxury Hotels portfolio, bringing a new boutique address to a 19th-century estate that was once the residence of Sweden’s Queen Victoria. But perhaps the most compelling reason to visit now is that it still feels like somewhere to be discovered. This is not simply Capri without the crowds; it is Capri with a different pace and a deeper sense of place. Here are some ideas for where to stay, eat and play in Anacapri. Where to stay in Anacapri Relais Caposcuro For something more intimate, Relais Caposcuro is the kind of family-run place that explains why staying in Anacapri can feel so different from Capri town. Formerly known as 2 Pini, the property grew out of the family’s old vineyards and has been welcoming guests since 1999. Sitting sweetly underneath the Monte Solaro chairlift, it is now being carried into its fourth generation, with Guido D’Auria and his wife Martina running the boutique hotel. “In 1999, we stopped the production of wine and the villa needed renovation, so Nonno Peppino, supported by his daughter Giulia [Guido’s mother], had to make a decision. Either they would sell the estate or transform it into a place where friends and guests could spend their holidays,” Martina explains. “They preferred the latter option so now, thanks to their vision, we welcome people from all around the world. This was formerly a family home, and Guido and I want to keep that feeling.” This is the stay for those who want to feel embedded in the village rather than insulated from it. Fancy taking part in a private cooking class or trying out local craft activities? The team pride themselves on offering bespoke experiences; just drop them a note in advance. Casa Caprile Opening in spring 2027 as part of the Small Luxury Hotels portfolio, Casa Caprile is one to watch. The 19th-century estate is being reimagined as a boutique hotel, with 12 bedrooms, a Mediterranean garden and a distinctly retro aesthetic, including the red-and-white striped awnings that give the property its old-school Riviera feel. Its arrival should add another characterful option to Anacapri’s hotel scene, particularly for travellers looking for something smaller and more design-led than the island’s grand hotels. Booking is now open from May 2027. Jumeirah Capri Palace The grande dame of Anacapri, Jumeirah Capri Palace has long been one of the island’s most polished places to stay. It feels more like an art-filled Mediterranean estate than a conventional luxury hotel. Creativity is woven throughout the experience, from suites decorated with tributes to artists to the hotel’s private collection of more than 100 works, known as the White Museum. The artistic journey begins on arrival, where Arnaldo Pomodoro’s Rive dei Mari, a 40-metre-long fibreglass-and-marble-dust wall installation inspired by Capri’s fishing history, runs the length of the entrance. A bronze helmet by Mimmo Paladino follows, with further works by Paladino, Giorgio de Chirico, Keith Haring and Fabrizio Plessi displayed throughout the property. The hotel’s annual partnership with Galleria Continua keeps the collection evolving, bringing a new international exhibition each year. We stayed in the imaginatively decorated Magritte Suite with a hand-painted pool featuring a mosaic bottom that depicts René Magritte’s iconic surrealist figure, The Man in the Bowler Hat. It sits in the most tranquil private garden. Architect Patricia Urquiola has redesigned a selection of suites and the hotel’s bar area, capturing Capri’s glamorous essence whilst incorporating local artisanal craftsmanship. The hotel also has an impressive medical spa with an internationally patented Leg School, a treatment that works wonders for your circulation. There is serious food here, too: L’Olivo holds two Michelin stars, while the fabulously flamboyant NOX Capri, designed by Campanian architect Antonio Girardi, is the place for post-dinner cocktails. Where to eat in Anacapri La Zagara For dinner in the heart of Anacapri, La Zagara is a wonderfully romantic choice. Tables are set beneath a canopy of lemon trees in the lush garden of Casa Mariantonia, where the menu takes traditional Capri flavours and gives them a contemporary spin. As the sun goes down, the garden lights up. It is also good for an aperitivo: the adjoining wine bar serves wines by the glass and small bites. Address: Via G. Orlandi, 180 80071 Anacapri Website: zagaracapri.com Columbus Just beside the chairlift to Monte Solaro, Columbus is a useful starting point for exploring Anacapri. The family behind the restaurant has worked the land here for generations, growing many of the vegetables and fruits used in the kitchen and producing its own Oro di Capri olive oil. The menu is rooted in uncomplicated island cooking, while the terrace makes this a good place for a drink as the village begins to wind down. Address: Salita Caposcuro 8, 80071 Anacapri Website: columbuscapri.com a-Ma-Re Capri For a memorable dinner by the water, head to a-Ma-Re Capri, set on lemon-filled terraces overlooking the sea near the Blue Grotto. The food has a Mediterranean feel, with chef Salvatore Elefante, who was born in nearby Gragnano, bringing plenty of Neapolitan character to the menu, alongside chef Nicola Giovanni Maiello, who has worked with him since 2019. Expect beautifully done versions of Italian favourites. My recommendation is the Il Professore wood-fired pizza with aubergine and dried basil pesto, best enjoyed with a lemon Negroni as the sun goes down and the lights of the coast begin to twinkle. Leave space for the restaurant’s twist on the Mille-feuille, prepared at your table. Address: Via Gradola 2, 80071 Anacapri Website: jumeirah.com Da Gelsomina Make the journey out to the Migliara for Da Gelsomina, a longstanding family-run restaurant tucked among Anacapri’s vineyards and countryside. It has been serving traditional island cooking since the 1950s, with recipes including ravioli capresi and pollo al mattone, alongside produce from the family garden and wine from its own vineyard. Come for a late lunch, but stay for the sunset: the restaurant sits close to the Belvedere della Migliara, with sweeping views towards the sea and Punta Carena. There is also a panoramic swimming pool. Address: Via Migliara, 72 - 80071 Anacapri Website: dagelsomina.com Il Riccio For a long, glamorous lunch, book a table at Il Riccio, Jumeirah Capri Palace’s glistening seaside restaurant overlooking the Blue Grotto. The setting is reason enough to come, but the seafood-focused menu has made it an institution. Lobster Caprese Style is a must to start, followed by the plate that inspired the restaurant, Ai Ricci Di Mare (spaghetti with sea urchins). There is lots of fun to be had here, especially in the famously over-the-top dessert room (aptly named The Temptation Room), which is a haven for sugar lovers. Little wonder the likes of the Clooneys, Matthew McConaughey and Jennifer Lopez have been spotted having a ball at Il Riccio. Address: Via Gradola, 4, 80071 Anacapri Website: jumeirah.com L’Olivo For a more elevated take on the flavours of the island, book L’Olivo. The restaurant has held two Michelin stars since 2011, with chef Andrea Migliaccio creating sophisticated interpretations of Neapolitan and Capri cooking. The lemon-scented tagliolini with red prawns is up there with one of the most delectable pasta dishes I have ever had the joy of eating whilst the risotto with Neapolitan ragout is another standout. The setting is as elegant as you might expect, with an intimate dining room and views towards the gardens and Bay of Naples. This is the destination dinner for a special occasion. Address: Via Capodimonte 14, 80071 Anacapri Website: jumeirah.com Il Solitario For a taste of the Anacapri of old, Il Solitario is hard to beat. The restaurant began life as a home and informal osteria in the 1960s, where locals would come to eat traditional dishes. Today, the Cappa family carries on that tradition, serving homemade pasta and classic Neapolitan recipes in a cosy setting of original tiles, ivy and twinkling lights. Order the lemon linguine, one of its signature dishes, and settle in for a delicious evening. Address: Via Giuseppe Orlandi 96, 80071 Anacapri Website: ilsolitarioanacapri.it What to do in Anacapri Monte Solaro The easiest way to understand Anacapri is from above. Take the chairlift from the centre of the village up Monte Solaro, Capri's highest point, for panoramic views across the island, the Bay of Naples and the Sorrento Peninsula. There is a restaurant and bar to welcome you and the sunsets here are as magical as you would hope. Address: Via Caposcuro, 10, 80071 Anacapri Website: montesolarocapri.it Belvedere della Migliara For a quieter alternative to Capri’s more famous viewpoints, follow the Via Migliara towards the southern edge of Anacapri. The path leads through the countryside to the Belvedere della Migliara, where the view opens out towards the Mediterranean and Punta Carena. At the end of the trail you will also find the Philosophical Park, designed and built by the Swedish economist Gunnar Adler-Karlsson. Address: Via Migliara, 72, 80071 Anacapri Website: philosophicalpark.com Punta Carena Make your way to the far southwestern tip of the island for a swim at Punta Carena, beneath the lighthouse. This is one of the best places to spend an afternoon by the sea away from the crowds, with the dramatic coastline providing the backdrop. The lighthouse itself dates back to the 19th century and is one of the island’s most distinctive landmarks. Pitch up at Lido del Faro beach club where you can stay until dusk. Address: Strada Faro di Carena, 80071 Anacapri Website: lidofaro.com Via Giuseppe Orlandi Anacapri’s main pedestrian street is lined with small shops, cafés, ceramics and local businesses, and has a much more village-like vibe than the designer-heavy streets around Capri’s Piazzetta. For signature dresses and shirts, pop into Mogador boutique, while Eureka is the place to pick up a fabulous ceramic piece. You cannot leave Capri without purchasing a pair of bespoke sandals. At La Capri Chic, owners Luca and Vincenzo will work with you to choose everything from the colour and sole to jewels and initials. Turn onto Piazza San Nicola, home to a small but mighty church built in 1719, to see the rather awe-inspiring majolica floor, crafted in 1761 by Leonardo Chiaiese to depict the Garden of Eden. Address Via Giuseppe Orlandi, Anacapri Websites: lacaprichic.com; eurekacapri.it; @mogadorcapri Casa Rossa Anacapri’s museum is hard to miss, with its vivid red façade standing beside an ancient Aragonese tower on Via Giuseppe Orlandi. Built between 1876 and 1899 by eccentric American colonel John Clay MacKowen, who made Capri his home, the house began as a private collection of antiquities and artworks gathered from around the island and beyond. Today, the Casa Museo displays archaeological finds from Capri and the wider Mediterranean, offering a glimpse into both the island’s ancient history and the eccentric community of artists, writers and intellectuals who were drawn here in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Address: Via Giuseppe Orlandi 78, 80071 Anacapri Website: museicapri.cultura.gov.it Villa San Michele Swedish physician and writer Axel Munthe’s Villa San Michele remains one of Anacapri’s essential visits, but it is worth going beyond the famous house itself. The property combines Munthe’s former home with terraces and gardens overlooking the sea, and offers a glimpse into the eccentric creative life that has long drawn artists, writers and intellectuals to the island. Address: Via Axel Munthe, 34, 80071 Anacapri Website: villasanmichele.eu

item.title: This sun-soaked destination has been named the best place for a last-minute autumn escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.44
As one record-breaking summer draws to a close and the guarantee of drizzle and plummeting temperatures hangs over us, the prospect of catching some last-minute autumn sunshine is extremely tempting. While there is no shortage of chic winter sun destinations on our radar, whether that’s Christmas in the Caribbean or banishing the January blues along Mexico’s Pacific coast, there’s still time to top up the vitamin D closer to home. But where should we be heading for sun-sure adventures this September and October? According to the number-crunchers at travel insurance site Quotezone.co.uk, Antalya is the best destination for an autumn sun getaway right now. The ancient Turkish city has long been a favourite destination among sun-seekers, with a plethora of sleek hotels and resorts catering to every type of escape along its glittering coast. With some of the best beaches in Turkey, plenty of history to uncover, a lively city centre and natural landscapes beloved by active travellers and adrenaline junkies, it’s the perfect place to don the swimwear one last time. To uncover the dreamiest autumn sun destinations, Quotezone selected ten of the most popular holiday spots in southern Europe and pitted them against each other across several factors. These include the average temperatures in September and October, sunshine hours, rainfall and sea temperature – plus the lowest price for a three-night stay. With an average temperature of 27.6°C, 9.5 sunshine hours and a particularly balmy sea temperature of 27.5°C, Antalya is a clear winner. In second place is the Canary Island of Tenerife, included in the survey as an autonomous community of Spain, with average temperatures of 26.3°C and some of the cheapest stays at £108 for three nights. The Cypriot city of Larnaca is third, also offering 9.5 hours of sunshine, while the largest and most southerly of the Greek islands, Crete, promises an escape from the northern hemisphere’s chill and 24.5°C waters for bathing.

item.title: These sleek holdalls for men will upgrade your next 48-hour getaway in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.41
Packing for a 48-hour getaway is an art form. It requires a bag that nails a delicate balance – it must have enough space for all your gear, while still being easy to tote manually (a long jaunt to a train station with an aching shoulder is never a good look). Essentially, your weekender needs to be large enough to hold an extra pair of shoes, wash bag and a change of clothes, while still compact enough to bypass the baggage carousel entirely. While a hard-shell suitcase has its place, for a quick hop, nothing is more seamless or stylish than a handsome holdall slung over your shoulder. Modern men’s weekenders are clever engineering feats, with padded tech sleeves to protect laptops, dedicated shoe compartments to keep clean outfits safe and pristine, and trolley pass-through sleeves that make navigating the airport a breeze on longer trips. There are options for all aesthetics and journeys, from rich full-grain oiled leather bags to rugged waxed organic canvas. Then there are the more technical options, made from lightweight waterproof fabrics built to bat off unpredictable British downpours with ease. Our editors have put the market’s top holdalls through rigorous real-world testing, pulling them on and off trains and planes, both at home and further afield. Below, we round up the standout men’s weekender bags for 2026 – from cheap and cheerful high street bargains to investment pieces to love and use for years to come. The best men’s weekender bags at a glance - Best for all-round organisation: Stubble & Co Gym Duffel - Best for wet weather trips & minimalist Scandi style: Rains Weekend Bag - Best small duffle bag: Carl Friedrik Compact Weekender - Best medium duffle bag: Away The Weekender - Best easyJet underseat bag: Antler Overnight Bag - Best leather duffle bag: Farrar & Tanner Oiled Leather Holdall - Best canvas duffle bag: Kovered Humber Waxed Canvas Holdall - Best for high street value: M&S Weekend Bag How we test the best men’s holdalls Our editors spent months testing out these weekend travel bags, bringing them on two-day getaways, overnights, and camping trips, and using them as our personal items on flights. We considered each bag's weight, capacity, design, and how well it held up after several trips. We also paid close attention to unique features that make a bag stand out against other options on the market, like having ample pockets or a separate shoe compartment.

item.title: 11 highest speed trains in the world: from 200mph bullet trains to bedrooms on rails: 10 epic railway adventures
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.40
The highest-speed trains in the world open up no end of possibilities for curious travellers. Whenever we head on an adventure that includes more time on the ground, it feels like a big win on the sustainability front – and, depending on the country and rail route, like stepping back in time. Whether it’s a long journey that flies by in a blur of bucolic scenes through the window or an overnight journey where you’re rocked to sleep, these are the high-speed rail adventures to know about. How many high-speed trains are there in the world? According to the UIC, there are an estimated 56,000km of high-speed lines (built to handle speeds of at least 250 km/h) in operation around the globe, and more than three billion of us use high-speed rail every year. Can a train travel at 400mph? Not yet. However, the Experimental Chinese Maglev trains using magnetic levitation have reportedly gone over 400mph. Shinkansen, Japan Japan’s Shinkansen, also known as the bullet train, is arguably the most iconic of all the world’s high-speed trains. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen line was launched ahead of the 1964 Tokyo Summer Olympics, connecting Japan’s four largest cities: Tōkyō, Yokohama, Nagoya and Ōsaka. Despite considerable expansion in the decades since, the first line remains the busiest, with more than 160 million passengers a year using the speedy route as a vital mode of transport. Carriages zoom across the country at speeds of up to 320km/h, services run every three minutes during peak hours, and it remains one of the safest rail networks in the world. For longer journeys, indulge in a Gran Class booking – Shinkansen’s equivalent of first class, with exceptional hospitality and plush, standalone seats that recline to 45 degrees. Booking: smart-ex.jp Shanghai Maglev, China It may be a short journey, but the roughly eight-minute trip between Shanghai Pudong International Airport and Longyang Road station is a particularly memorable experience for jetsetting railfans. The Shanghai Maglev uses magnetic levitation to reach a maximum operational speed of 431km/h, although the maximum cruising speed utilised on the route as of 2026 is 300km/h. Booking: trip.com Eurostar With a top operational speed of 300km/h, Eurostar services remain among the highest-speed trains in the world. Services began between London and Paris in 1994 following the completion of the Channel Tunnel, and the service now spans five countries: France, the UK, the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland. It’s a super-efficient service for international rail travel, and while journey times naturally take longer than flight times, the city-centre station drop-offs and the lack of need to travel between airports make it a popular choice for weekend breaks and business travellers. The latter favour Eurostar Premier, which offers extra leg room, larger reclining seats and access to priority lanes and lounges. Booking: eurostar.com CR400AF ‘Fuxing’, China Able to reach a maximum speed of 420km/h, China’s electric CR400AF remains among the fastest trains in the world. There are several versions of the CR400AF design, but all variants are compatible and currently operate at speeds of up to 350km/h. They include the CR400AF–AE, a 16-carriage sleeper train that operates between Beijing West/Shanghai-Hongqiao and Hong Kong West Kowloon, and the CR400AF–Z variant currently being used on most of the high-speed railway in China. Booking: trip.com ICE3, Germany This high-speed railway icon, built to whisk passengers between cities at speeds more commonly associated with air travel, was introduced in 2000. The sleek electric train can reach about 330km/h in regular service on suitable high-speed lines, while its aerodynamic design and distributed traction help it maintain impressive speed through Germany’s extensive rail network. Booking: int.bahn.de TGV, France France’s TGV is one of the world’s most famous high-speed trains, synonymous with speed, sleek engineering and effortless journeys through the gorgeous French countryside. Since 1981, the trains have transformed travel between major cities, with its fastest services now reaching around the 320km/h mark on some lines and routes. The network connects Paris with destinations including Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille, while international TGV services extend into neighbouring countries. Booking: sncf-connect.com Al Boraq, Morocco Al Boraq has transformed rail travel across North Africa, bringing high-speed journeys to a country better known for ancient medinas, desert landscapes and Atlas Mountain adventures Since 2018, the service has connected Tangier with Casablanca via the rails, offering a sustainable alternative to hopping from A to B on short, internal flights. The name refers to the mythical winged creature said to have carried the Prophet Muhammad, giving the modern service a distinctly Moroccan identity. Travellers can cover the journey between Tangier and Casablanca in around two hours, Booking: moroccotrains.com Acela, USA Acela is one of the United States’ most recognisable high-speed trains, connecting major cities between Boston and Washington, DC. The latest generation of Acela trains, introduced in 2025, can reach 320km/h on sections of specially upgraded track, although their overall operating speed is lower because of the corridor’s varied infrastructure. Built by Alstom, the new trains feature faster acceleration, more spacious interiors and improved passenger amenities compared to the trains of the past. Booking: amtrak.com Frecciarossa 1000, Italy Italy’s Frecciarossa 1000 is a striking symbol of the country’s high-speed rail ambitions, connecting cities from Turin and Milan to Bologna, Florence, Rome and Naples. The train has been specifically engineered for international travel, with services extending beyond Italy into France and Spain – wherever will your next rail adventure take you? Booking: trenitalia.com KTX-Cheongryong, South Korea These trains are among the most recent additions to South Korea’s rail network. The trains can whizz through the country at around 320km/h. Most intriguingly, KTX-Cheongryong uses distributed traction, with motors positioned throughout the train rather than concentrated in dedicated power cars. This allows it to accelerate quickly, helping reduce journey times on South Korea’s high-speed network. Booking: korail.com AVE S-103, Spain Last but by no means least comes the appearance of my shadow. Spain’s AVE S-103 is one of the most recognisable trains on the country’s high-speed railway network, linking major cities including Madrid, Barcelona, Zaragoza and Tarragona at remarkable speeds. Booking: grupo.renfe.com

item.title: 21 best hotels in Mykonos to book for a slick and stylish stay
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.24
Though you wouldn’t know it now, it wasn’t until the 1980s that Mykonos opened its first luxury hotel on the island’s south coast – and thus began the influx of the best hotels on the island. While this hotel, Myconian Ambassador, still stands, Mykonos today has become synonymous with luxury: hotels, restaurants, beach bars and beyond. It's best known as a place to party, but there’s a lot more to this Greek island, with beats-until-dawn bars mainly confined to the (actually fairly small) area of Mykonos Town. More than ever before, visitors are starting to notice everything Mykonos has to offer away from the late-night dining and dancing scene and are choosing to explore the island’s wild, less-crowded coastlines instead. Where tourists wander, hoteliers follow: over the last few years, there’s been a boom in openings along the island’s south-east coast, from Kalafati beach, where you’ll find Cali Mykonos, to Elia beach, where Four Seasons Mykonos is set to open, the second Greek property from the brand, following its 2019 Athens Riviera launch. See our edit of what to pack for three nights in Mykonos here. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Mykonos - Best for luxury: Four Seasons Mykonos - Best for honeymoons: Amyth of Mykonos - Best beach location: Myconian Sunrise Relais & Chateaux Hotel - Best for a girls' trip: Fouquet's Mykonos - Best boutique hotel: Deos Mykonos - Best for families: Santa Marina, a Luxury Collection Resort What are the best areas in Mykonos to stay in? For all of its hype, Mykonos is relatively small. The island is only 10 kilometres, so wherever you stay, you're pretty close to the action and beaches. Some of the hotels on this list are found along the popular Ornos Beach on the island's southwest. If you want to be based around some hubbub, this option has plenty of shops, restaurants and bars nearby. To be in the thick of the party scene, look to hotels like Mykonos Theoxenia and Bohème, located right in Mykonos town. If you'd prefer to be far removed from it all, Cali Mykonos is hidden away in the reclusive (and exclusive) coastal village Kalafati. When to go to Mykonos The height of the season is July and August, but things are already hotting up in early summer when the fresh produce is better and there are less crowds. If you favour a slightly slower pace, with more comfortable temperatures and less crowds, book a trip to Mykonos in either of the shoulder season months: May or September. How to get to Mykonos Flights from London: Mykonos has an airport serviced by domestic flights from Athens and direct flights from the UK. EasyJet flies directly from the UK to Mykonos; Olympic Air and Aegean Airlines fly to Mykonos via Athens. By ferry from within Greece: Mykonos is easy to reach from Athens' two ports (Piraeus and Rafina) by boat, especially in summer when ferry companies add to their scheduled journeys. Car ferries tend to be comfortable but slow, taking approximately seven hours to get to the island, while modern high-speed catamarans and Sea Jets are more than twice as fast, but not as steady in rough seas. You can also reach Mykonos via other Greek islands if you want to island-hop. How we choose the best hotels in Mykonos Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: The 10 best hotels in the Bahamas for a postcard-perfect stay in the Caribbean in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.18
When Nasa astronaut Scott Kelly spent a year in the inky, star-filled skies of the International Space Station in 2015, it was the vivid azure waters of the Bahamas that he called "the most beautiful place from space.” With 700 islands teeming with endlessly soft, empty beaches and towns filled with brightly coloured clapboard cottages, swaying palms and creeping bougainvillaea, it’s even better when you’re dipping your toes directly in it. The turquoise shallows of the Bahamas are an underwater sensation thanks to its barrier reef, making it one of the best countries in the Caribbean for snorkelling and diving. There’s a dizzying amount of hotels on offer, from postcard-pretty cottages on the A-list favourite Harbour Island to the all-singing, all-dancing family-friendly resorts in the capital of Nassau; here’s our pick of the best hotels in the Bahamas. Editor's picks - For luxury: Coral Sands Inn & Cottages - For couples: Eleven Bahama House - For families: The Royal Atlantis Bahamas When is the best time to visit the Bahamas? For low humidity and plenty of sunshine, the Bahamas is at its best between December and April. December is the peak season and while that will certainly keep the beaches busy, it also means perfect weather. Our tip: strike out for Harbour Island, a three-mile-long, mile-and-a-half-wide sliver of sensational, pink-sand stretches, where there are always enough sunbeds to go around. For less crowds and lower prices while still enjoying good weather, aim to visit between May to June or Mid-November. The island's peak hurricane season usually hits between June to November. How we choose the best hotels in the Bahamas Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We're always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: How to embrace the autumn equinox this year
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.99
Growing up in Australia, I didn’t experience the changing seasons. So now that I live in the UK, I am thrilled by the long shadows cast by the evening's low, orange sun or the prospect of snuggling up for a candlelit movie night as soon as autumn rolls in. In an age of burnout, digital fatigue and social exhaustion, there's something delightful about engaging in analogue activities to hail a new season. Historically, pagans celebrated autumn after the light-filled joy of spring and summer: it symbolised a final opportunity to gather the Earth’s bounty before the frost settled. The equinoctial split between night and day was honoured as a symbol of balance and harmony – qualities many of us seek today. And darkness was something to be embraced, as both successor and precursor to the light. What is the autumn equinox? The autumnal equinox is the astronomical event that marks the official first day of the season. Autumn – the equinox, especially – represents something unique in terms of the inexorable march of time and nature. A buffer between the excesses of a heady summer and festive winter, it’s a time to reflect, recharge and reset. The UK, in particular, lends itself to such fallow times – partly because its position in the Northern Hemisphere so beautifully harnesses the split between light and darkness, but also because of the country’s agricultural and pagan history. When is the autumn equinox 2026? This year's autumn equinox is on Wednesday 23 September 2026 at 1:05am BST, according to the Met Office. So, light the candles, draw the curtains – and venture out only if it’s going to nurture you as fulsomely as one of these events. Here are the best ways to celebrate the autumn equinox this year. At the time of writing, these events are still available across the UK. How to celebrate the autumn equinox Stretch it out at an autumn yoga retreat Autumn and its falling leaves offer a timely reminder to let go of the old, and this day-long yoga retreat will help with release and grounding through movement, mindfulness and meditation in a gorgeous Lake District setting. All levels are welcome, and a vegetarian lunch and cakes are included in the price. When: Saturday September 26, 10am-4pm Website: lakesyoga.co.uk Address: Rayrigg Farm Studio D, Windermere, LA23 1BW Embark on a Full Moon Labyrinth walk Embark on a guided walk of a church garden labyrinth under the light of a full moon; connect with the wild, folkloric powers of hawthorn; contemplate; journal and reconnect with yourself, the earth, and those around you on this dreamy moonlit walk. When: Saturday 26 September, 7.30-9pm Website: events.humanitix.com Address: St James the Less, Church Hall, Penicuik, EH26 9EE, Scotland Head to the forest for a women-only nature escape An all-female afternoon of immersion in a forest landscape, complete with foraging, fungi identification and the possibility of a wild swim. Followed by a wholesome and nourishing feast, participants are encouraged to bring a sense of adventure and experience the magic. When: Saturday 16 September, 1-5pm Website: tickettailor.com Address: Tollymore Forest Park, Co. Down, Northern Ireland, BT33 0PR Embrace total wellness in Wales Set within beautiful Welsh countryside, this two-day retreat combines yoga, guided meditation, a floating sound bath, cold water immersion and sauna, creative activities, a fire circle and cacao ceremony, as well as restorative time in nature and space to reflect. When: 21-23 September Website: eventbrite.co.uk Address: Golden Grove, Gelli Aur, Carmarthenshire SA32 8LS Feel zen with a candlelit soundbath Led by spiritual wellness guide Alexandra Wilby, this candlelit soundbath will transport you into a state of deep relaxation, allowing space to release tension and to connect with the season’s rhythm. A guided meditation will encourage you to let go of what no longer serves you, helping you to feel renewed and grounded as winter approaches. When: 18 October, 6.30-7.30pm Website: tickettailor.com Address: Christ Church with St Philip, Worcester Park, KT4 8LG Start new holistic rituals An immersive journey honouring the natural rhythm of the seasons, this three-hour event combines gentle yoga, journalling, meditation, a sound bath, a symbolic release ceremony and a sauna experience. Closing with an ohm circle and intention setting, there’s an invitation to stay for an informal vegan and vegetarian meal afterwards. When: Saturday 26 September, 4-7pm Website: eventbrite.co.uk Address: Eastway Baths, 80 Eastway, London E9 5JH Get witchy on a nocturnal bat walk Darker skies call for swooping, squeaking bats; they’re a popular familiar for those of a witchy bent, too. A series of nocturnal, 90-minute walks in London’s Hyde Park and Kensington Gardens will help participants to spot and identify different species, complete with ‘detectors’ designed to help the human ear hear the critters’ calls. When: Various dates and times from Wednesday 23 September Website: royalparks.org.uk Discover floromancy Dine on a four-course, harvest-inspired meal within a walled garden, accompanied by astro-botanical alchemist Jemma Foster talking guests through the symbolism of the botanicals in each dish. There’ll also be the opportunity to enjoy the first pouring of the estate’s own spirit, crafted from herbs and flowers foraged from the garden. After the meal, guests will be invited to set an intention and cast it into a firepit in a symbolic celebration of new beginnings. When: September 23, 5.30pm Website: iscabordehill.co.uk Address: Isca, Borde Hill, Borde Hill Lane, Haywards Heath, RH16 1XP Go on a nurturing day retreat A day retreat designed to nurture and nourish, and to allow participants to leave with a sense of intention and clarity as the new season takes hold. Expect a cacao ceremony, transformational Kundalini activation, a sacred fire ceremony and a transportive soundbath, as well as a hearty, wholesome lunch – all within an intimate setting surrounded by beautiful English countryside. When: September 26, 12-6pm Website: eventbrite.co.uk Address: The Roundhouse Haven, Ashley Road, Market Harborough, LE16 8PL

item.title: Why we're obsessing over the Balkans right now: 5 destinations to visit before the crowds arrive
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.87
A region of mountains, beaches, waterfalls and wonder, the Balkans feel like West shading into East. You can taste it in the food and hear it when different religions pray. The cognoscenti have been heading to these eccentric nations for years, lured by lower costs and visitor numbers compared with Western Europe – but travel insiders are only just cottoning on. I have been visiting the Balkans for a decade. I’ve enjoyed hanging out of the window of a smoky train carriage clattering through the hills from Mostar to Sarajevo, exploring the remains of the 1960s vision of a futuristic Skopje and taking a cable car up Mount Dajti outside Tirana. The game-changer this year, though, is the EES chaos, which has ruined so many previously simple EU hops. In non-Schengen Kosovo, Serbia, Bosnia, Montenegro, Albania and North Macedonia you don’t have to worry about missing your plane while you’re stuck in a passport queue, and the entry and exit process is a breeze. The topography of the Balkans is dramatic to say the least. There aren’t bulky hotels or giant developments, and the region feels smaller and more friendly than the rest of Europe. The mountains provide a glorious backdrop for climbing and walking galore – one of Europe's most stunning international hikes is the Peaks of the Balkans, which connects Kosovo, Albania and Montenegro in a 124-mile loop. As well as hiking, wellness retreats have been booming here in southeastern Europe, but they’re unlike their counterparts in other European countries, largely because they aren’t on the same scale. Here you can really unwind at spa resorts, spend time in nature, wild swim and paddleboard on deserted lakes, then clamber up paths not chock-a-block with tourists. Coastal hotels have more space, and jagged coastlines mean smaller beaches, remote coves and dreamy turquoise waters. The Balkans have pushed back against million-dollar hotels and large resorts, embracing ecotourism. Montenegro established the Eco Fund in 2020 and has committed, as far back as 1991, to becoming an environmentally sustainable country. Eco-resorts are blossoming, with the likes of Oblun offering an alternative vision to mass tourism: glamping, gardening and kayaking in the heart of the countryside, surrounded by orange, fig and pomegranate trees while you practise yoga. Visitors are also discovering the lesser-known cities of the Balkans. Pristina, Kosovo, is a fascinating and friendly spot, home to incredible socialist murals and gorgeous period architecture. The National Library of Kosovo, by Andrija Mutnjaković, from 1982, is a wild and wonderful journey into the soul of Kosovan heritage, inspired by mosque domes and books – it is the architectural highlight of Europe’s newest capital. Albania’s second city, Durrës, is also on the rise, with easy access to the country’s increasingly popular beaches. Skopje, meanwhile, attracts fans of 1960s Japanese genius Kenzō Tange, who redesigned the city and built the modern train station in a so-called metabolist style following the catastrophic 1963 earthquake. There's plenty to explore in the Balkan cities and the wilderness beyond – here we round up the best destinations to add to your travel wishlist. The best Balkan destinations to visit Montenegro This is the year to visit Montenegro – the country on everyone’s lips. Kotor Bay is flashy these days, and the super-rich who don’t want to die young flock to wellness retreats such as Siro Boka Place. Underrated capital Podgorica is where design-literate travellers are heading. Svetlana Kana Radević was a heroine of Montenegrin design who became the most famous female architect in the former Yugoslavia. Her Hotel Podgorica is remarkable – its exterior is clad in stone from the Morača river bed, and she designed the building as a series of steps blending into the side of the river valley. Montenegro also offers serene mountains, chances to sail along its coast and homely eateries such as family-run indie Scala Santa, open since 1996 and serving fish pâté and octopus salad in Kotor Old Town. Lake Ohrid, North Macedonia This year marks 25 years since the Ohrid Agreement was signed in this pretty North Macedonian town, bringing peace to the country then known as Macedonia. Today the lake and town both attract visitors seeking peace and quiet. The surrounding hills are ideal for walks, and Ohrid is famous for the ancient remains you can dive into the lake to see and the Monastery of St Naum on the lakeshore. The iconic money shot visitors want is of the 13th-century Church of St John at Kaneo, which overlooks the lake's cool waters. With 17 native fish species, angling is a way to unwind here, and fish feature heavily in the local cuisine – lake trout and clear fish soup are classic dishes. The coast of Albania With prices skyrocketing in Greece, Albania makes perfect sense as a coastal destination. Hike to Gjipe Beach and wild camp a stone’s throw from soft sand and dramatic cliffs. The peaceful, secluded Mirror Beach has the kind of turquoise water that'll have you plotting your return before you've left. Albania is heading towards a classy version of style-led, low-impact tourism. Zoe Hora in Dhërmi is telegraphing a different way forward – this design hotel is built around a series of houses. Aragosta overlooks the sea in Durrës, and serves fish pizza, qofte meatballs – Albania’s unofficial national dish – and trileçe, a milk cake with caramel. Check out the newly restored and reopened Pyramid cultural centre in the capital, Tirana, a city being radically renewed with pedestrianisation and outdoor art. Bosnia Spomen or Spomeniks are the defining feature of the Bosnian countryside, and can be found all across the former Yugoslavia. Most were erected by former president Tito, commemorating the partisan army who fought Nazism in the mountains. In Bosnia you can hike the Kozara National Park to the Kozara Spomenik – titled Monument to the Revolution. A two-and-a-half-hour trail leads you through forests and over streams to this historical site. Spomenik Database is the best resource if you’re on the hunt for Spomeniks. Mostar is full of ancient charm, and its famous bridge attracts the world’s best divers; Sarajevo has become a lively European city in the past decade, with bars, restaurants and rooftop venues. Bosnia also has a sliver of coast at the intriguing town of Neum. Serbia Belgrade is preparing for its year as an international host city, with Expo 2027 kicking off in May. The event, with the theme “Play for Humanity – Sport and Music for All”, will feature exhibitions, pavilions and talks encompassing architecture, technology and the arts. Although it won’t be ready for May, a new metro – a project that began decades ago – is finally set to be completed in 2027. More proof that Belgrade is ready for a new breed of in-the-know travellers is the opening of the newest outpost from the French design-hotel mini-chain Mama Shelter. Outside the capital, Novi Sad surprises with its Hungarian architecture and extensive riverside beaches, where the city goes to relax, and the mountains are ripe and ready for travellers looking for ski escapes that won’t break the bank.

item.title: Where was ‘MobLand’ filmed? Pierce Brosnan takes us behind the scenes of Season 2
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.14
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was MobLand filmed? Warring families, London gangsters, teetering drug empires… There’s nothing quite like a good crime drama, and MobLand is surely one of the best in recent memory. Season one left us on the edge of our seats, and we’ve been (im)patiently waiting to see what will come of the Harrigans and the Da Souzas ever since. Luckily, the second season promises much of the blood, guts and gore of the first – we spoke to Pierce Brosnan about what it was like returning to Conrad Harrigan, and his favourite places to film Season 2 of Mobland. “When Guy [Ritchie] came to me with this idea two years ago, Helen [Mirren] and I had been working together on The Thursday Murder Club,” Brosnan says. “She said, ‘Do you like it? Are you going to do it?’ I said, 'Yes, I want to go back to London. I want to be back here in this wonderful city where my career started.’ And she said, ‘Okay, good. Well, if you are doing it, I'll do it.' And both of us just jumped right in there. We get on very well together.” Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren play the husband-and-wife duo of Conrad and Maeve Harrigan. They are both totally ruthless, power-hungry and seemingly incapable of empathy – their sole goal is control, and they don’t care who they manipulate, maim or kill along the way, even within their own family. “It was wonderful to go back to Conrad,” he continues. “I enjoy playing this character so much. He's happened at a great time in my life, and to be working with Dame Helen Mirren and this magnificent cast, Tom Hardy and the rest of our company, has been a joy. The writing by Jez Butterworth is so rich and textured and nuanced, and it works on so many different levels. It's like putting on an old coat, really. There's something so familiar about it.” The series takes place mainly in London, depicting mob families as they battle for control over the city's drug scenes. “London is an ever-changing city. Londinium has been the epicentre of many great events historically, culturally, and certainly from the world of the arts and a filmmaker like Guy Ritchie, who he's born of this land and he knows it so well, whether it be the interior life of the city or the countryside. So as a storyteller, he is the perfect gentleman to create this world of MobLand." For the Harrigans, their name and identity is something to be protected at all cost. The way they are viewed and respected, and how they fit into the warring dynasties of London, is of utmost importance. For Brosnan, understanding Conrad’s background and how he became the man he is was a big part of preparing for the role. “I think there's a strong identification for me with Conrad because of being a transplant. I left Ireland when I was 11 years of age – August 12th, 1964. I landed and was rejoined with my mother, and we lived in Putney. So filming in and around London was a lot of fun.” “I didn't do in-depth study or preparation for Conrad, but when I spoke to Guy Ritchie for the first time after reading the initial five episodes, I started talking about the character and where he was from, as a Londoner with an Irish background, because so many Irish folks who live in North or South London have lost their accents. So I was trying to define the character and the accent but he said, look, and this was the phone call, and the first phone call, he said, “Don't worry about it. We'll sort it out on the day. Put it out of your mind.” So I kept it as simple as possible and I more or less made it up on the day.” "These characters that we play – Maeve, Conrad – are these Irish, rebellious outsiders, these from-the-streets folks who have created this wealth of life through really extreme circumstances of violence. They do what certain rich people do in life, whether they be rock stars or artists who become very wealthy – they buy the country estate, but they really know nothing about living in the countryside. So in the series you go from the Cotswolds to the East End of London and back again. It was brilliant.” “I'm as much an audience member as I am a participant. My family love this show; they've never wanted to watch me as much as they do on this show, and so we all celebrate it.” Below, Pierce Brosnan tells us about his favourite places to film Mobland Season 2, from the UK's oldest film studios to the lush lands of the Cotswolds. Where was MobLand Season 2 filmed? Ealing Studios, London “My world consists mainly of Ealing Studios, where we film,” Brosnan says. “Ealing Studios is one of the great bastions of English film work, and it has a whole history of some of the great Ealing comedies.” It opened in 1902 as the UK’s first film studio, and still operates today – making it the UK’s oldest continuously working film studio. Kentish Town, London “Conrad does a scene sequence driving the Bentley around Kentish Town, and I went to drama school up in Chalk Farm, so on that particular day we did a tour of my old haunts. Tom Hardy [who plays Harry Da Souza] and I went to the same drama school – I was many years ahead of him, but we were taught by the same teachers in the world of method acting. It was a drama school called the Drama Centre in Chalk Farm, and I graduated in 76, so I was many, many, many years ahead of Tom. Michael Fassbender and Colin Firth both went there, too. It felt full circle going back, although it was quite weird because I was actually driving the Bentley with a camera truck in front, so I had to be aware and focus because I was actually on the streets and being filmed. Guy Ritchie and all the directors, they make such a feast of the action sequences. I'm very impressed by the driving sequences in MobLand.” Scott’s, Mayfair, London The first scene in season one of MobLand begins in the basement of a glitzy London restaurant, and between scenes at The Midland Grand inside the St Pancras Renaissance Hotel to Loulou’s nightclub in Mayfair, you’d be safe to assume Season 2 will have more high-end London settings, too. “We shoot at Scott's,” Brosnan says. “Maeve and I, we go to meet Serafina [played by Mandeep Dhillon]. And Maeve is all out there. She's all absolutely bedecked like a queen, like an empress. So we shot there, and then we shot down and around Harley Street.” Oxford Stadium, Oxford Season 1 ends with Maeve and Conrad in prison, but Season 2 sees them back in the game – this time, gambling at a local dog track. “Well, the opening scene is at the dog races. So episode one is at the dog races,” Brosnan says. The races are set at White Hart Stadium, a venue that has now been demolished but was once the sport's main track. But the scenes were actually shot in Oxford, at the Oxford Stadium greyhound track on Sandy Lane in Cowley. “That was a wonderful day's work,” adds Pierce. "It was quite spectacular, and it's a major kind of shootout. Blood and guts everywhere." Mallorca, Spain “We go off to Mallorca at one point. I don't think I'm giving anything away by telling you that,” laughs Brosnan. "We had a week in Mallorca, and we stayed at a delightful hotel on the ocean front. It's a gorgeous part of the world. One of the highlights for me was going to Miro's studio [Fundació Miró Mallorca]. I'm a painter, and so seeing the life of the great artist Joan Miró was a highlight for me. The Cotswolds Season 2 sees the Harrigans back in their main residence in the Cotswolds. “It's an absolute joy – everyone loves going to the dear Cotswolds,” says Brosnan. “There folks down there are probably thinking: ‘please no more, please do not show any more of our beautiful landscape!’ We went back to the same house. It's just outside of Bourton-on-the-Water, near Broadway. It really is a lovely time to be there too – we always start this show in November, so we're in the winter months, but to be down in Broadway, near that part of the world at Christmastime is just pure magic.” “My favourite place to stay is the Dormy House in the Cotswolds. It's a beautiful hotel. They look after us so well. It's charming, and you can tramp along and walk across the fields. Stayed at the Soho Farmhouse for a while, too. There are some beautiful walks, and you just get out, and if you feel like you're in the middle of nowhere, it's so stunning around there. We stayed at Estelle Manor, too, which is quite magnificent. It's a beautiful old home and a stately home. Conrad would probably like Estelle Manor. He'd pull up in the Bentley. It's all people who want to be seen and they're all very important, feeling very important. But Dormy House has my heart. I just like it. It's quiet and it's just my speed. It's intimate, small. The food is very good, and the staff are just charming and lovely.” Tyrella Beach, Northern Ireland In December 2025, Belfast Live reported that the cast and crew were seen shooting on Tyrella Beach in County Down, Northern Ireland. “They shot some scenes in Northern Ireland. I didn't shoot anything there, but two of the characters go off to Northern Ireland.” The pictures show Eddie Harrigan and Gina Da Souza walking along the shore. In a production interview, Helen Mirren said that Season 2 will "broaden the landscape out of North London and especially the younger members of the family are seeing that there’s a globalisation element to it.” We see this with the Northern Ireland and Mallorca scenes, but is there scope for a shoot even further afield in future seasons? “Helen and I were just talking about this, actually. We'd love to go to Italy. Helen lives in Puglia, so we've talked about maybe some cross-pollination between families and the mafia. It would be very good. Well, I think Jez and his company of writers have already got season three more or less in the bag. I'm not sure, to tell you the truth, but we haven't seen it, so we never know where it's going. But yes, I would love to continue.”

item.title: The best Barbados villas let you do island life like you own the place in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.05
Barbados’s vibrant mix of breathtaking beaches, Colonial-style architecture, botanical gardens and characteristic Caribbean hospitality makes it a natural beacon for those seeking sun, sand, rum punch and a warm island breeze. Despite a slim 21-mile radius, there’s a surprising number of excellent hotels bringing historical charm, plush beds and unrivalled sea views to restore peace to weary travellers. But for a proper pulse-slowing immersion onto island time, a private stay is best. You don’t even have to compromise on hotel amenities, as plenty are fully staffed with private chefs, butlers and concierges ready to attend to your every whim. Whether you’re bound for the sights and sounds of carnival season, the joyful food scene, or simply to recline on idyllic white sands, there’s a slew of exceptional homes across the island ready to call home. Below, six of the best villas in Barbados to book now, or see our guide to the best villas in the Caribbean. Editors’ picks of the best villas in Barbados - For couples: Calypso Harmonies, Gibbs Beach - For families: Villa Sugar Hill, St James - For big groups: Modern House, Speightstown - For proximity to the sea: Sea Haven, West Coast How we choose the best villas in the Caribbean We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. All listings featured on Condé Nast Traveller are independently selected by our editors. If you book something through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
