item.title: Discover Fall at Its Best in West Virginia’s State Parks
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.02
Fall colors in West Virginia. (Photo: West Virginia Department of Tourism) As autumn sweeps through the gorges, mountains, and valleys of West Virginia, the state’s “Almost Heaven” slogan seems like an understatement. Suddenly, there’s very little “almost” about it. With a kaleidoscope of foliage marching over the rolling hills and complementing the deep greens of the pines, fall in the Mountain State is something to behold. Here’s where—and how—to see the show across West Virginia’s State Parks. With more than 40 waterfalls on the West Virginia Waterfall Trail, visiting one (or several) is a great way to experience the serenity of the season. Each one offers something different, along with the best kinds of similarities—cascading water, stunning foliage, and the feeling of full immersion in nature. See them all, check in, and earn prizes with the West Virginia Waterfall Trail. There’s no better way to end an autumn day than by returning to a forest cabin. And in West Virginia, you hardly even need to leave the trail to find your home away from home—more than 20 state parks have cabin rentals available. One of the best places to lay your head come fall is the scenic Blackwater Falls State Park. There, a day of hiking, biking, or fishing can end at one of 39 fully furnished cabins. Or, for a completely unique cabin experience, head to Coopers Rock State Forest, where you’ll find five stargazing cabins equipped with skylights and floor-to-ceiling windows that let you take in the night sky while enjoying the comforts of home. One of the best ways to experience West Virginia’s colorful fall forests? From above. There are several places to enjoy sweeping mountain views across the state, including the scenic chairlift ride at Canaan Valley Resort State Park and the Aerial Tram at Pipestem Resort State Park. At Pipestem, you even have the unique opportunity to travel over the rim of the Bluestone Gorge and down to the Bluestone River, enjoying the view as you sink into the scenery. As you explore the Mountain State, keep your eyes peeled for West Virginia’s iconic Almost Heaven swings. With more than 50 spread across some of the most scenic state parks, towns, and points of interest in the state, you’re bound to find a spot to pull over, stretch your legs, and commemorate a fall trip done right.

item.title: Paddle, Bike, Run at These Adventurous Multisport Events
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.75
You don't have to swim to compete in a multisport event. These athletes competing in (clockwise from top left) Ski to Sea, Gut Check Cape Cod, The Great American Triathlon, and The Big Hurt get to paddle their way through the water on race day. (Photo: Clockwise from top left: Whatcom Events, Jittipong Rakritikul, Capital Road Race Management, Matt Sagen | Cascadia Films) For most new triathletes, the open-water swim is the most intimidating discipline. If you’re not ready to take the plunge, you can still experience multisport adventures. At most of these unconventional triathlons, the swim leg is replaced by a kayak, canoe, or stand-up paddleboard leg. Ranging from New Jersey to California, these fun adventure races give you a taste of the multisport experience without getting your feet (too) wet. September Nebo, North Carolina North Carolina is home to a number of adventure races, but the Pisgah 12-Hour Adventure Race is truly unique. Unlike a traditional triathlon, athletes will embark on an orienteering adventure with the goal to gather as many punches as possible from checkpoints on the course within the allotted time. The team with the most points in the least amount of time wins. It’s based around Lake James State Park at the edge of Linville Gorge in Nebo, North Carolina, and 2026 will be the seventh time the race has been held in this location. Expect bushwacking, mountain biking on single track, and scenic paddling. You can race solo, but it’s more fun with friends, so create a team of 2-4 people. You’ll need to know how to read a map, use a compass, and even though you paddle, you’ll still get wet, so dress accordingly. Race with a head lamp in the dark and carry fluid and snacks for the duration. It’s the most fun you can have in the woods with a hundred of your newest friends. September Brewster, Massachusetts Gut Check Cape Cod isn’t your typical triathlon. While it definitely falls into the “adventure race” category, this event is more of a point-to-point, outdoor quest. What’s unique is that each year, the course is different, so nobody knows exactly what they’re in for until minutes before the race start. Gut Check began in 2019 and takes place in the 2,000-acre Nickerson State Park. Described as a “unique journey across land and water,” the race includes 1,000 vertical feet of trail running, 1,000 vertical feet of road cycling, and water crossings that can be completed by swimming or paddling. The number of checkpoints is kept a secret until race morning, but there’s an anticipated finish time of 1.5 to 3 hours. There will be no more than four swim segments, and each is a half mile or less. If you choose to paddle, those segments may be a bit longer. How do you prepare for a race like this? Organizers suggest being able to run 4-6 miles on trails, ride 5-10 miles, swim a total of 1,500 yards, and paddle up to 1.5 miles total. This race involves orienteering by map, and you must reach several checkpoints along the way. The objective is to use “your wits and fitness to scramble your way to the last cliff climb.” You can race solo or in a 2-4-person team. In 2025, the race sold out, so don’t wait to sign up for this one. September Lenox, Massachusetts The Great Josh Billings Runaground has a long and storied history (almost 50 years!) in the Berkshires of Western Massachusetts. The race consists of a 27-mile bike ride, 5-mile paddle, and 6.4-mile run. If you think you’re up for the challenge, the first step is to assemble a team. The Tin category consists of two athletes who divide the three legs between themselves. For example, one athlete rides the bike, both paddle, and the second athlete runs. The Iron category is for a single athlete who wants to complete all three legs of the race. The cycling leg marks the start of the event in Great Barrington. Athletes will ride 27 miles through five different towns on the way to Stockbridge Bowl. Expect scenic country roads and rolling hills on this route with five climbs and 1,750 feet of elevation gain. After the ride, the cyclist will hand off a wristband to the next teammate waiting at the lake. That athlete will use a canoe, kayak, or SUP to paddle 5 miles around the lake finishing at Camp Mah-Kee-Nac. After the paddling leg, that athlete must hand the wristband to a runner waiting on the beach. The final leg of the race is a 6.4-mile run around the lake to the finish line at the Tanglewood Main Gate. So, who is Josh Billings? It’s actually the pen name of Henry Wheeler Shaw, a writer and noted humorist from the 19th century. Known as a “cracker-barrel philosopher,” he penned a number of sayings, such as “to finish is to win,” which is the motto of The Great Josh Billings Runaground. This bike-canoe-run triathlon is one of the oldest and largest in the country. It’s fun-loving, eccentric, and a bit wacky, much like its namesake. After the race, stick around for “The Bash” to enjoy live music, a beer tent, massages, food, photo booth, and a kids race. September Bay City, Michigan If you had any doubts about whether or not this race involves swimming, the Bay City Morning Rotary put it right in the title for you. This is a “Driathlon,” which means you won’t get wet (unless you fall out of your kayak). This year marks the 16th annual Driathlon in Bay City, Michigan. Described as a “triathlon with a twist,” the event includes a paddle, bike, and run. It’s a fundraiser for the Bay City Morning Rotary and allows the organization to distribute funds to local charities. Groups of two can compete in either a relay format, in a team format where each athlete does all three events, or you can choose the individual kayak division. Athletes begin the race with a 5K paddle in a kayak or canoe on the Kawkawlin River. The second leg is a 20K, three-loop route on Bangor Township roads. The final leg is a 5K run along the river. The transition area is located at Castaways Bay City where there will be pre-race coffee, donuts, and bagels available. Post-race, you can look forward to ShineWater, water, and fruit, as well as the musical stylings of the race DJ. September Port Angeles, Washington This four-leg adventure race takes athletes from the foothills of the Olympic Mountains to the shores of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Home base is Pebble Beach Park in downtown Port Angeles. Athletes begin their adventure with a 16-mile mountain bike on the Foothills Trail System. Then, they will transfer to a kayak to paddle 2.6 miles in Port Angeles Harbor. Next, hop on the road bike for 30 miles on rural roads in Clallam County. The final leg is a 10K run on the Waterfront Trail. This race can be done solo or in a relay consisting of 2-4 people. With a central transition area, beer garden, and music, this is a very spectator-friendly event. Stick around the next day for The Little Hurt, a youth race for kids pre-K to eighth grade. September Point Pleasant, New Jersey The DQ Treasure Island Sprint Triathlon has something for everyone: a triathlon, duathlon, aquabike, relay, and kayak triathlon. The kayak triathlon consists of a 1.5K paddle, 10.5-mile bike ride, and 3-mile run. Athletes will paddle into the Manasquan River and around Osborn Island before finishing at Maxson Avenue Beach. Then, there’s a four-lap bike ride, followed by an out-and-back run. Because this is part of the DQ Grand Prix and Club Challenge, points accumulate throughout the series. Cash prizes are awarded to overall winners, and awards are presented to age group, Clydesdale/Athena, adaptive category, relay divisions, and more. May Whatcom County, Washington Round up 2-7 of your most adventurous friends to compete in the original team relay race at Ski To Sea. This popular event takes athletes across snow, land, and sea from Mount Baker to Bellingham Bay. It started in 1973 and is held annually on Memorial Day weekend in Whatcom County, Washington. The format involves teams of 3-8 athletes competing in seven different sports to cover a total of 91 miles. In order of event, athletes will complete a cross-country ski (5K), downhill ski/snowboard (4K), run (8 miles), road bike (41 miles), canoe (18.5 miles), cyclocross bike (11 miles), and sea kayak (5 miles). The course takes athletes through Glacier, Maple Falls, Kendall, Everson, Lynden, Ferndale, and finishes in the historic Fairhaven district of Bellingham. Once the final athlete reaches the finish at Marine Park, they will hop out of their kayak, run up the hill, and ring the finisher’s bell. The afterparty includes an awards ceremony, Kulshan Brewing Beer Garden, and food from several local vendors. July Sacramento, California The Great American Triathlon showcases the beauty of the American River Parkway in California’s state capital with a run/bike/paddle. The unique format begins with a 5.8-mile run, followed by a 12.5-mile bike ride, and a 6.1-mile paddle. The entire route travels along the American River Parkway. The run begins at William B. Pond Park in Carmichael and heads downriver to Cal State University, Sacramento. The bike goes from Sacramento to the Sunrise Bridge in Fair Oaks. The paddle leg is a scenic route from the bridge to River Bend Park in Rancho Cordova. You have the option to compete as an individual or part of a team. Space is limited to 250 teams and 600 individual racers. This event raises money to preserve the American River Parkway and benefits local children’s charities.

item.title: Buried in 2 Feet of Snow With No Overnight Gear, a Hike in the Enchantments Just Turned Deadly
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.47
Two people in the Enchantments at the summit of Asgard Pass in the Cascade Mountains (Photo: Tegra Stone Nuess/Getty Images) An Oklahoma woman died of hypothermia while attempting a thru-hike of the Enchantments, a renowned high-alpine region in Washington state’s Cascade Mountain Range. Sybil Claborn, 45, was hiking with her husband on September 13 when an early-season snowstorm struck the trail, according to the Chelan County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO). Several feet of snow buried the couple, both of whom suffered severe hypothermia. Claborn succumbed to the cold. “The area the couple was at is approximately 7,000 to 8,000 feet in elevation, with either trailhead approximately eight to ten miles away,” CCSO Chief Ryan Moody said in a statement sent to Outside. “Storms had persisted throughout the day, producing significant snowfall in the area. The male reported that both individuals’ clothing was soaked and that they did not have overnight gear.” Authorities have not released the man’s name, age, or condition. The Enchantments is a coveted alpine hiking area known for mountain goats, turquoise lakes, and jagged peaks. The Washington Trail Association (WTA) categorizes the 18-mile one-way hike as being “hard,” with 4,500 feet of elevation gain and a high point of 7,800 feet. The couple was in the so-called “core zone” of the Enchantments, which is a high plateau filled with lakes, authorities say. A high-alpine basin forms the centerpiece of the Enchantments traverse. Camping along the Enchantments traverse is only allowed by securing a competitive permit. Some hikers will attempt the entire trek in a day to avoid one, but weather conditions can turn violent quickly, especially at high elevations, putting unprepared mountaineers at an extreme risk of rapid hypothermia. Although large amounts of snow don’t typically accumulate until November, variable weather is common through these alpine peaks. “Those undertaking the Enchantments thru-traverse in September should be aware of variable conditions brought by the onset of autumn in the alpine,” WTA writes on its website. “Conditions can vary greatly this time of year—it is not uncommon for 30-plus degree temperature swings to occur in a single day.” September 13, 5:30 P.M. The husband placed the initial SOS call, reporting his wife was unable to move. 5:50 P.M. A second call confirmed the couple was buried in one to two feet of snow under an emergency blanket. Air rescue was grounded due to severe weather. 8:00 to 10:50 P.M. Army helicopter pilots make multiple attempts from Yakima, Washington, to reach the couple but fail due to storm conditions. September 14, 3:30 A.M. Ground rescuers from Chelan County Mountain Rescue reach the site on foot, finding Claborn deceased and her husband suffering from severe hypothermia. 9:00 A.M. Air evacuation clears, transporting the surviving hiker to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth. CCSO provided Outside with a detailed timeline of the rescue. Just before 5:30 P.M. on September 13, authorities say they received an initial emergency call from a man who reported his wife was unable to move, and that he couldn’t carry her out on the trail. Twenty minutes later, the man called again to say the woman was under an emergency blanket and the couple was buried between one and two feet of snow. Weather conditions were quickly deteriorating, and responders determined that it wasn’t safe to fly a helicopter in to evacuate the couple. “At that point, the only other option was to get a ground team in as quickly as possible to try to warm her up,” Moody said. “A ground rescue team was requested from Chelan County Mountain Rescue (CCMR). They provide the quickest ground response possible.” CCSO requested a hoist-capable helicopter before 7 P.M. if weather conditions improved. An hour later, an Army helicopter launched from Yakima, Washington, located about 100 miles away. Weather again prevented responders from reaching the pair. Throughout the evening, CCSO said that the man continued to communicate about his wife’s condition and the possibility that she may die. The Army again tried to fly a helicopter into the area at 10:50 P.M., but the weather was still too dangerous. At 3:30 A.M. on September 14, two CCMR personnel reached the couple on foot. At this point, the woman had died, and the man was suffering from severe hypothermia. Responders warmed the man in a tent rescuers brought, the Sheriff’s office said. Later that morning, a helicopter arrived to transport the man and two CCMR rescuers. They landed at the Leavenworth Fish Hatchery, about ten miles from the trailhead, around 9:00 A.M. Officials transported the man by ambulance to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth for treatment. By 10 A.M., the sheriff’s office sent in a recovery flight to recover the deceased woman. She was transported to the Chelan County Coroner’s office Additional information regarding the cause and manner of her death is under investigation, authorities say.

item.title: 5 Workouts to Build Serious Uphill Hiking Strength
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.69
(Photo: Peter Amend/Getty) The first time I ever went backpacking abroad, I was so unprepared for the climbs that I couldn’t complete my planned itinerary. The route in question should have been a dream loop through the Italian Dolomites. But instead of frolicking through alpine passes, I found myself two days in, on the verge of tears, staring down yet another 6,000-foot climb. The sun was about to set, and my quads were Jell-O. I couldn’t do it. I booked a room in an inn I couldn’t afford, climbed the pass the next morning, and then took a bus to my endpoint. While there’s no shame in calling a trip early, it’s a bummer to miss out on miles of beauty just because your hiking fitness isn’t where you thought it was. And while it’s relatively easy to train for a route if you have similar terrain close to home, it can be tough to prep for truly enormous climbs—like the kind you’ll find in the Colorado Rockies, the Italian Dolomites, or the French Alps. “It’s especially hard to train in America for stuff like the Alps or the Dolomites because those mountains are so steep,” explains Alexa Hasman, a mountain athlete, personal trainer, and founder of Rise Ultra Coaching. The trick, she says, is to combine endurance training with hill repeats and gym time to build serious muscular power. Here are a few of her favorite hill workouts. Your first order of business is to build a strong endurance base. For this, Hasman recommends finding the longest hill you can (or setting your treadmill to its maximum incline) and climbing at a consistent pace for one to two hours. Ideally, you’ll carry a little weight: Hasman suggests starting with ten percent of your bodyweight and hiking for 60 minutes. Add 15 minutes each week. You can also play with weight, adding about five pounds per week until you’re at 20 percent of your bodyweight. Hasman cautions against carrying any more than that. Upwards of 20 percent, the likelihood of injury outweighs the diminishing strength gains. (Also avoid increasing weight and distance in the same week—up one or the other, but not both.) Throughout, stick to a pace that’s engaged but sustainable. “You should be conversational,” Hasman says. “If you can say three sentences at a time without gasping for breath, that’s where I want you.” A single long hike is great, but it doesn’t quite simulate the back-to-back days of serious vert that you’ll encounter on a backpacking trip. To prepare, Hasman recommends doing two endurance workouts per week on consecutive days. “Cumulative fatigue is really important there,” Hasman says. “It teaches your body to work on tired legs. You might feel stiff, sore, or heavy the next day, but that’s normal. This is just as much about mental training as it is physical.” Once you have a strong endurance base—i.e., you can reliably hike uphill for 90 to 120 minutes while carrying 15 to 20 percent of your bodyweight—it’s time to start building speed and power. Find a steep hill and charge up it at close to your max effort for ten seconds. Walk slowly down to the base of the hill, then do it again. Your goal is four total reps. Over time, build up to reps of 30 seconds, then 60 seconds, then two minutes, then three minutes. If you live near a hill that’s long enough for a three-minute interval, great. If not, do this on a treadmill at its maximum incline setting. “If you’re an uphill athlete, then you’re also by nature a downhill athlete,” Hasman says. And if you’ve ever done a long descent with weight on your back, you’re probably aware that downhills are the real quad-killers. To avoid jellified quads during your trip, Hasman recommends training downhills specifically. One way to do this is to reverse the above workout. Walk slowly up a hill, then charge down it as fast as you can go without being reckless. Do this for four reps. You can also combine these two workouts: Book it up the hill, then book it down, and take your rest at the bottom. Welcome to the least-fun workout on this list—but perhaps the most effective. “Wall sits are my secret sauce for downhill,” Hasman says. They’re great because they hold you in an exaggerated, active downhill-hiking position for an extended period. “I start my athletes with one-minute wall sits a couple of times a week. After a few weeks, we go until failure. Then we add weight.” Once you can sit with a ten-pound plate on your lap for a minute or two, you’re ready for boss level: single-leg wall sits. “Most people can only hold them for a second or two—it’s almost like marching while sitting against a wall,” Hasman says. “If you can hold it for 30 seconds, you’re an absolute beast.” Nothing beats single-leg exercises for building uphill strength and stability. To this end, Hasman recommends getting into the gym at least twice a week during the meat of your training. Focus on your glutes, quads, hamstrings, and core. While there are tons of relevant exercises, Hasman says step-ups are a particular must-do. “Do 15 to 30 reps on one leg, then switch,” she recommends. Start with three sets. Every week, either add a set or add five pounds of additional weight to make it harder. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: A New Approach to Disaster Relief
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.53
Participants carrying Amazon’s portable rapid response technology systems during their disaster relief training exercise. (Photo: Pete Kiehart) From this summer’s intense wildfires to back-to-back earthquakes to a brewing Super El Niño, one thing is clear: The growing threat of natural disasters is hard to ignore. Supercharged by climate change, events like wildfires, earthquakes, hurricanes, and floods now occur more regularly, often in places that aren’t prepared for them. This reality means billions of people worldwide need stronger preparedness and resilience measures. This new era of heightened risk requires a new era of heightened response, from innovative tools to strong relationships to advanced preparation. Enter Amazon. “When I spoke with first responders, I kept hearing the same failures repeat over and over—disasters affecting their ability to communicate, provide relief quickly, or even access resources as basic as clean water,” said Jeffrey Schweitzer, Amazon’s disaster relief innovation lead. Along with nonprofit partners, Schweitzer and his team developed new, customizable rapid response technology systems to restore critical services, all in suitcase-sized packages that one person can carry and set up in just a few minutes. “During disasters, responders need to understand the landscape, the impact, where survivors are, and who needs help,” said Rodney Cooper, who serves as national director for technology and programs with the Information Technology Disaster Resource Center (ITDRC). “During Hurricane Helene, everything was dark. Survivors could not reach out to each other.” That’s exactly the kind of situation this new tech is made for: restoring services within hours, so communities don’t have to wait weeks to call loved ones or turn the lights back on. Amazon’s rapid response tech includes 10-plus configurations that relief personnel can set up: solar microgrids, satellite Wi-Fi, water purification devices, even terrain-mapping drones. The drone systems alone can cost up to $250,000, but Amazon provides them to partners at no cost. And the tech is reusable: After a disaster response ends, nonprofits ship the systems back to Amazon for inspection, refurbishment, and restocking. Meaning one system can serve multiple communities, across multiple disasters. The systems can power hospitals, emergency shelters, fire departments, and community centers. A single system can keep a 50-bed hospital running for 72 hours or serve more than 2,600 hot meals—and they’ve already been crucial for restoring communities after recent disasters. Following the recent twin earthquakes in Venezuela, where telecommunications were completely severed near the epicenter in La Guaira, Amazon worked with nonprofit partners on the ground to deliver portable Wi-Fi systems to connect clinics, shelters, and community hubs. One system was placed on a car roof to create a movie night for kids. And in Jamaica, after Hurricane Melissa, portable solar batteries and satellite Wi-Fi units restored power and communications within minutes so doctors could coordinate patient care. Solar systems even allowed World Central Kitchen to power its food trucks and serve hot meals after dark. “For Amazon, preparedness means prepositioning. It’s having the people trained. It’s having everything from pallets of diapers to satellite communications ready to go,” said Abe Diaz, senior manager for disaster relief at Amazon. “That means the time it takes for the community to get back on their feet is shorter, and ultimately that means recovery time is shorter.” Amazon will make 2,000 of these systems available to nonprofit partners in 2027, with 800 ready to ship from the company’s disaster relief hub in Tennessee this hurricane season. Preparation also requires coordination and practice. At a recent training exercise in a small Maryland town, Amazon brought together two dozen organizations—including local fire and rescue, nonprofit partners, and government agencies—to practice how people, technology, and partnerships can work together to strengthen disaster response. Participants launched into a series of hands-on missions, including a river crossing into an isolated flood-affected community, a simulated search-and-rescue mission, and helicopter-assisted aid delivery. Each mission was designed to put Amazon’s rapid response technology to the test in real-world conditions and allow local communities, companies, and government agencies to get hands-on experience with both the tech and each other. “You don’t want everyone exchanging business cards and meeting each other in the middle of a disaster itself,” said Civil Affairs Major Alex Haseley, an emergency management specialist with the U.S. Army. “Events like this, we’re getting to meet each other, we’re building some trust, we’re figuring out how to contact each other on relatively short notice. Emergency management is such a magical mission: When people feel what it’s like to truly help a survivor, it’s like a drug and you want to keep doing it.” During a disaster, hot meals do more than sustain people—they restore dignity and normalcy when communities need it most. For the training exercise, nonprofit organization Operation BBQ Relief used Amazon’s technology systems to power hot-meal preparation for dozens of people, including police officers and firefighters who serve the town daily. “A lot of times, the last thing you’re thinking about is nourishing yourself—you’re worried about your home, belongings,” said Chris Huggins, head of logistics and inventory for Operation BBQ Relief. “Barbecue brings hope and comfort—you’ve never sat down to a plate of barbecue and been sad, y’know? Taking five minutes to share a hot meal with a loved one is like saying, ‘Hey, there’s gonna be a better tomorrow. You’re not alone, and we’re here for you.’ This groundbreaking tech is a natural evolution of Amazon’s commitment to aid global communities threatened by sudden disaster. Since 2017, Amazon has donated and delivered over 30 million emergency supplies to support communities impacted by more than 200 disasters globally. Amazon leverages the same logistics network, aviation capabilities, and cloud technology that power its day-to-day operations to deliver rapid aid to communities facing crisis. “When a major disaster strikes, every minute a community spends without power, clean water, or connectivity is critical,” Schweitzer said. “Amazon is uniquely positioned to repurpose our existing delivery network, fulfillment hubs, and tech capabilities to get essential aid where it’s needed in hours, so even when infrastructures fail, recovery can start sooner.” When disasters strike, Amazon uses the same strengths that get packages to doorsteps to bring critical aid where it’s needed, fast. Since 2017, Amazon has donated and delivered more than 30 million relief items to support communities impacted by 200-plus disasters worldwide. For more information, visit AboutAmazon.com.

item.title: Diving with Giant Manta Rays in Mexico’s Remote Revillagigedo Islands
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.75
(Photo: Jay Clue) My dive watch shows I am 78 feet deep. Even though this is my 17th dive in four days, I feel my heart race and nerves bubble up as we descend into plankton blooms, which are not affording us the crystal-clear diving conditions we’ve experienced in days prior. With nothing to focus my gaze on in these hazy waters, my mind is flooded with thoughts I’ve pushed away this week, including just how far out in the Pacific Ocean I am. Suddenly, I see the now-familiar silhouette of a massive winged creature emerging from the blue. As it gets closer, I stay still—a tip that’s provided me with numerous close encounters this week. It circles me, so close I can see its depthless purple eye, the size of a tennis ball, watching me. And then comes another. A giant oceanic manta ray (Mobula birostris) with a wingspan of 20 feet appears out of the abyss. A handful of other divers quickly kick over, camera rigs pointed forward like shields. Before they reach us, my giant friend hovers a mere four feet above me. I hang motionless. Time seems to slow as the manta reveals its chevron belly, unfurling its scars. And then it’s gone. An immense wave of awe washes over me; my eyes water behind my mask. We are 250 nautical miles—more than 24 hours by boat—from Cabo San Lucas, on the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula. That’s the closest civilization, so to speak, from us in the ultra-remote Revillagigedo archipelago. Uninhabited by humans, these four volcanic islands are often referred to as the “Galápagos of Mexico” due to their dramatic underwater pinnacles, exceptional biodiversity, and waters teeming with large pelagic species like giant manta rays, sharks, and whales. In 2016, UNESCO declared the islands a World Heritage Site, and in 2017, it became the largest marine protected area in North America. The only way to visit these remote islands is via a liveaboard boat. And while a Mexican Navy base houses roughly 250 caretakers and their families for this protected area, regular tourists aren’t allowed to step foot on the islands—permits are almost exclusively given for scientific research. But everyone’s here for what’s below the surface: hammerhead sharks galore, singing humpbacks, 20-ton polka-dotted whale sharks, and the islands’ biggest attraction—friendly manta rays that can reach up to 22 feet long. Conditions can be challenging this far out, and out of the group of 20 divers on our seven-day liveaboard trip, I’m the least experienced arriving with only 45 dives. In comparison, some of my fellow divers have several thousand under their belt. Our guide is Jay Clue, the owner and founder of Dive Ninja Expeditions, the first designated PADI Eco Center in Mexico and one of the first in the world. Dive Ninja leads eco-minded big marine animal diving expeditions all over the world. An award-winning photographer, Clue has a deep passion for marine conservation and sustainable tourism that proves these manta rays (and other endangered species) are more valuable alive than dead. On this particular trip, there are many aspiring Clues who want to hone their underwater photography skills. So while my fellow divers are kitted out with the best and biggest camera rigs, I have chosen to dive without even a GoPro. With strong currents and sustained depths, a camera would be one more thing I’d have to think about. This camera-free choice affords me closer encounters, too—apparently, mantas want to look into our eyes, not our lenses. Research suggests mantas are some of the most intelligent fish on our planet. They have massive brains, can recognize themselves in mirrors, and can recognize us, too, it seems. “I was unexpectedly greeted by two familiar faces once,” says Clue, who has led more than 20 trips to these islands in the last decade. “A few mantas I’ve spent time photographing on past trips swam directly up to me, then proceeded to unroll their cephalic fins as they glided, motionless, eye-to-eye only a few feet away.” Almost as if they were saying hello to an old friend, says Clue. “Is this just a rare coincidence my human brain is trying to turn into something it isn’t,” he wonders, “or could it be something more?” Robert Rubin, PhD, the region’s foremost expert on these “flying carpets of ebony silk,” as he calls them, has been studying gigantic oceanic manta rays in Mexico for more than three decades. The founder and director of the Pacific Manta Research Group, he believes manta rays are sentient, intelligent creatures that merit protection. Inspired by Rubin’s research, Clue set out to create dive trips that combine awe-inspiring marine encounters with conservation education and citizen science. “You can dive with manta rays all over the world, but here they have a different behavior than we see anywhere else. They seem to seek out interactions with divers. You can see their eyes tracking you. It feels like they want to have a conversation with us,” says Clue. Several evenings on the trip, he gives presentations on Rubin’s research and Pacific Manta Research Group’s manta identification effort, which is a citizen science project anyone can get involved in. “Whether you have a tiny GoPro or a $10,000 camera, it doesn’t really matter. Anyone can take photos of the mantas’ bellies and submit them,” says Clue. This crowdsourced data helps researchers identify specific individuals to track migrations and protect critical aggregation sites. Today, the biggest threats to mantas are overtourism (in mainland Mexico and worldwide) and boat strikes, both around the islands and on their migratory travels. “As Revillagigedo is a remote location, technically protected by both a national park and the World Heritage Site, it’s largely a safe space for these animals,” says Karey Kumli, project manager at Pacific Manta Research Group. Responsible tourism, however, plays a powerful role in protecting the manta rays. “It wasn’t until all the tourist boats came [to Revillagigedo] that the fishing [ban] really was enforced. So it’s crucial that there’s tourists there,” says Cody Sheehy, director of The Last Dive, a new film about these islands and the mantas making its way across festival circuits this year. “The money and the jobs brought to those islands showed the Mexican government could justify their position on keeping it in the national park and [staving off] fishing,” he adds. Individual mantas have been tracked through photo identification for up to 33 years—the worldwide age record for the oceanic (giant) mantas. When they look back at photo sets taken 10 to 40 years ago, 95 percent of those animals have made at least two appearances, says Kumli. Our dive trip alone added 44 new mantas to the research database. I added a manta to the database and named her Artemis. Inspired from the 2026 Artemis II historic lunar flyby where a crew traveled farther from Earth than any humans in history. It seemed a fitting name, as this dive trip felt like it was the closest I’d ever get to floating weightlessness in space. After each dive at different islands throughout the week, we’d find ourselves elated, rehashing all our incredible encounters on the top deck at sunset. Gina, a veteran diver from Florida, said it best: “My version of heaven is where all questions are answered. Including what the mantas are thinking.” Diving this far out, deep in the blue, felt like a spiritual, mysterious realm to me. And while we haven’t found out what mantas are thinking just yet, the fact that these creatures still trust us in this world feels like heaven enough. This article is from the Summer 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here.

item.title: How to Clean, Sanitize, and Store a Water Filter in the Off-season
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 3.93
It's important to clean and sanitize your backcountry water filter or purifier before storing it during the off-season and winter months. A simple three-stage process involves cleaning the filter to improve flow rate, sanitizing it to kill microorganisms, and drying it before storing it until you're ready to use it again. Step 1: Backflush Your Water Filter or Purifier Many backcountry water filters and purifiers can be backflushed, meaning you reverse the normal flow of water through the filter element. This unclogs debris or contaminants stuck in the filter, flushes them out, and improves the filter's flow rate. Many filters and purifiers come with a hose or a syringe, like the Sawyer Squeeze that you can use to perform this backflushing operation. to clean it. If you've used your water filter or purifier recently, you only need to backflush/clean it a few times. If you haven't used it recently and the filter element is “dry”, it's best to run water through the filter in the normal direction to wet it out before commencing the backflushing operation. Try not to apply extra pressure when you backflush the filter element because it can rip or deform the internal element, which may be paper, depending on the product you use. Sawyer claims their filters are pretty tough, but others are not, and I think it's prudent to be firm but gentle during the backflushing process. Step 2: Sanitize the Filter Element In this next stage, you need to sanitize the filter/purification element and kill any microorganisms that may remain inside. You don't want these to keep growing over the winter because they can permanently clog or damage the filter element. Different manufacturers suggest slightly different procedures, so check their website recommendations. The two most common ways people sanitize their water filter/purification element are to flush it with a diluted bleach solution made with one capful of fragrance-free bleach per Liter of tap water. A few liters should do the trick. Filter these as you would in the field with raw water. Once finished, filter a quart or two of plain tap water through to remove any remaining chemicals so you don't get a mouthful when you start using the filter next season. Alternatively, you can treat a liter or two of water with Aquamira drops or Katadyn Micropur tablets to sanitize your filter. These contain chlorine dioxide, which is an ultralight way to purify backcountry water sources without filtering. If you use one, you don't need to rinse your filter afterward, as the water you'll backflush or clean your filter with is completely potable. In fact, many city and town water supplies use chlorine dioxide to treat their tap water. Step 3: Drying and Storage Let your filter/purifier dry slowly and naturally by placing it in a warm, well-ventilated location, out of direct sunlight. After a week, move it to a drawer or closet in the heated part of your home. Come next season, it will be ready to use. Note: Some manufacturers suggest slightly different procedures, so check their website recommendations. For instance, rather than letting your filter dry, some recommend storing it wet after sanitizing. That's all there is to it! Updated September 2026. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. Some municipalities have enough metals in their water that flushing with your tap water as a final step may lead to a stubborn clog in the spring. It generally requires some sort of acidic flush to get those minerals about. Citric acid is recommended by some manufacturers for this.

item.title: Burrata and beyond: a foodie tour of northern Puglia, Italy
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.43
‘I don’t eat mozzarella outside Puglia,” says our friend Savio. “It’s not the same.” Savio is a very opinionated foodie, so I take his words with a pinch of good Puglian sea salt (see below). He was adamant about the superiority of the stretched-curd cheese from his home turf. Puglia is also the birthplace of ingredient du jour burrata, which originated in Andria, a few miles from Savio’s home town of Barletta. Andria forms one part of the triangular Barletta-Andria-Trani (BAT) province, but despite the cheese connection and Barletta having miles of palm-backed, sandy beaches, it is often passed over for better-known parts of Puglia. So I asked Savio’s company, Unexpected Italy, an app that calls itself the antidote to overtourism, to organise a trip to the area. About a century ago, in the hills outside Andria, farmer Lorenzo Bianchino was snowed in and couldn’t get his milk to market. To save what he could, he revived an old technique for preserving butter (burro, hence burrata), stuffing cream mixed with mozzarella scraps (stracciatella) in a casing of the stretched-curd cheese. There are now several burrata makers in Andria, the most famous being Caseificio Olanda, which offers demos, tastings and a museum. Late one morning, we watch Riccardo “Dino” Olanda, son of the founders, work his magic. He adds almost-boiling water to the curds, then mixes with hands red from doing this every day. As he stretches and massages the curds, a smooth velvety mass forms. “See how it’s shiny?” he says. “Means it’s ready.” Working quickly, he squeezes out round lumps between thumb and forefinger into the familiar mozzarella balls. This action is mozzare, hence the name. He also makes little knots and plaits before moving on to burrata. Taking a warm mozzarella ball, he works it into a hollow bag with his fingers then fills it with cream and stracciatella before tying the top with string. Afterwards, a dairy-heavy meal totally worth the cholesterol and calories: mozzarella and burrata to start, then bread with chunks of caciocavallo (a stretched-curd cheese), and a dessert of heart-shaped fresh ricotta with strawberry jam or cocoa. And, I have to say, Savio is right. The mozzarella and burrata have a juicy, elastic texture and a gorgeous cheesy, umami flavour; the salt and flavour leached out by the whey the cheeses later sit in. How will I ever settle for Tesco Finest after this? Over the next few days, eating our way around the province’s restaurants and food producers, I wonder whether it’s because the ingredients are so good that this area has so many food obsessives, or the other way round. Barletta sees few foreign tourists, but it is full of Italian life. There are lots of independent shops, a Norman castle and cathedral to visit, and every evening people pour into the bars, clubs and gelaterie of the sette strade, seven parallel streets in the old town. Down the coast, Trani, with its sea-facing romanesque cathedral and pretty harbour, attracts some tourists, but they are not in evidence at 7am when the fishing boats return. The men complain of rough seas and a poor catch, but from the back of the boats they’re soon selling mullet, octopus, skate, fat sea snails, monkfish and palombo (small shark) to restaurateurs and fishmongers. Thirtysomething Nicola says he went out at midday and got back at 3am. When does he sleep? “Never.” A fifth-generation fisher, he began helping on the boats aged six. We’ll eat fish later, but today is for pizza. Portento in Barletta is run by food nut Luigi Lacerenza. He has us try so many local products as antipasti – caprino goat’s cheese tasting of green mountains, grilled caciocavallo from an old couple who make just six a week and small-batch salami – that we’re almost too full for pizzas. But they are wonderful: one with sausage, olives, oyster mushrooms and yellow tomatoes; another with aubergines and grated cacioricotta. In Cerignola, west of Barletta, Rosario Didonna used the money he won on a TV standup competition to turn his family’s deli into a cosy, wood- panelled restaurant, U’ Vulèsce (dialect for “peckish”). Rosario knows fishers by name, works with small farmers and wine producers, and invites nonne from all over southern Italy to demonstrate recipes in his kitchens. We start with tasty goat prosciutto and plum-sized local olives called bella di Cerignola. Then an unforgettable prawn tartare served in sea urchin shells, hairy crab spaghetti (“the juice is better than lobster”), octopus with bean puree, and sea bass with orange mayo. He waves away our thanks: “I’m doing the best job in the world!” Nicola Barbera at Masseria Barbera, a farm restaurant in the Alta Murgia national park, is equally inspired, but rather by what grows on the estate founded by his great-great-great-great-grandfather Riccardo, who fought with Garibaldi. Exuberantly bouncing us around the farm – it produces 90% of what the 100-cover restaurant needs – he shows us olives and vines, but also the “weeds” growing around them. “They’re eatable,” he says, grabbing handfuls of peppery rocket, and bitter but delicate wild chicory. From the abundant kitchen garden, he makes eight varieties of tomato sauce. We tuck into a lot of this for lunch: a pie with white onions, anchovy and sultanas; courgettes with mint and garlic; spaghetti with yellow tomatoes. (“I call it bastard sauce,” says Nicola. “Those tomatoes take three times as long to pick.”) Then, something I never thought I’d eat: grilled donkey fillet. I feel bad about the patient, mild-tempered beasts, but this is healthy, low-fat food, never intensively farmed. It’s also the best meat I’ve ever tasted. Good food is made better by good olive oil, and producers here include Muraglia, known for organic oil in hand-painted, rainbow-stripe ceramic bottles, and Sabino Leone, offering tours of its ancient groves and oil mill for €15, plus tastings. This area also offers plenty to do between meals. Barletta was the home of Italian painter Giuseppe De Nittis, who hung out with Degas and Manet, and took part in the first impressionist exhibition in Paris, in 1874. Over 200 of his works are now displayed in the 16th-century Palazzo della Marra (€6). At Europe’s biggest salt pan, Salina Margherita di Savoia, there’s an expanse of peaceful ponds with a snow-white salt mountain to climb. Another day, an exhilarating ebike ride in the Alta Murgia with Filippo Tito of Cycling ’n’ Trek, through dense forest to peer with awe into an old bauxite mine that resembles a mini grand canyon. We get back ravenous, but in this corner of northern Puglia, that’s a blessing. Where to stay Until this century, Barletta had little tourist accommodation. Pick of the few B&Bs is Antica Dimora (doubles from €97), a restored 17th-century palazzo run by Lilly and Riccardo Manna. There are three smart bedrooms with lots of plants and breakfast features different local specialities each day. Lama di Luna (doubles from €230) is an organic farm in deep countryside, with six rooms set around an 18th-century stone courtyard. A well and solar panels make it energy and water self-sufficient; half of its 200 hectares are left wild, the rest are planted with olives, vines, almonds and cherries. There’s a cinema, a library and a large pool shaded by 600-year-old olive trees. Where (else) to eat Barletta’s 60-year-old Mosé bakery is revered for its krapfen filled doughnuts and sourdough croissants. There are also chocolates, ice-cream and cakes, all housemade, and great coffee. Puglia has hundreds of gelaterie but experts rate Scoop in Canosa (which is called Puglia’s “Little Rome” for its catacombs, temple ruins and Roman bridge). Francesco Di Nunno makes ice-cream with local seasonal ingredients: raspberry and strawberry sorbets are available only in early summer; percoca yellow peach until mid-August. There’s affordable fine dining at chef Luciano Matera’s Il Turracciolo in central Andria. Highlights for me are broad bean and chicory “meatballs”, bright green inside; a “hidden mushroom” under baked eggy topping; and pasta discs with whole and pureed green beans and peas. At A Sud dell’Anima, chef Nadia Tamburrano uses modern techniques and hyper-local ingredients to make food of astonishing quality for a small hilltop town (Minervino, population under 8,000). Her antipasti explode with flavour thanks to house-cured capers and homemade mustard, syrups and purees. A main of sweetbreads wrapped in intestines feels a bit out-there, but is delicious, the intestines crispy as crackling. The trip was organised by Unexpected Italy, which offers personalised itineraries for Barletta and the surrounding area Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Wine tasting, swimming holes and honky-tonks: A road trip through the Texas Hill Country
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.24
Wine tasting, swimming holes and honky-tonks: A road trip through the Texas Hill Country The Texas Hill Country has arguably the most photogenic landscape in the Lone Star State. Comprising a 25-county swatch of limestone and granite hills, ridges and caverns, this region forms the geographical boundary between the wetter, greener southeastern side of the state and the sunnier, drier southwestern side. On a road trip along the rocky bluffs, lush aquifer-fed valleys and semi-arid stands of yucca, juniper and live oak, you can fully sense that you're at the intersection of two major continental zones. Although this largely rural region abounds with wilderness parks, hiking trails and swimming holes, it's also home to a pair of urban cultural hubs, Austin and San Antonio. Related: What is the best gas rewards program for saving at the pump in 2026? Texas Hill Country road trip planning Although this itinerary starts and ends in San Antonio, you can just as easily use Austin as your base. Because the heart of the Hill Country is relatively compact, you could spend your entire stay in either of these cities, exploring the countryside on a series of day trips. But to fully appreciate the area's welcoming vibe and verdant countryside, spend at least a couple of nights in a smaller town, such as Fredericksburg, with its growing cache of stylish lodgings, or perhaps Boerne, Marble Falls or Gruene. Budgeting your time Give yourself at least three days to immerse yourself and fully appreciate the region's mellow personality. This part of the world is best appreciated at a leisurely pace. This way, you can spend a couple of nights in one of the aforementioned smaller towns, plus a night in either Austin or San Antonio. If you're able to budget a full week, you'll have time for some in-depth winery-hopping, longer hikes and rafting trips and live music shows — and you can check out the highlights of both Austin and San Antonio. Related: The best rental car loyalty programs in 2026 Getting to the Texas Hill Country The region is served by two large international airports, Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) and San Antonio International Airport (SAT). Related: Delta to offer more connections in Austin focus city. Will it ever be a hub? The best months to visit the Texas Hill Country Every season here has its charms. Spring is tops for strolling through colorful wildflower meadows, autumn offers a chance to see the changing foliage of maple and cypress trees, while winter has milder weather, fewer crowds and a cozy vibe. These seasons are more temperate than Texas summers, during which you may contend with highs in the triple digits. But there's also something appealing about eating barbecue brisket and listening to a bluegrass band on a hot summer night. Keep in mind that powerful rainstorms sometimes soak the Hill Country, especially May through October. The tragic and deadly floods of July 2025, for example, significantly damaged the western side of the region, around Kerrville and Hunt. This event largely spared the towns covered on this itinerary. A Hill Country hotel boom The Hill Country is right in the midst of a lodging boom, and several noteworthy hotels and resorts are in the works as of this writing. The eco-chic 1 Hotel Austin recently opened in Aug. 2026 in a gleaming 74-story tower in the bustling Rainey District downtown. Fredericksburg has a pair of high-profile properties on the horizon, including the Kimpton Fredericksburg, with an anticipated 2027 opening, and the Waldorf Astoria Texas Hill Country, the luxury brand's first resort in the state, with plans to open by early 2028. The Ophelia Hotel Marble Falls, part of Hilton's Tapestry Collection, is now accepting reservations from Feb. 2027. Exploring San Antonio Although this city sprawls over a 500-square-mile area, most of the key attractions lie within a narrow north-south corridor bisected by the San Antonio River. Start south of downtown by exploring the linear San Antonio Missions National Historical Park, a trail of four missions developed by the Spaniards in the late-17th and early-18th centuries. The largest and best restored is Mission San Jose. As you enter downtown, drive along St. Mary's Street past the ornate Victorian mansions of the King William Historic District, pausing for a bite at one of Southtown's hip eateries. Then park around La Villita Historic Arts Village, a collection of colorful crafts and art galleries established by the WPA in 1939. Here you can access the Downtown Reach loop of the iconic San Antonio River Walk, a captivating promenade that wends through the city's heart. The downtown section is lined with touristy restaurant terraces, but its twinkly lights and colorful umbrellas are festive nonetheless. Emerge from the River Walk to visit The Alamo — its exhibits relate the stirring tale of the building's ill-fated yet inspiring role in the 1836 Texas Revolution. Follow the River Walk north through the three-mile Museum Reach section, which is hands-down the most appealing stretch, with its lush greenery and whimsical public art. Allow at least an hour to visit the outstanding San Antonio Museum of Art before strolling north to the buzzy Pearl District, a hive of stylish eateries and boutiques fashioned out of an ornately designed late-Victorian brewery complex. Enjoy dinner at Down on Grayson or Southerleigh Fine Food and Brewery. Where to stay in San Antonio In the Pearl District along the River Walk, the striking 146-room Hotel Emma (rates start at $445 per night) occupies a magnificently transformed 19th-century brewery building with inviting common spaces and stylish restaurants. It's a member of the American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts collection, offering perks like complimentary daily breakfast for two to select cardholders. North of downtown and well-situated to begin your exploration of the surrounding greenery, the posh JW Marriott San Antonio Hill Country Resort & Spa (rates start at $359 or 52,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night) has a nine-acre water park, a spa and several fine dining options. Hyatt loyalists can head west of downtown to check into the Hyatt Regency Hill Country Resort and Villas (rates start at $413 or 15,000 World of Hyatt points per night), which recently wrapped up a $100 million renovation with the opening of a 2.2-acre lagoon. San Antonio to Fredericksburg Depart San Antonio and head north up U.S. Highway 281, turning left onto Highway 46 in Bulverde, making the short detour north to Guadalupe River State Park. Hop out for a light hike on the easy but rewarding Bald Cypress Trail, then cool off with a dip in the river. Continue about 15 miles west on Highway 46 into Boerne (pronounced Bur-nee). Bisected by Cibolo Creek, this charming town was, like so many in this part of the state, settled in the mid-19th century by German immigrants. Stroll along Cibolo Creek in River Road Park, with its stately bald cypress trees and cheerful chorus of ducks and geese. In town, grab a latte from Black Rifle Coffee or a malty kolsch from Free Roam Brewing Company (a good bet for pizzas too). Continue north on rural Highway 474, then turn left onto Highway 473, with a potential detour to Hillbillyz or, in nearby Sisterdale, Black Board Bar-B-Q for mouthwatering barbecue. Drop by Sister Creek Vineyards for a wine flight, then continue west to tiny Toonstone, and turn north onto Old 9 Road to Old Tunnel State Park, where you can hike down to an old railroad tunnel and witness about 3 million Mexican free-tailed bats flutter out at dusk each evening (May through October). From here, follow the road north through Grapetown into Fredericksburg. Fredericksburg This picturesque town of around 12,000 residents has steadily blossomed into one of Hill Country's most appealing getaways. Stretching about 10 blocks along Main Street, the downtown Fredericksburg Historic District is framed by stately limestone buildings, many with ornate German-style wooden or iron trim. A few of these contain museums, such as the informative Pioneer Museum and the octagonal Vereins Kirche Museum. The National Museum of the Pacific War — an affiliate of the Smithsonian — contains thought-provoking exhibits on World War II and has just finished a renovation. Allow a half-day to explore downtown's distinctive shops and savor lunch at one of the old-world German restaurants, such as The Auslander or Old German Bakery. Just southeast of town, tiny Luckenbach is one of the Lone Star State's greatest and weirdest treasures. This legendary live music venue is set amid the rustic grounds of a mid-19th-century German trading post and had been essentially abandoned when eccentric entrepreneurs bought it and turned it into a music hall in the early 1970s. Immortalized in the 1977 Waylon Jennings song "Luckenbach, Texas," it's a memorable place to watch leading country, bluegrass and folk singers perform. Llano and Marble Falls Loop From Fredericksburg, it's an easy day trip to explore some of the Hill Country's most dramatic scenery. Head north on Highway 965 for 17 miles to Enchanted Rock State Natural Area, the dominant feature of which is an imposing pink-granite dome that rises several hundred feet above the arid landscape. Continue to Highway 16 and into downtown Llano for a lunch of Cajun and Tex-Mex cooking at the Barrel House, and a stop by the Llano Fine Arts Guild and Gallery to view its impressive selection of artwork by regional talents. The drive continues east on Highway 29 along the southern shore of rippling Buchanan Lake, and then on to Inks Lake State Park, where you can swim amid the pink granite outcroppings of Devil's Waterhole. This is also a great park for wildflower hikes and kayak paddles (rentals are available). You can break up the day with a tasting at Perissos Vineyard and Winery or Uplift Vineyard, then continue to Longhorn Cavern State Park for a guided 1.1-mile round-trip tour of its limestone cave. Have a look at the stately museum and other stone structures built in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). Drive east to U.S. Highway 281, following it south to the oft-photographed Bluebonnet House, anchored by a once gracious but now dilapidated mid-19th-century farmhouse surrounded by spectacular wildflower meadows. The next stop is Marble Falls, a dapper town on a scenic stretch of the Colorado River that's popular for stand-up paddleboarding and kayaking. Many of its attractive limestone storefronts house art galleries and wine-tasting rooms, and the beloved Blue Bonnet Cafe has been serving satisfying chicken and dumplings and pecan pies since 1929. From here, it's about an hour drive back to Fredericksburg. Where to stay in Fredericksburg A sleek mix of contemporary and beautifully restored historic downtown buildings, the Albert Hotel (rates start at $265 per night) opened in 2025 with 105 rooms, superb restaurants and bars and a serene spa with an extensive spa menu. A few blocks away, the Winchester Lodge (rates start at $188 per night) offers 16 spacious suites, many with Jacuzzi tubs, kitchenettes, balconies and fireplaces. Fredericksburg to Austin It's an 80-mile straight shot east on U.S. Highway 290 to Austin, and there's plenty to see along the way, including more than half of the Hill Country's 100+ wineries, some with downtown tasting rooms but many in the surrounding vineyard-dotted countryside, where you'll also find pecan, peach and other farms. The glass-walled tasting room and gracious patio at William Chris Vineyards are a gorgeous backdrop for sampling Rhone-style blends and listening to live music. Slate Theory Winery stands out for its industrial-chic design and fascinating tours of its vast underground cellar, and at Signor Vineyards, you can savor an exceptional cheese-charcuterie board while you sip a crisp Sauvignon Blanc amid the manicured gardens and sweeping lawns. In Hye, you can also drop by Garrison Brothers Distillery for a tour and to taste the exceptionally smooth and complex bourbons. The tiny town of Stonewall is closely associated with the 36th U.S. president, Lyndon B. Johnson, who resided here on a sprawling riverside ranch known as the Texas White House. Learn about his storied, if at times controversial, life at Lyndon B. Johnson National Historical Park, which you can explore on a self-guided driving tour that begins at an engaging museum in adjacent Lyndon B. Johnson State Park & Historic Site and includes the reconstructed modest dwelling he was born in and the cemetery where he was laid to rest. Note that parts of the park are currently closed during a major restoration project that's expected to wrap up in 2027. Johnson City and Blanco About 15 miles east in Johnson City, you can visit a second unit of the national historical park. It includes the Victorian home where LBJ grew up and a visitor center with exhibits about him and his wife, Lady Bird. Continue down U.S. Highway 281 through Blanco, which appeared prominently in the Coen Brothers' acclaimed remake of "True Grit." If it's a hot day, dip your toes in the spring-fed waters of Blanco State Park. Then order a venison burger at the Redbud Cafe and Pub, located in a vintage storefront on the town square. Check out the owners' sturdy yet stunning stoneware pottery, which they sell in their adjacent gallery. From here, head east along rural Highway 165 through tiny Henly, rejoining U.S. Highway 290 to Dripping Springs. Exploring Austin Take Highway 12 north from Dripping Springs to Bee Cave, and then follow Highway 620 toward the pretty eastern shoreline of Lake Travis, which is actually a dammed reservoir along the 862-mile Colorado River (not to be confused with that other Colorado River that flows through the Grand Canyon). On the western outskirts of Austin, Lake Travis is a fine spot for boating, swimming and sunbathing. You can work up an adrenaline rush riding the ropes at Lake Travis Zipline Adventures, saunter sans-Speedo along the clothing-optional (and LGBTQ+-popular) stone terraces of Hippie Hollow Park or sip margaritas and nosh on shrimp fajitas at the Oasis on Lake Travis, a rambling multistory cantina that sits high on a precipice with stunning water views. Follow Highway 2222 east into Austin, stopping for the short but slightly strenuous trek up the 106 steps to the 705-foot summit of Mount Bonnell for a great view of the river. Yet another Texas city that's undergone incredibly rapid growth over the past few decades, the once-easygoing college town (University of Texas) and state capital, Austin, has doubled in population since 1990 and now has more than a million residents. Traversed by a wide stretch of the Colorado River known here as Lady Bird Lake, Austin is more a place to explore hip neighborhoods than museums. Still, the imposing 10-story LBJ Presidential Library on the leafy campus of the University of Texas is an interesting stop for history buffs, as is the Bullock Texas State History Museum, with its extensive collections touching on everything from the state's rich Native American heritage to its considerable contributions to space exploration. It's also worth taking a tour of the elegant Renaissance Revival–style Texas State Capitol building, which dates to 1885 and has a beautiful interior and grounds. On sunny days, stroll amid the fragrant plantings and trees of Zilker Botanical Garden and refresh yourself at nearby Barton Springs Pool, an outdoor swimming hole fed by natural underground springs that keep it at a constant temperature of around 70 degrees. One of the best ways to experience this high-tech hub of creative design and exceptional eating and drinking is to walk around one of Austin's buzzy neighborhoods, which pulse with celebrated restaurants, music clubs, and indie shops. Excellent areas for this include downtown 2nd Street, Rainey Street, the Warehouse District, East Austin and South Congress. Where to stay in Austin With an ideal downtown location adjacent to the famous Austin City Limits Live music venue and steps from the trails along Lady Bird Lake, the 36-story W Austin (rates start at $378 or 52,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night) unveiled a dramatic redesign in 2024 and features some of the cushiest digs in town, plus an exceptional spa and a hip speakeasy cocktail bar, the Blue Room. Out in the countryside closer to Lake Travis, book one of the dapper rooms at the Omni Barton Creek Resort & Spa (rates start at $349 per night), with its sweeping views of the surrounding hills, four world-class golf courses and an expansive sun terrace with three pools and a full spa. Austin to San Antonio Although Interstate 35 provides a fast but unexciting route between these two cities, you'll have a much more interesting time sticking with the meandering backroads, which snake through a handful of quirky little towns. Take Highway 1 southwest from Austin, stopping for a lazy ramble amid the lush 284-acre grounds of the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center. Continue on Highway 1826 to Dripping Springs, a quintessential Hill Country town that's home to more than a few celebs, including Kyle Chandler and Woody Harrelson. Stop for a prodigious plate of slow-smoked brisket at the famous — and mammoth — Salt Lick BBQ restaurant, or if you're favoring a more intimate vibe, follow Highway 12 south to Wimberley. Wimberley In this endearingly offbeat creekside hamlet, you could spend the better part of an afternoon browsing folk art, fashion and housewares. Countless boutiques, cafés and restaurants are clustered in the center of town, some along the banks of tree-shaded Cypress Creek, a lazy tributary of the Blanco River. For lunch, grab a seat on one of the three-shaded patios at Community Pizza and Beer Garden or the Longleaf Craft Kitchen + Bar. Gruene and New Braunfels Budget a half-hour or so for the drive south along curving backcountry roads to the rollicking community of Gruene (pronounced "Green"), which sits along a plateau above the serpentine Guadalupe River. Here you'll find funky shops and down-home eateries with oak-shaded patios, like the Gristmill River Restaurant & Bar, with its lushly landscaped decks above the river. Definitely see what's on at the renowned music venue, Gruene Hall, the oldest dance hall in Texas (it dates back to 1878). It's a short hop farther south — following the course of the Guadalupe River — to New Braunfels, a handsome city of around 125,000 that enthusiastically embraces its German roots. The best time to visit is early November, for the 10-day Wurstfest celebration (think Bavarian dancing, beer and bratwurst). From here, it's just a 35-minute drive down Interstate 35 to San Antonio. Where to stay in Gruene and New Braunfels Set dramatically on a bluff above the Guadalupe River, the adults-only Gruene River Hotel & Retreat (rates start at $305 per night) has 17 rooms, many with hot tubs, and rates include a gourmet breakfast and an evening happy hour. In downtown New Braunfels, the stately 1929 Faust Hotel (rates start at $283 per night) opened in May 2026, following a three-year closure and an ambitious $4.5 million renovation that preserved its stunning tilework, enormous windows, and bold art deco aesthetic. Related reading:

item.title: Leaf-peeping season is almost here: Where to see spectacular fall foliage across the US in 2026
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.20
Leaf-peeping season is almost here: Where to see spectacular fall foliage across the US in 2026 Editor's Note Autumn officially begins on Sept. 22, and that means leaf-peeping season will soon be here. Where and when the foliage will be most dramatic depends on location, altitude and weather. Leaves turn earlier in places with higher elevations and lower temperatures, so some parts of the northern and western U.S. are starting to see some color, while other destinations may not kick off their leaf-peeping seasons until October. If you'd like to plan a leaf-peeping trip this year, we've got you covered. Here are the best destinations you can visit over the coming weeks to see spectacular foliage. Related: Fall foliage cruises in New England, Canada and beyond When and where can we see fall foliage at its peak? Each fall, various forecast tools aim to predict the arrival of autumn foliage across the U.S. using precipitation and temperature statistics, historic trends for peak leaf peeping, local observations, and model outputs from previous years. Our favorites include The Old Farmer's Almanac and the Smoky Mountains Fall Foliage Prediction Map. Plus, camping app Hipcamp launched an interactive map to help you find campgrounds for leaf-peeping trips. Even with these tools, no one can guarantee exactly where and when foliage will peak — especially with unusual weather patterns on the rise. "Of course, past results do not necessarily indicate what will happen this year, but it should give you a fairly good idea of how fall leaves typically progress," an Old Farmer's Almanac representative said. Here, we'll cover the country's top destinations for leaf peeping, and when to visit each for your best chance at seeing spectacular fall colors. Best places in the US to see fall foliage Northeast For travelers on the East Coast, the foliage is just beginning to turn in New England's most popular leaf-peeping states. Prime destinations include the Vermont ski town of Stowe, the Berkshires mountain range in Massachusetts and Acadia National Park in Maine. You can expect mountainous regions to reach maximum color toward the end of September and early October. Lower-elevation areas, like the Hudson Valley in New York and Bar Harbor, Maine, may peak a little later. However, unexpected weather can shift these dates. Last year, a flash drought caused Vermont's leaves to drop early, while unseasonably warm weather in Pennsylvania delayed the leaf-peeping season. To stay updated on your destination, check local reports. Many states and regions offer fall foliage reports with predictions and regular updates throughout the season; Maine and the Poconos have already launched theirs for 2026. You can even sign up for local leaf-peeping newsletters to get updates in your inbox. Related: My first all-inclusive experience at a super-luxe upstate New York resort West The mountains of Colorado — known for their glorious gold and crimson aspen forests — are changing color earlier this year due to the state's prolonged drought. Peak foliage is expected to start in mid-September in the northern part of the state and travel south over the following weeks. The aptly named mountain town of Aspen is a great option, but there are plenty of brilliantly colored areas closer to Denver, such as Guanella Pass near Georgetown and Golden Gate Canyon State Park outside Golden. Utah's unearthly landscapes may be best known for their sandstone cliffs and gravity-defying arches, but they're also great places to enjoy the fall foliage of canyon maple, scrub oak and more come early to mid-October. Plus, the autumnal light illuminates the red rocks spectacularly. On the West Coast, Oregon's wild landscapes explode with color every fall. This year, Portland's foliage is expected to peak in mid- to late October. Take a steamboat ride to admire the changing leaves from the river, or drive the Columbia River Highway, a stretch of interstate designed specifically for its scenic vistas. Related: A points-fueled autumn road trip through Oregon's natural wonders Midwest Due to the Great Lakes' insulating effect, Michigan enjoys a long leaf-peeping season. This year's is already starting, with peak color forecast for early October in northern parts of the state and progressing south through late October. The famous M-119 road, also known as "Tunnel of Trees," recently reopened some sections after devastating floods earlier this year. Parts of Missouri, such as Lake of the Ozarks, are great candidates for a leaf-peeping trip as well. By Nov. 1, the maple, oak, hickory and ash trees along the lake's 1,150 miles of shoreline will be a riot of painterly hues. However, the American smoke tree, which turns an almost electric shade of pink, tends to peak much earlier. For a change of scenery, consider Lexington, Kentucky, where you can experience fall foliage from the water with a paddling tour along the Kentucky River or Elkhorn Creek. The leaves are expected to peak in the middle of November. Related: 5 stunning fall foliage road trips in the Midwest Mid-Atlantic and Southeast For endless views this fall, plan a road trip along the Blue Ridge Parkway or the North Carolina coast. The state boasts a long leaf-peeping season thanks to a wide range of elevations. You can see spectacular color in the Great Smoky Mountains on the state's western side starting in early October, and that peak will shift east over the coming weeks, hitting the coast in early November. Virginia's plentiful deciduous trees and varied landscape provide a long fall foliage season as well. The season should start in earnest toward the end of September, at which point the Virginia Department of Forestry will start updating its fall foliage report weekly. For thinner crowds, consider Columbia, South Carolina. This hidden gem will be packed with color in late October and early November, whether you stay in town to explore Riverbanks Zoo and Three Rivers Greenway or head to nearby Congaree National Park — home to some of the country's oldest and tallest deciduous trees. Related: The best national parks for a weekend getaway South The farther south you go, the later leaf-peeping season starts, giving you a few extra weeks to plan a trip. Plus, you may not have to contend with as many crowds in these colorful Southern destinations. For example, Louisiana has plenty of top spots for leaf peeping from late October through mid-November, including Chemin-A-Haut State Park, Lake Claiborne State Park and Jimmie Davis State Park. Experience the vibrant red leaves of the bigtooth maple trees in Lost Maples State Natural Area outside San Antonio. The leaves likely won't start to change until late October; check back here for updates. Or try Garner State Park in southern Texas, where you can explore 11 miles of hiking trails and take in the varied hues of cypress, oak, mesquite and persimmon trees. The town of Eureka Springs, Arkansas, is surrounded by enough blazing mountainsides to rival northern leaf-peeping spots — and it offers preserved Victorian buildings and therapeutic natural hot springs. Mid-October through early November is the best time to go. Related: Air Canada will return to San Antonio in 3-route expansion Bottom line If you're dreaming of a leaf-peeping trip, now is the time to book it. Even better, it doesn't have to eat up your travel budget or vacation days — with so many stellar destinations in the U.S., you can experience the magic of the season while staying close to home. Though tools like the ones we mentioned can't make any guarantees, they are useful guides for determining where and when to travel for optimal fall colors. This is especially true for the maps, which update based on real-world user data gathered as the season unfolds. But remember, any weather changes over the coming weeks could adjust the predicted peak timing for any of these places, so try to be as flexible as possible with your plans. We recommend booking changeable flights and hotel stays whenever possible.
